practice_questions.text: Give one thing you should note about a performer's vocal delivery when watching a live production.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for any one of: pitch / pace / pause / volume / accent / intonation / phrasing / emotional range / projection / timing. Accept any precise vocal skill.

practice_questions.text: What is meant by the term 'directorial concept'?
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying that it refers to the director's vision or intention; 1 mark for explaining that it shapes all performance and design decisions so the production communicates a unified meaning.

practice_questions.text: Explain how keeping a production log within 24 hours of seeing a performance helps a student write a stronger live theatre review.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks: 1 mark for identifying that specific detail fades quickly from memory; 1 mark for explaining that a log captures precise technical details (lantern type, colour, moment); 1 mark for explaining that these details support analytical writing rather than general impressions; 1 mark for linking this to the What / How / Why scaffold or to the exam's requirement for technical specificity.

practice_questions.text: Analyse how the stage configuration of a production affects the way an audience experiences a performer's use of proxemics.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks: 1 mark for identifying a named stage configuration (e.g. theatre in the round, proscenium arch, thrust stage); 1 mark for defining or explaining proxemics in the context of performer-audience relationship; 1 mark for analytical development of how the configuration changes how the audience reads spatial distance (e.g. in the round, every seat sees a different set of relationships; on a proscenium, the front-of-house sightline privileges downstage centre positions); 1 mark for a concrete example or evaluative statement about effect on audience.

practice_questions.text: Imagine you saw a production of a ghost story at a fictional touring theatre in 2024. In a key scene, the lead performer plays a character confronting the ghost for the first time. As a performer, explain the vocal and physical choices you would make to communicate the character's fear and disbelief at that moment. Refer to specific vocal and physical skills.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (7-8): Response names at least one precise vocal choice (e.g. a sudden drop to near-whisper, broken phrasing with involuntary pauses, a rising pitch before the voice cracks) AND at least one precise physical choice (e.g. the body recoiling to upstage left, hands raised palms-outward, a sustained freeze of three beats before slow retreat), both anchored to this specific confrontation moment; effect on the audience is named and substantiated (e.g. the sudden stillness makes the audience hold its breath in empathy); language is technically fluent.
Secure (5-6): Names a vocal and a physical choice, generally anchored to the moment; explains at least one effect on the audience; mostly specific but may have one generic descriptor (e.g. 'her voice was quiet' without further detail).
Developing (3-4): Relevant choices mentioned but described in general terms ('she looked scared', 'her voice was soft'); little or no named effect on audience; limited technical vocabulary.
Emerging (1-2): Basic listing of general feelings or actions with no technical vocabulary and no reference to specific moment or audience effect.

practice_questions.text: Analyse and evaluate the live theatre production you have seen. In your answer, explain how specific performer choices and at least one design choice communicated meaning to the audience. Reach a substantiated evaluative judgement about how successfully meaning was communicated overall.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (25-32): Sustained analytical writing anchored to named moments; every performer choice is specific (named vocal quality, named physical action, named moment); every design choice is concrete (lantern type, gobo, sound texture, costume fabric or colour); each choice is linked to a clearly stated effect on the audience; a confident, substantiated evaluative judgement is made about why the production succeeded or did not in communicating its central meaning; technical vocabulary used accurately throughout.
Secure (17-24): Most choices are specific; at least two performer choices and one design choice are named and explained with effect; an evaluative judgement is present though it may lack full substantiation; technical vocabulary mostly accurate.
Developing (9-16): Relevant choices identified but often general ('the lighting was dark', 'the actor seemed sad'); some attempt at explaining effect on audience; little or no evaluative judgement; limited technical vocabulary.
Emerging (1-8): Largely descriptive or plot-based; choices listed rather than analysed; no evaluative judgement or audience effect; minimal technical vocabulary.

practice_questions.text: Identify the setting in which almost all the action of A Taste of Honey takes place.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for: a rented flat / a bedsit / a damp flat in Salford. Accept any specific reference to the flat/bedsit in Salford.

practice_questions.text: What is meant by the term 'kitchen-sink drama'?
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying it as a British theatre movement from the late 1950s; 1 mark for explaining that it placed working-class characters and domestic settings at the centre of drama, replacing upper-middle-class drawing-room subjects.

practice_questions.text: Analyse how Delaney uses the single-setting flat to communicate Jo's situation to the audience.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks: identification of the single-setting device (1), explanation of how it creates a sense of entrapment or poverty (1), reference to a specific staging or design element that reinforces this (1), link to the audience's understanding of Jo's circumstances or the play's themes (1).

practice_questions.text: Explain how the live jazz musicians on stage contribute to the audience's experience of the play's structure.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks: identification of the jazz musicians as a Theatre Workshop / Brechtian device (1), explanation of their structural role in marking scene transitions or commenting on action (1), explanation of how they prevent the audience from fully immersing in naturalism (1), link to their effect on the audience's relationship with the story or characters (1).

practice_questions.text: Analyse how Delaney uses the two-act structure of A Taste of Honey to communicate her intentions about Jo's situation and the cycle of poverty and neglect. Refer to specific moments in the play's structure.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Perceptive analysis of how the circular two-act structure (both acts ending with Jo abandoned) communicates a deliberate argument about cycles of poverty and neglect; identifies the symmetry between Act One's end and Act Two's end; discusses at least one specific structural moment (e.g. the opening and closing mirroring each other) and explains the intended effect on the audience with precision; may reference the Brechtian influence of Theatre Workshop.

Secure: Clear analysis of the two-act structure with reference to at least two moments; understands that Delaney intends an argument not just a story; generally accurate effect on audience identified.

Developing: Relevant points but mainly descriptive; identifies the circular structure but does not fully explain the intention; effect on audience vague.

Emerging: Basic description of what happens in each act; little or no analysis of Delaney's intentions.

practice_questions.text: As a director staging A Taste of Honey, explain how you would use set design, lighting and the positioning of the jazz musicians to communicate to the audience the contrast between the naturalistic domestic world of the flat and the presentational, Brechtian quality of the live music. Refer to specific moments in the play.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Detailed, concrete staging across set design, lighting and musician positioning; each choice is anchored to a named moment (e.g. the opening arrival, the canal scene, Geof's exit) with a specific effect on the audience stated; discusses the hybrid naturalistic-Brechtian form intelligently; set design choices are specific (materials, levels, props as symbols); lighting choices include lantern types, colour, state changes; musician placement considers sightlines and the Brechtian function; shows clear directorial intention throughout.

Secure: Most design areas covered; at least one named moment per design discipline; generally concrete choices; effect on audience identified in most cases; some sense of the hybrid form.

Developing: Some staging ideas but generic ('dark lighting for sad scenes'); few named moments; limited engagement with the Brechtian-naturalistic tension.

Emerging: Basic listing of staging ideas with little justification; no named moments; descriptive rather than analytical.

practice_questions.text: Name the theatre company that first produced Dominic Cooke's stage adaptation of Noughts and Crosses in 2007.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for: the Royal Shakespeare Company (RSC). Accept 'RSC' as a correct abbreviation.

practice_questions.text: Define the term 'episodic structure' as it applies to Cooke's adaptation of Noughts and Crosses.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying that episodic structure is built from short, self-contained scenes; 1 mark for explaining that this allows large spans of time to be compressed into stage time, or that scenes are linked by transitions (lighting, sound) rather than continuous action.

practice_questions.text: Analyse how the dual-narrator device shapes the audience's relationship to the story in Noughts and Crosses.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks: identification of what the device is (1); explanation of how it positions the audience as witnesses or creates direct address (1); reference to the Brechtian dimension or dramatic irony generated (1); link to a specific moment or staging implication (e.g. the narrator steps into a lighting special at downstage centre) (1).

practice_questions.text: Explain how a lighting designer might track the lighting state across the structural arc of Noughts and Crosses to communicate the play's movement from childhood innocence to political tragedy. Refer to at least one specific scene or moment.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks: identification of a lighting choice for the opening beach scene (e.g. warm wash, open angles) (1); identification of a contrasting lighting choice for the later political scenes (e.g. cold blue, directional side light, harsh shadows) (1); explanation of the effect on the audience (1); link to a named moment of the play and its dramatic meaning (1).

practice_questions.text: Analyse how Cooke's two-act structure with epilogue shapes what the playwright wants the audience to understand about the relationship between personal love and political violence in Noughts and Crosses.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Argues that the two-act structure enacts the lovers' trajectory from possibility to inevitability; analyses how Act One's episodic compression creates an accelerating sense of threat while Act Two strips away options; connects the epilogue's final monologue and tableau to the playwright's intention that the audience sit with tragedy rather than closure; references at least two named moments (e.g. the opening beach scene and the execution); links structural choices to design implications (lighting, soundscape, staging configuration) with named, concrete elements.

Secure: Identifies the two-act shape and connects it to the tragic arc; explains how the epilogue resists easy resolution; references at least one named moment; makes at least one link to a staging or design choice.

Developing: Describes the structure (two acts, epilogue) without fully analysing what it communicates; may describe what happens rather than what the audience is made to feel or understand; staging references are generic.

Emerging: Identifies that the play has a two-act structure with little analysis of its effect; no reference to staging or design.

practice_questions.text: As a director staging the opening beach scene and the final epilogue of Noughts and Crosses, discuss how you would use staging configuration, lighting design, sound design, and performer positioning to communicate the contrast between the world at the play's opening and the world at its close. Refer to specific choices across at least two design disciplines and explain the effect on the audience.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Presents a coherent directorial vision spanning both moments; specifies a staging configuration (e.g. thrust stage) and explains how it serves the dual-narrator direct address; names concrete lighting choices for the beach opening (e.g. a wide warm straw wash from overhead Fresnels, haze to suggest open air) and contrasts with the epilogue's isolated lighting special (e.g. single profile lantern, cold blue gel, tight focus on Sephy downstage centre); names specific sound choices (e.g. open ambient soundscape of waves and birdsong for the opening, giving way to silence or a sustained low underscore for the epilogue); explains how performer positioning (proxemics, levels) reinforces the isolation of the final moment; all choices are anchored to named dramatic moments and justified with reference to audience effect and the play's themes.

Secure: Addresses both moments with mostly concrete design choices; includes at least one named lighting element and one sound element; explains the effect on the audience; staging configuration is mentioned if not fully justified.

Developing: Addresses one moment more fully than the other; design choices are sometimes generic ('dark lighting for the sad ending'); effect on audience is implied rather than stated.

Emerging: Lists some design ideas without relating them to the specific moments or explaining effects; response is largely descriptive.

practice_questions.text: Name the theatre role responsible for calling all technical cues during a live performance.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for: stage manager.

practice_questions.text: What is an understudy?
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying that an understudy is a performer; 1 mark for explaining that they learn another actor's role in order to cover the part at short notice if the scheduled performer cannot appear.

practice_questions.text: Explain the contribution a costume designer makes to a production, and how their choices affect the audience's understanding of character.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks: 1 mark for naming the costume designer's role; 1 mark for a specific design element (e.g. colour, fabric, silhouette, fit, accessories, hair, make-up); 1 mark for explaining how that element communicates character to the audience; 1 mark for a concrete example or development (e.g. linking period detail, social class, or character psychology to a specific choice).

practice_questions.text: Explain what a playwright does and how their work differs from the director's in a professional production.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks: 1 mark for accurately describing the playwright's role (writes the script, dialogue, stage directions); 1 mark for noting the playwright typically hands over creative authority after delivering the script; 1 mark for describing the director's role (interprets the text, guides creative vision, runs rehearsals); 1 mark for explaining the distinction (the director makes staging choices the playwright does not control — e.g. two directors can produce very different versions of the same script).

practice_questions.text: Analyse how a director and set designer might collaborate to communicate a production's overall concept to the audience. In your answer, refer to at least one specific set design element and its intended effect on the audience.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: sustained analysis of how director's intention is translated into a specific set design choice (e.g. a bare stage with a single chair to communicate isolation; a revolve to show the passage of time); the effect on the audience is precisely named (e.g. 'the audience is positioned as witness to the character's entrapment'); at least one concrete design element is analysed for its symbolic or atmospheric meaning; both roles are clearly distinguished throughout.

Secure: clear explanation of how director and designer collaborate; at least one design element described with its effect; some distinction between the roles' responsibilities.

Developing: relevant points about design or direction but limited analysis; effect on audience implied rather than stated; roles may be conflated.

Emerging: basic description of what a set looks like with little or no analysis of intention or audience effect.

practice_questions.text: As a director, explain how you would use the stage space and the contributions of two design roles to communicate a clear concept to the audience in the opening moments of a production. Refer to specific staging and design choices.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: a clearly stated directorial concept; specific, concrete choices from at least two design disciplines (e.g. lighting state — lantern type, colour, intensity; set — material, scale, level; costume — silhouette, colour, period); each choice is anchored to the opening moment and linked to a precise intended effect on the audience; performer positioning is described with staging vocabulary (upstage, downstage, proxemics, focus); the two design contributions are distinct and their interaction is analysed.

Secure: directorial concept is present; at least two design disciplines referenced with mostly concrete choices; audience effect generally described; staging vocabulary used, though not always precisely.

Developing: general staging ideas with limited specificity; design choices tend toward generic descriptors ('dark lighting', 'period costume'); audience effect implied; staging vocabulary limited.

Emerging: broad description of a scene with little staging specificity; design choices listed without justification; no clear directorial concept; staging vocabulary largely absent.

practice_questions.text: Name the playwright of Things I Know to Be True.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for: Andrew Bovell.

practice_questions.text: What is meant by the term 'dramatic structure'?
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for a basic correct answer (e.g. the way a play is organised or divided into sections); 1 mark for development linking structure to the creation of meaning or effect on the audience (e.g. the sequencing of scenes and revelations to build tension or surprise).

practice_questions.text: Analyse how Bovell uses the seasonal frame to give structural shape to the play's four revelations.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks: identification of the seasonal structure and its mapping to four children (1); explanation of how one or more seasons carries a specific emotional charge that contrasts with or amplifies its revelation (1); reference to accumulation of revelations and audience effect (1); reference to a specific structural device such as direct address or the shock ending (1).

practice_questions.text: Explain the effect of placing Bob's rose garden at the centre of the play's staging. How might a set designer communicate the garden's symbolic function?
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying the garden as a symbol of Bob's emotional life or sense of order; 1 mark for a specific design choice (e.g. a single rose bush as a focal point, or soil under Bob's feet contrasting with the kitchen's hard floor); 1 mark for explaining the effect of that choice on audience understanding of Bob's character; 1 mark for linking the garden's staging to a named moment or transition in the play.

practice_questions.text: Analyse how Bovell uses dramatic structure to control the audience's understanding of Bob Price across the four seasons. Consider what is revealed, what is withheld, and what effect the late revelation has on the audience's experience of the earlier scenes.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Detailed analysis of Bovell's structural intentions, including the seasonal frame as a deliberate device, the function of Rosie's direct-address monologues in creating dramatic irony, the withholding of information about Bob, and the retrospective re-ordering the shock ending creates. The student explains the intended effect on the audience at specific structural moments with concrete reference to dramatic methods. No plot summary.

Secure: Identifies seasonal structure and the shock ending, explains that Bovell withholds information about Bob, and makes some reference to audience effect. One or two structural devices mentioned (e.g. direct address, seasonal arc). Mostly analytical rather than descriptive.

Developing: Describes what happens in the four seasons without sustained analysis of why Bovell structures the play this way. Some attempt to address audience effect but largely plot-driven.

Emerging: Retells the plot across the seasons with little or no analysis of playwright's intentions or structural choices.

practice_questions.text: As a director staging the moment when the final revelation about Bob is made in winter, explain how you would use lighting, set, proxemics and at least one performer choice to communicate the shock to the audience. Refer to specific choices and their intended effects.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Full range of staging disciplines addressed. Lighting: specific state change named (e.g. a sudden shift from an amber wash to cold white or near-blackout, using a profile lantern to isolate Bob); set: a specific design choice for the garden in winter (e.g. bare rose stems, frost effect on the ground cloth); proxemics: specific positioning of characters at the moment of revelation, with justification; performer: specific vocal (e.g. a drop in volume, a pause before a line) and physical choice (e.g. stillness contrasting with movement elsewhere). Every choice anchored to the named moment with an explanation of the effect on the audience.

Secure: Most disciplines covered; at least one named lighting choice and one named performer choice; generally concrete but perhaps one area described generically (e.g. 'dark lighting' without naming lantern type or state change); audience effect mostly addressed.

Developing: Relevant staging ideas but generic language ('sad lighting', 'slow movement'); disciplines covered superficially; limited or no reference to the named moment; effect on audience implied rather than explained.

Emerging: List of ideas without justification or reference to specific staging choices; mostly descriptive; no reference to the named moment.

practice_questions.text: Name the narrative device Shakespeare uses before Act One to tell the audience the lovers will die.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for: the prologue / the chorus / a choric prologue (any of these accepted).

practice_questions.text: What is meant by the term 'proxemics' in performance?
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for a basic definition (the distance between performers / physical relationships on stage); 1 mark for specifying what proxemics communicates (status, intimacy, conflict, relationship).

practice_questions.text: Explain how a director might use blocking and proxemics in the shared sonnet at the Capulet feast to communicate the rapid development of Romeo and Juliet's attraction to an audience.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks: identification of the staging device (1), explanation of a specific blocking choice e.g. the distance closing line by line (1), reference to the named moment (1), link to the effect on the audience or to character meaning (1).

practice_questions.text: Explain how the lighting and sound design might change at the moment Romeo kills Tybalt in Act Three, Scene One to communicate the structural turning point of the play to the audience.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks: naming a specific lighting change with a justification (1), naming a specific sound change with a justification (1), linking the design shift to the play's structural turn from comedy to tragedy (1), describing the intended effect on the audience (1).

practice_questions.text: Analyse how Shakespeare uses the compressed five-day timeline to communicate his intentions about fate and the power of the feud. Refer to at least two moments in the play.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: the student analyses how the compressed timeline amplifies the sense of fate and inevitability; they name at least two specific moments (e.g. the wedding within 24 hours of meeting; the failure of the letter in Act Five) and explain what Shakespeare wants the audience to feel at each; analysis extends to how a director might physicalise the sense of relentless pace through staging; judgement is sustained and considers the audience's dual awareness (knowing the ending from the prologue).

Secure: the student identifies the compressed timeline as thematically significant, names two moments, and explains the effect on the audience's sense of fate; staging reference may be present but not fully developed.

Developing: the student describes the timeline without fully analysing Shakespeare's intentions; moments are mentioned but not closely examined; little or no reference to staging or audience effect.

Emerging: the student retells events in order without analysis; no clear sense of Shakespeare's intentions or the audience's experience.

practice_questions.text: You are directing the tomb scene in Act Five. Discuss how you would use set design, lighting, sound and performer choices to communicate the tragedy of the double death to the audience. Refer to specific staging decisions throughout.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: the student designs the tomb scene with specific, justified choices across all four disciplines plus performer choices; set design specifies materials, levels and configuration (e.g. a raised stone platform downstage centre, cold grey stone tiles, the bodies visible and framed by the architecture); lighting names lantern types, angles, colours and states (e.g. a single low-angle profile casting long shadows across the stone, shifting from deep red as Paris dies to cold blue-white as Juliet wakes); sound design distinguishes diegetic and non-diegetic elements (e.g. silence broken only by Romeo's footsteps, then a low string underscore as he discovers Juliet); performer choices specify vocal and physical qualities for at least one named character at a named moment; every choice is justified with reference to effect on audience and thematic meaning; a directorial throughline is evident.

Secure: the student covers most of the four disciplines and offers performer choices; choices are generally concrete with at least one named element per discipline; justification is present but may not be fully developed for all choices.

Developing: the student covers two or three disciplines but choices are generic (dark lighting, sad music, slow movements); performer choices described in emotional terms without specific vocal or physical translation; limited reference to audience effect.

Emerging: the student lists design ideas without explanation; little or no reference to specific staging choices or their meaning; narrative description of what happens rather than how it would be staged.

practice_questions.text: Identify the staging configuration used for the 2013 New Vic production of Around the World in 80 Days.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for: theatre-in-the-round (accept: in-the-round / round staging).

practice_questions.text: What is meant by the term 'episodic structure' in drama?
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying that the play is built from a series of short or self-contained scenes; 1 mark for explaining that these scenes are linked by a through-line (e.g. the countdown or the chase) rather than forming one continuous unfolding action.

practice_questions.text: Analyse how Eason's use of multi-roling contributes to the theatrical energy of Around the World in 80 Days.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks: identification of what multi-roling is in this play (1); explanation of how it creates theatrical pleasure for the audience (e.g. rapid transformation, visible skill) (1); reference to a named moment or role type where multi-roling is used (e.g. ensemble as steam engine, elephant, or crowd) (1); comment on how it suits the episodic structure or the physical-theatre form (1).

practice_questions.text: Explain how a director might use lighting to signal the shift between a narrator moment and a full dramatic scene in Around the World in 80 Days. Refer to at least two specific lighting choices.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks: one clear lighting choice for the narrator moment (e.g. single profile lantern, tight top-light, cool white special) (1); explanation of how it isolates the narrator and signals a step outside the fiction to the audience (1); one contrasting lighting choice for dramatic scenes (e.g. warm general wash, multiple lanterns from different angles) (1); explanation of how this contrast in lighting state helps the audience follow the storytelling structure (1).

practice_questions.text: Analyse how Eason uses episodic structure and direct address narration to communicate the theme of time and the urgency of Fogg's wager to the audience.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: The response analyses episodic structure as a deliberate choice to keep the countdown audible throughout the play, explaining that Eason intends each new episode to reset and increase the tension rather than resolve it. Direct address narration is analysed as a device that makes the audience co-witnesses of the clock ticking, positioning them as stakeholders in the wager. Concrete staging references are made (e.g. narrator stepping into a pool of light to update the audience on days remaining; blackout between episodes signalling time lost). The response considers how both methods together create a cumulative audience experience of urgency. A substantiated judgement is made about how effectively this communicates Verne's original theme.
Secure: Most of the above is present; at least one staging reference is concrete; the link between structure and audience experience is generally accurate.
Developing: Relevant points about the structure are made but staging implications are generic or absent; the connection to the theme of time is implied rather than analysed.
Emerging: The response describes what happens in the play or lists features of episodic structure without explaining their effect on the audience.

practice_questions.text: You are directing Around the World in 80 Days. Discuss how you would use the staging space, the ensemble's physical skills, and lighting and sound design to bring the Reform Club opening scene and the first departure from London to life. Refer to specific staging choices across at least three theatrical elements.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: The response makes specific choices across multiple theatrical elements with clear justification for each. Staging configuration is discussed (e.g. in-the-round: Reform Club chairs arranged centre stage, Fogg placed upstage centre to dominate sightlines from all sides). Ensemble physical work is described precisely (e.g. the Reform Club gentlemen creating a formal tableau, rigid posture and synchronised movement to signal Victorian social constraint; the physical shift to the first locomotive created by performers forming a line downstage, arms pumping, a percussive soundscape built from breath and stamp). Lighting choices are named (e.g. warm amber wash for the Reform Club interior; a sharp blackout and then a cooler blue-white chase of side-lights to suggest movement as Fogg departs). Sound design is referenced (e.g. ticking clock underscoring Fogg's opening speech; a steam whistle cue as the journey begins). Every choice is linked to the play's themes (precision, momentum, the ticking clock). A directorial intention is stated and sustained throughout.
Secure: Most elements are covered; choices are mostly concrete; directorial intention is generally clear; at least two theatrical disciplines addressed in detail.
Developing: Some staging ideas are present but choices are described generically (e.g. 'the lighting would be dramatic'); fewer than two disciplines addressed with specific detail.
Emerging: The response lists ideas without explaining how they would work on stage or what effect they would create for the audience.

practice_questions.text: Identify one structural device Willy Russell uses to frame Blood Brothers.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for any one of: circular structure / framing device / Narrator / prologue / tableau / the play opens and closes on the same scene.

practice_questions.text: What is meant by the term 'circular structure' in drama?
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for a basic definition (e.g. the ending returns to or mirrors the beginning); 1 mark for development or a linked dramatic effect (e.g. it creates a sense of inevitability or dramatic irony, because the audience knows the outcome from the start).

practice_questions.text: Explain how the use of the Narrator in the prologue of Blood Brothers might affect an audience's experience of the rest of the play.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks: identification of the Narrator's role (1); explanation of how direct address or fourth wall breaking creates distance (1); analysis of how knowing the ending affects the audience's emotional engagement throughout (1); reference to a specific structural moment or design choice that reinforces this effect (1).

practice_questions.text: Explain how a lighting or set designer might communicate the circular structure of Blood Brothers to the audience. Focus on the prologue tableau and the closing tableau, and name at least two specific design choices.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks: naming a specific lighting state for the prologue (e.g. deep red wash, tight overhead special) with a linked effect on the audience (1); naming a matching or contrasting lighting choice for the close (1); naming a set or costume element used in both tableaux that creates visual symmetry (1); explaining what this repetition communicates to the audience about fate or inevitability (1).

practice_questions.text: Analyse Russell's intentions in choosing to reveal the deaths of Mickey and Edward at the very start of Blood Brothers rather than saving the ending as a surprise. What does this structural choice communicate to the audience about the play's central concerns?
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sustained analysis of Russell's intentions across the full structural arc. Identifies that the circular structure is not a spoiler but a political statement — the audience is asked to watch a class system at work, not simply to be surprised by a twist. Explains how dramatic irony operates throughout (childhood innocence shadowed by knowledge of the ending). Discusses how the Narrator's role reinforces this intentional transparency. References at least one concrete staging moment and links it to what Russell wants the audience to think and feel. Reaches a substantiated judgement about Russell's social and theatrical purpose.

Secure: Clear identification of Russell's intentions with good explanation of dramatic irony and the social critique embedded in the circular structure. At least one reference to a named moment. Effect on the audience generally accurate.

Developing: Relevant but largely plot-based. Identifies the circular structure but focuses on what happens rather than why Russell chose this shape. Little analysis of audience effect or social intent.

Emerging: Basic description of the story opening with the deaths. Little or no analysis of intention or structural effect.

practice_questions.text: As a director, discuss how you would stage the prologue tableau and the closing tableau of Blood Brothers to communicate the play's circular structure to the audience. In your answer, refer to performer positioning, lighting design and at least one further design discipline.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Comprehensive response that treats the prologue and final tableau as a matched pair. Specifies performer positioning for both (e.g. the two bodies downstage centre, Mrs Johnstone upstage, Narrator at a fixed point throughout); names a specific lighting state for both that creates visual symmetry (e.g. deep red gel wash, profiles at a steep downward angle); discusses a further design element (sound: a slow underscore that bookends the play; costume: desaturated adult tones contrasting with brighter childhood palette); explains the intended effect on the audience for each choice; reaches a directorial judgement about how the staging serves Russell's social purpose.

Secure: Covers performer positioning and at least two design disciplines with generally concrete choices. Effect on the audience addressed. Structural link between prologue and close is made.

Developing: Some staging ideas but generic (dark lighting, sad music). Little named detail. The structural argument is present but underdeveloped.

Emerging: Basic listing of staging ideas with no named detail, no link between prologue and close, and little explanation of audience effect.

practice_questions.text: Name the playwright of The Great Wave.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for: Francis Turnly.

practice_questions.text: What is meant by the term 'cross-cutting' in the context of dramatic structure?
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying cross-cutting as alternating between two or more storylines; 1 mark for explaining that this creates juxtaposition or dramatic irony between the separate storylines.

practice_questions.text: Analyse how the opening beach-storm scene functions structurally in The Great Wave. Refer to one staging or design technique a director might use.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks: identification of the scene's structural function (1); explanation of what it establishes for the audience (1); reference to a specific staging or design choice, e.g. soundscape, lighting state, blocking (1); explanation of the effect that choice creates for the audience (1).

practice_questions.text: Explain how a sound designer might use the sea soundscape across the two parallel storylines to communicate the separation of the Tanaka family. Refer to specific sound design choices and their effect on the audience.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks: identification of the sea as a recurring sound motif (1); a specific sound design choice, e.g. varying the wave volume at key transitions, using directional surround-sound speakers (1); explanation of how this creates the effect of geographic or emotional separation (1); reference to a named moment of the play where this choice would be most effective, e.g. the opening beach scene or a cross-cut transition (1).

practice_questions.text: Analyse how Turnly uses the dual-timeline structure of The Great Wave to communicate the theme of state power over individual lives. Consider how a director might make this structural argument visible to the audience through staging.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Identifies Turnly's intention to place the audience in the position of a witness who knows more than the characters do; analyses the cross-cutting as the formal equivalent of the political argument (state power creates enforced parallel lives); discusses specific directorial choices — lighting state contrasts between Japan and North Korea, costume differentiation, blocking that physically separates the two worlds — and anchors each choice to a named moment with a named effect on the audience. Reaches a substantiated judgement about what the structural choice asks the audience to feel. Secure: Discusses dual timelines and offers some design or performer choices; may be less precise about specific moments or the audience's experience. Developing: Describes the two storylines but treats structure as a plot summary rather than a dramaturgical choice; design references are generic. Emerging: Brief identification of the dual timeline with little analysis of intention or effect.

practice_questions.text: As a director, discuss how you would stage the transition scenes between the Japan and North Korea storylines in The Great Wave. Consider lighting, sound and the physical positioning of the performers to make each cross-cut transition meaningful for the audience. You should refer to at least two named moments of transition in the play.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Full discussion of at least two named transition moments; lighting choices are concrete (lantern type, colour temperature, intensity — e.g. a cold 6200K profile wash fading to black for North Korea vs a warm 3200K Fresnel for the Japanese domestic scenes); sound design choices are specific (wave soundscape swelling, then cutting to silence, then propaganda music underscore); blocking is described precisely (performers freezing downstage left in one storyline while new scene opens upstage right); costume differentiation is described; the cumulative effect on the audience of these repeated transitions is analysed. Substantiated directorial judgement about which design choice carries the most structural weight. Secure: Two design disciplines discussed, most choices concrete, at least one named moment, generally accurate audience effect. Developing: Aware of the transitions but describes design in general terms (dark for North Korea, bright for Japan); no specific lantern type, gobo or soundscape texture; limited reference to named moments. Emerging: Lists design elements with little explanation of how they work in performance.

practice_questions.text: Name the historical event that took place in 1887 and provides the opening context of The Empress.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for: Queen Victoria's Golden Jubilee (accept: the Jubilee celebrations / the 50th anniversary of Victoria's reign).

practice_questions.text: What is meant by the term 'parallel storylines' in a play?
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying that two or more separate narrative threads run alongside each other; 1 mark for explaining that these threads are intercut or juxtaposed so that each illuminates the other (accept equivalent explanation).

practice_questions.text: Explain how a lighting designer could use contrasting lighting states when the play moves between the Windsor Castle scenes and the East End scenes in The Empress. Refer to specific lighting choices.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks: identification of a specific Windsor lighting choice (1) such as a warm amber or gold wash to signal wealth and formality; identification of a contrasting East End lighting choice (1) such as a cooler white or pale blue wash to suggest poverty and natural London light; explanation of the effect on the audience of the contrast (1) e.g. the shift encodes social hierarchy visually so the audience is reminded of inequality with every transition; link to the play's structural meaning (1) e.g. the lighting state contrast reinforces Gupta's dramaturgical juxtaposition of the two worlds of the British Empire.

practice_questions.text: Analyse how the structure of The Empress — specifically the intercut parallel storylines — creates dramatic tension for the audience.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks: identification of the intercut structure (1); explanation of the technique's effect, e.g. that cutting between Rani's vulnerability and the court's opulence creates irony (1); analysis of how the structure builds towards the convergence near the play's end (1); reference to a specific named moment in one of the two storylines (1).

practice_questions.text: Analyse Gupta's intentions in choosing to open The Empress with the scene at Tilbury Docks in which Rani is paid off and abandoned. What does Gupta want the audience to think and feel at this moment?
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (10–12): Detailed analysis of Gupta's multiple intentions — to establish Rani's vulnerability as the audience's entry point into the play; to make the systemic nature of the ayahs' exploitation concrete and immediate rather than abstract; to root the play's political argument in a personal, emotionally engaging story. Candidate links these intentions to specific dramatic methods (the choice of a public dockside setting, the power imbalance in staging terms, the contrast between Rani's isolation and the bustle of the docks) and explains the intended audience effect at each. Substantiated judgement about which intention is primary.

Secure (7–9): Two of the above intentions clearly articulated with some reference to dramatic methods; the effect on the audience is identified though not always fully developed.

Developing (4–6): One intention identified; limited reference to dramatic method; effect on audience implied rather than explained.

Emerging (1–3): Describes what happens at the docks rather than analysing why Gupta chose to begin there and what she wants the audience to understand.

practice_questions.text: You are directing the moment in The Empress when the two storylines converge near the play's end and characters from Rani's world and Abdul's world briefly share the stage. How would you stage this moment to communicate the play's themes of solidarity and survival to the audience? Refer to set design, lighting, sound and at least one performer's vocal or physical choices.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (17–20): Specific, justified choices across all four design disciplines and at least one named performer's vocal and physical choices, all anchored to this named convergence moment. Set design choice (e.g. the divide between the Windsor staging area and the East End area dissolving as characters cross the stage threshold), lighting choice (e.g. a slow cross-fade from two separate lighting states into a unified warm gold wash as the characters meet), sound choice (e.g. a Hindi underscore that swells as they converge, then holds under the final dialogue), costume contrast still legible onstage (Rani's worn sari fabric against Abdul's court livery). Performer choice: specific vocal quality and physical positioning (proxemics) for Rani in this moment. Choices are justified with reference to what the audience is meant to feel. Substantiated directorial judgement.

Secure (11–16): Most of the design areas covered with some concrete choices; at least one named performer choice; effect on audience identified for most choices.

Developing (6–10): Some relevant staging ideas but generic (e.g. 'warm lighting', 'Indian music'); little justification of how each choice creates meaning; performer choices vague.

Emerging (1–5): Basic listing of staging ideas with minimal explanation; no named performer choices; descriptive rather than analytical.

practice_questions.text: Name the theatre that Stanislavski co-founded in 1898.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for: the Moscow Art Theatre.

practice_questions.text: What is meant by the term 'magic if' in Stanislavski's system?
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying that it is an imaginative technique; 1 mark for explaining that the actor asks what they would do if they were genuinely in the character's circumstances, to generate truthful behaviour on stage.

practice_questions.text: Explain how a performer might use Stanislavski's concept of 'given circumstances' to prepare for a scene in which their character receives devastating news.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks: 1 mark for defining given circumstances (all the facts about the character's world provided by the text); 1 mark for identifying a relevant circumstance (e.g. location, relationship, preceding events); 1 mark for explaining how awareness of that circumstance shapes a specific physical or vocal choice; 1 mark for linking the choice to the effect on the audience's reading of the scene.

practice_questions.text: As a performer playing a character who slowly realises they have been deceived by someone they love, explain how you would use vocal and physical skills to communicate that dawning realisation to the audience. Refer to a specific moment in the scene.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (7-8): The response identifies a specific moment and makes precise, named vocal choices (e.g. pace slows to a deliberate pause; pitch drops; a single word spoken at reduced volume) alongside equally precise physical choices (e.g. body goes still at centre stage; hands lower slowly to the sides; eye contact with the other performer held then broken as the realisation lands). Effect on the audience is named (e.g. the stillness creates unease; the audience shares the character's sense of the world collapsing). Both Stanislavskian technique (magic if, given circumstances) and stagecraft are referenced.

Secure (5-6): Vocal AND physical choices are both present and reasonably specific. A named moment is used. Effect on audience is mentioned but may be brief.

Developing (3-4): Choices are present but generic ('I would speak quietly and look sad'). The moment may be vague. Effect is implied but not explained.

Emerging (1-2): Basic list of emotions or feelings with little translation into vocal or physical action. No named moment.

practice_questions.text: Analyse how a director applying Stanislavski's principles might use naturalistic staging to communicate the social and emotional tension between two characters meeting for the first time in an unfamiliar setting. What might the director intend the audience to understand about these characters' relationship?
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (10-12): The response analyses specific directorial choices rooted in Stanislavski's principles — representational set (period furniture, authentic props), naturalistic lighting (low-intensity Fresnel wash suggesting a window light), blocking that uses proxemics to communicate power or discomfort, and performer objectives that drive the action. The analysis explains what the audience is meant to understand (e.g. the power imbalance between the characters is expressed through who controls the space) and why those choices serve the playwright's intentions. Multiple choices are analysed, not just listed.

Secure (7-9): Most choices are present and analysed. Naturalism and at least one Stanislavskian technique are referenced. Effect on audience is explained.

Developing (4-6): Some choices are named but analysis is thin; focus may drift to plot description rather than directorial intention.

Emerging (1-3): Basic description of staging with little or no analysis of intention or audience effect.

practice_questions.text: You are directing a naturalistic production of a play in which the central character is isolated from those around them by secrets they cannot share. Explain how you would use the principles of Stanislavski's system — including given circumstances, objectives and the fourth wall convention — alongside specific design choices (set, lighting, sound and costume) to communicate the character's isolation to the audience. Refer to at least two distinct moments in the play.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (17-20): The response demonstrates sustained, detailed application of Stanislavski's system. Given circumstances are used to explain why the character behaves as they do. Objectives drive blocking choices — e.g. the character's super-objective is to maintain control while their scene objectives repeatedly conflict with this. The fourth wall is maintained and its effect on the audience is analysed. Design choices are specific: set uses levels and isolated areas of furniture to communicate physical and social distance; lighting uses a naturalistic Fresnel wash with one area left in shadow to signal the character's inner world; costume choices are period-accurate but mark the character's difference from others (a slightly worn collar, a darker colour palette). Two distinct moments are developed in detail with named performer and design choices and their effects on the audience.

Secure (13-16): Stanislavski's principles are applied correctly and most design disciplines are addressed. At least two moments are used. Choices are mostly specific.

Developing (8-12): Relevant Stanislavskian ideas are present but may be superficially applied. Design choices may be generic. Only one moment is developed in detail.

Emerging (1-7): Basic knowledge of Stanislavski is shown with limited application. Design choices are vague. No named moments.

practice_questions.text: Name the act of The Crucible in which the courtroom confrontation takes place.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for: Act 3.

practice_questions.text: What is meant by the term 'dramatic climax'?
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying the term as the point of highest tension or turning point in a play's structure; 1 mark for development, e.g. noting it is the moment after which events move towards resolution or catastrophe, and that in The Crucible this falls in Act 3 with Proctor's failed attempt to expose Abigail in court.

practice_questions.text: Analyse how Miller uses the four-act structure of The Crucible to create a sense of inevitability for the audience.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks: 1 mark for identifying the structural pattern (exposition through to denouement); 1 mark for a specific structural observation (e.g. each act closes the space available to Proctor, or the move from domestic to public to jail shrinks the world); 1 mark for linking this to audience effect (e.g. the audience feels helpless as options close); 1 mark for connecting the structure to Miller's allegorical purpose (the pattern mirrors how McCarthyite accusation trapped individuals).

practice_questions.text: Explain how a set designer could use levels and proxemics in the Act 3 courtroom scene to communicate the power imbalance between Judge Danforth and John Proctor.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks: 1 mark for a named design element with specific detail (e.g. Danforth elevated on a raised platform upstage centre, placing him at a higher level than Proctor); 1 mark for explaining the proxemic effect on audience (e.g. the physical height creates visible dominance, the audience reads authority before a word is spoken); 1 mark for a second design choice (e.g. Proctor positioned downstage centre, closer to the audience, creating an uncomfortable proximity that generates sympathy); 1 mark for linking the combined choices to the play's meaning (the design makes the audience feel the injustice of a system that cannot be challenged).

practice_questions.text: How does Miller use the structure of Act 4 to communicate his intentions about conscience and personal integrity to the audience? In your answer, refer to specific moments and Miller's broader purpose.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: The response analyses how Miller uses Act 4's structural features (the slow pace, reduced cast, prison setting) to force the audience into a contemplation of moral choice. The candidate identifies Miller's dual intentions: the personal (Proctor's redemption through refusal) and the political (the allegory of refusing to name names under McCarthyite pressure). Analysis is anchored to specific moments (e.g. the signed then torn confession, Elizabeth's final words) and explains the effect each has on the audience. Staging or performance implications are noted with concrete choices (e.g. the isolation of Proctor in a tight lighting special as he tears the paper). Judgement is substantiated.

Secure: The response identifies Miller's intentions (integrity, the cost of honesty) and links them to structural features of Act 4. At least one specific moment is named and explained. Some reference to audience effect. Generally accurate but less fully developed.

Developing: The response describes what happens in Act 4 rather than analysing Miller's intentions. Some awareness of themes but effect on audience is asserted rather than explained. Generic staging reference if any.

Emerging: Basic plot summary with limited analytical engagement. Little or no reference to structural choices or audience effect.

practice_questions.text: You are a director staging the opening of Act 1 and the opening of Act 4 of The Crucible as a double image for the audience. Discuss how you would use set, lighting, sound and performer positioning to communicate the difference between these two moments and what they reveal about the play's tragic arc.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: The response offers a detailed and coherent staging concept for both acts with clear awareness of the tragic arc. Set choices are specific (materials, levels, spatial arrangement); lighting choices name lantern type, colour, intensity and cue (e.g. a tight Fresnel special over Betty's bed in Act 1, a low-intensity warm side-light on Proctor's face in Act 4 as he faces his death); sound choices name source and quality (e.g. diegetic wind and prayer from offstage in Act 1, near-total silence with a single tolling bell in Act 4); performer positioning is described precisely (upstage, downstage, proxemic distance between characters). Every choice is justified with reference to the play's meaning and the audience's emotional journey. A substantiated directorial judgement closes the response.

Secure: Staging choices cover most disciplines; mostly concrete with at least one named technical detail per skill area; both acts addressed; generally accurate effect on audience; some link to tragic arc.

Developing: Staging choices are present but generic ('dark lighting', 'sad music'); one or both acts under-developed; limited link to tragic arc or Miller's intentions.

Emerging: Basic listing of ideas with minimal explanation; one act may be ignored; no reference to tragic structure or audience effect.

practice_questions.text: Name the real historical South Asian politician whose career inspired the character Hari Mohan Lal in The Empress.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for: Dadabhai Naoroji (accept: the first Indian/South Asian MP, the first South Asian MP for Finsbury).

practice_questions.text: What is meant by the term 'gestus' in Brechtian theatre?
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying that gestus refers to a social gesture or attitude; 1 mark for explaining that it is embodied in a specific physical action that reveals a character's class, status or relationship to power (accept equivalent explanation drawing on Brecht's concept).

practice_questions.text: Explain how a costume designer could use specific costume choices for Hari Mohan Lal to communicate his position between two cultural identities in The Empress.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks: identification of a specific Western costume element (1) e.g. a dark wool frock coat or tailored suit in the Victorian parliamentary style; identification of a South Asian element in the same costume (1) e.g. a silk pocket square in a sari colour, or an embroidered collar in a Bengali pattern; explanation of how the combination signals Hari's assimilation into the political world (1); explanation of how the retained South Asian detail signals his preserved cultural identity and the tension between the two (1).

practice_questions.text: Analyse how proxemics in the docks scene could communicate the power relationship between Mrs Wormwood and Rani to the audience.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks: identification of a specific proxemic positioning for Mrs Wormwood (1) e.g. upstage and elevated; identification of a contrasting position for Rani (1) e.g. downstage and at floor level; analysis of how the spatial separation communicates the power differential between employer and abandoned servant (1); link to the audience's understanding of the play's wider argument about domestic service and the Empire (1).

practice_questions.text: As a performer playing Rani in the moment she realises the English family has left without arranging her return passage, explain the vocal and physical choices you would make to communicate her situation to the audience. Refer to specific performer skills.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (7–8): Specific named vocal choice anchored to this moment (e.g. a drop in volume to barely above a whisper, a lengthened pause before she speaks her first reaction, a flattening of pitch that drains emotion from her voice as shock sets in) AND a specific named physical choice (e.g. a stillness spreading from her hands outward, a slight forward lean then arrested as she registers the absence, a controlled facial expression that suppresses panic behind a mask of dignity). Both choices are justified with reference to what this communicates to the audience about Rani's inner life and her external situation. Candidate demonstrates awareness of how these choices set up Rani's character for the rest of the play.

Secure (5–6): Clear vocal and physical choices, both relevant to this moment; some justification of the audience effect; not fully developed for both choices.

Developing (3–4): At least one valid performer choice, but described in general terms (e.g. 'I would look shocked') without specifying the exact vocal quality or physical action.

Emerging (1–2): Basic description of what Rani feels with little or no translation into named vocal or physical skills.

practice_questions.text: As a director, explain how you would stage the scene in The Empress in which Abdul Karim first appears in Victoria's household to communicate both his personal dignity and his precarious position as a racial outsider at court. Refer to set design, lighting, performer choices and proxemics.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (17–20): Specific, justified staging choices across all required areas. Set design: use of levels, Victorian interior materials (heavy drapes, a formal dais for Victoria's chair) that communicate court hierarchy; a clear sightline across which Abdul must cross to reach Victoria. Lighting: a warm directional spotlight on Victoria's space contrasted with the cooler, more exposed ambient light in which Abdul stands, making him visible and scrutinised. Performer (Abdul): specific physical choices communicating controlled dignity (upright posture, measured pace, deliberate stillness of the hands) and the inner cost of that control (a fractional hesitation before each courtly gesture). Proxemics: the court figures arranged upstage in a semi-circle that encloses the space Abdul must enter, so that the stage architecture itself embodies the hostile gaze. Costume: Abdul's court livery as a sign of his official role, but in a cut or colour that marks him as different from the English courtiers. All choices justified with reference to the intended effect on the audience and the play's wider themes.

Secure (11–16): Most areas covered with concrete choices; proxemics and at least two design disciplines addressed; performer choices present; effect on audience identified.

Developing (6–10): Some relevant ideas but generic descriptions; limited justification; one or more areas missing.

Emerging (1–5): Basic listing of staging ideas with minimal explanation; no named performer choices; descriptive rather than analytical.

practice_questions.text: Name the character in Romeo and Juliet who belongs to neither the Montague nor the Capulet family but is killed as a result of the feud.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for: Mercutio.

practice_questions.text: What is meant by 'levels' as a staging term?
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for a basic definition (different heights on stage / use of raised platforms or floor positions); 1 mark for explaining what levels communicate (status, power, relationship or emotion between performers).

practice_questions.text: Explain how a costume designer might use fabric and colour to communicate Juliet's youth and the constraints of her Capulet household to the audience.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks: naming a specific fabric or colour choice (1), explaining the effect of that choice on the audience's reading of Juliet (1), linking the costume to her age or social context (1), describing how the choice might change across the play to reflect her situation (1).

practice_questions.text: As a performer playing Mercutio, explain the vocal and physical choices you would make to communicate his mercurial energy and its contrast with Tybalt in the duel scene. Refer to at least one specific moment.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: the student specifies distinct vocal choices for Mercutio (e.g. rapid pace, rising pitch as the Queen Mab speech accelerates, then a clipped, flat tone as he acknowledges his wound) and distinct physical choices (e.g. wide use of stage space, loose limbs, improvisational movement contrasting with Tybalt's rigid, formal stance); the contrast between the two performers' physical languages is directly addressed; a named moment is used as an anchor; the effect on the audience is described.

Secure: the student names vocal and physical choices for Mercutio and mentions the contrast with Tybalt; choices are generally concrete; one named moment present; effect on audience implied.

Developing: the student describes Mercutio's energy in general terms without naming specific vocal or physical skills; contrast with Tybalt mentioned but not developed; no named moment.

Emerging: the student describes what Mercutio is like as a character without translating this into performance choices; descriptive rather than analytical.

practice_questions.text: Discuss how you would use set design, lighting and costume to communicate the power dynamic between Lord Capulet and Juliet in the scene in Act Three where he threatens her for refusing to marry Paris. Refer to specific staging choices throughout.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: the student makes specific, justified design choices across set, lighting and costume, plus performer choices; set design describes the physical relationship of the space to the power dynamic (e.g. a raised bed as Juliet's only refuge, Capulet commanding the floor level); lighting describes specific lantern choices and states that externalise the power shift (e.g. a top-light on Capulet alone, Juliet in softer downstage light); costume distinguishes the characters' social status; performer choices for both Capulet and Juliet specify vocal and physical qualities at named moments; every choice justified with audience effect and thematic meaning.

Secure: the student covers most disciplines with generally concrete choices; performer choices present for at least one character; justification present but may not extend to all choices.

Developing: the student covers two or three disciplines with generic choices; staging ideas described but not fully justified; performer choices in emotional terms only.

Emerging: the student lists ideas without staging specificity; descriptive rather than analytical; no clear sense of intended audience effect.

practice_questions.text: Analyse how Shakespeare uses the contrast between the Nurse and Friar Lawrence to communicate his intentions about adult authority and its failure. Refer to at least two moments in the play.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: the student analyses the contrast between the Nurse and Friar Lawrence as surrogate adults who fail the lovers; they name two specific moments (e.g. the Nurse's advice to accept Paris in Act Three versus Friar Lawrence's botched potion plan) and explain what Shakespeare wants the audience to understand about adult responsibility; analysis includes how staging choices might reinforce the intended meaning; judgement is sustained.

Secure: the student identifies both characters as adult guides who fail, names two moments, and explains the effect on the audience's view of authority; staging reference may be present.

Developing: the student describes what the characters do without fully analysing Shakespeare's intentions; moments named but not closely examined.

Emerging: the student retells events involving the Nurse or Friar without analysis of Shakespeare's intentions.

practice_questions.text: Identify one character in A Taste of Honey who is described as a queer art student.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for: Geof.

practice_questions.text: What is meant by the term 'proxemics' in a theatrical context?
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying that proxemics refers to distance or spatial relationships between performers on stage; 1 mark for explaining that it is used to communicate meaning such as power, intimacy, hostility or vulnerability between characters.

practice_questions.text: Explain how a director might use proxemics to communicate the change in Jo's relationship with the Boy across their scenes together.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks: identification of proxemics as a tool for communicating emotional distance or closeness (1), explanation of how starting with greater distance between Jo and the Boy signals her initial guardedness (1), explanation of how gradually reducing that distance communicates growing trust or affection (1), link to the effect this creates for the audience watching the relationship develop (1).

practice_questions.text: As a performer playing Jo, explain how you would use vocal and physical choices to communicate her two contrasting registers — defensive wit and suppressed vulnerability — in the scene when she is left alone after Helen departs with Peter.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Both vocal and physical choices are named and specific, anchored to the moment after Helen's departure; vocal choices distinguish between the two registers (e.g. fast pace and sharp consonants for the wit; a drop in volume and a pause before a single syllable for the vulnerability); physical choices are equally specific (e.g. a sharp movement away from the door followed by stillness; a hand reaching towards where Helen stood then pulling back); the effect on the audience is clearly stated.

Secure: Both registers addressed; at least one specific vocal and one specific physical choice named for each; effect on audience identified; generally anchored to the named moment.

Developing: One register addressed more than the other; choices are relevant but generic ('sad voice', 'looks upset'); limited anchoring to the specific moment.

Emerging: Describes what Jo feels rather than how a performer would show it; no distinction between vocal and physical; no named moment.

practice_questions.text: Explain how a designer might use lighting and costume to communicate the contrast between Helen and Jo to the audience throughout the play.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks: identification of a specific lighting contrast between the two characters (1), explanation of how that lighting choice communicates something about each character's function or situation (1), identification of a costume choice that contrasts the two women (1), explanation of how that costume choice communicates their different relationships to femininity, class or age (1).

practice_questions.text: As a director staging A Taste of Honey, explain how you would use proxemics, blocking and design choices to communicate the contrasting relationships Jo has with Helen and with Geof. Refer to specific moments in the play.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Perceptive, specific staging that addresses proxemics, blocking and at least two design disciplines (lighting, costume, set or sound) for both relationships; choices are anchored to named moments (e.g. Helen's return in Act Two, Geof and Jo making a home); each choice is justified with a clear effect on the audience; shows understanding of the thematic significance of the contrast between the two relationships; all choices are concrete rather than generic.

Secure: Both relationships addressed with at least one named moment each; proxemics and at least one design discipline covered; generally concrete choices; effect on audience identified.

Developing: Some staging ideas but mainly general; one relationship addressed more fully than the other; limited named moments; effect on audience implied not stated.

Emerging: Basic description of the two relationships without staging specificity; few or no named moments; descriptive rather than analytical.

practice_questions.text: What role does Kamal Hadley hold in the world of Noughts and Crosses?
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for: a senior Cross politician (accept: Home Secretary equivalent, government minister, Sephy's father who holds political power).

practice_questions.text: Define the term 'multi-roling' and explain why it is used for state officials in productions of Noughts and Crosses.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for a definition of multi-roling (one performer plays more than one role in the same production); 1 mark for explaining that it communicates the interchangeable, institutional nature of the state's agents, or that the system rather than individuals is the antagonist.

practice_questions.text: Explain how a costume designer could use fabric and silhouette to communicate the difference in social status between Jasmine Hadley and Meggie McGregor. Refer to at least one specific choice for each character.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks: a specific fabric choice for Jasmine (e.g. fine wool, silk, tailored fit) with explanation of what it communicates (1); a contrasting fabric or silhouette choice for Meggie (e.g. cotton, worn, practical cut) with explanation (1); at least one reference to how the choice signals status within the play's racial hierarchy (1); a link to the effect on the audience's understanding of the two characters' relationship (1).

practice_questions.text: As a performer playing Callum in the school integration scene, explain the vocal and physical choices you would make to communicate the conflict between his inner intelligence and the self-policing the Cross school demands of him. Refer to at least one specific moment of the scene.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Names at least one specific vocal choice anchored to the scene (e.g. reduced volume, measured pace, clipped delivery when addressing Cross teachers) and at least one specific physical choice (e.g. reduced gesture, arms closer to body, deliberately slowed pace on entering the school space, gaze directed downward in Cross company); explains the effect of each choice on the audience's understanding of the play's power dynamics; links the choices to a named moment of the scene; the response reads as a detailed, justified interpretation rather than a list.

Secure: Names at least one vocal and one physical choice; links them to the scene; explains at least one effect on the audience.

Developing: Identifies relevant choices but describes the character's feelings rather than translating them into specific vocal and physical terms; effect on audience is implied.

Emerging: Makes basic suggestions ('I would be nervous', 'speak quietly') without specifying how or anchoring to a named moment.

practice_questions.text: Analyse how Cooke constructs the character of Callum to make the audience understand the play's argument about systemic inequality. Refer to at least two moments of the play.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Argues that Callum is constructed as living proof that noughts are denied rather than inferior, and that Cooke places him in specific situations (the school integration scene, his relationship with Sephy, the Liberation Militia sequences) to force the audience to witness the mechanism of exclusion; analyses how staging choices (blocking, proxemics, lighting) at named moments reinforce this; discusses how Callum's arc towards radicalisation is presented as an effect of injustice rather than a character flaw; reaches a judgement about Cooke's overall intention.

Secure: Identifies Callum's significance as a nought who is bright but excluded; references at least two moments; explains at least one staging implication; reaches a general judgement.

Developing: Describes Callum's situation rather than analysing Cooke's intentions; references to staging are vague or absent.

Emerging: Summarises Callum's story without addressing what the playwright intends the audience to understand.

practice_questions.text: As a director staging the scenes that contrast Sephy and Callum's home environments in Noughts and Crosses, discuss how you would use set design, lighting and costume to communicate the inequality between their worlds to the audience. Refer to specific choices across at least two design disciplines.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Presents a coherent design concept for both environments; specifies set elements for the Hadley household (e.g. levels, elevated furniture, warm textured materials, a sense of space) and contrasts with the McGregor home (e.g. a smaller floor area, functional furniture at a lower level, cooler or more desaturated colours); names specific lighting choices for each space (e.g. warm directional side light with a soft golden gel for the Hadley interior, a flatter cooler wash with a single practical light source for the McGregors); names costume choices anchored to specific characters (fabric, condition, silhouette) and justifies each; explains the effect of the contrast on the audience's understanding of the play's political world; response is anchored to named moments rather than generalised.

Secure: Addresses both environments with mostly concrete choices; at least one named lighting and one set element per space; costume choices are specific for at least one character; effect on audience is explained.

Developing: Contrasts the two homes in general terms; design choices are sometimes vague; effect on audience is implied rather than argued.

Emerging: Identifies that the homes are different without specifying design choices; response is largely descriptive.

practice_questions.text: Identify one vocal skill a performer might use to communicate a character's authority.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for any one of: a slow, measured pace / a low pitch / a loud, projected volume / a deliberate pause before speaking / a clipped, precise intonation. Accept any precise vocal skill linked plausibly to authority.

practice_questions.text: What is meant by the term 'tableau'?
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying that it is a still, frozen stage picture; 1 mark for explaining that it uses the positions and relationships of performers' bodies to communicate meaning without movement or speech.

practice_questions.text: Explain how a performer's use of stillness at a key moment in a live production can have a powerful effect on the audience.
