practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks: 1 mark for identifying what stillness is (a deliberate absence of movement at a chosen moment); 1 mark for explaining how it draws focus (the eye is drawn to the still performer amid movement, or to the performer whose stillness signals internal change); 1 mark for a specific audience effect (e.g. the audience becomes quiet, leans in, anticipates what comes next); 1 mark for a developed link to meaning or character (e.g. stillness can communicate suppressed emotion, moral weight or a moment of decision more powerfully than action).

practice_questions.text: Analyse how the interaction between two performers in the live production you have seen communicated the relationship between their characters at a specific moment.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks: 1 mark for naming a specific moment or scene; 1 mark for identifying a specific interaction (e.g. one performer's gaze held, broken or avoided; the proxemic distance decreasing or increasing; a gesture directed at rather than away from the other); 1 mark for analytical development of what the interaction communicated about the characters' relationship (power, intimacy, conflict, dependency); 1 mark for a statement about audience effect or evaluative comment on how effectively the relationship was communicated.

practice_questions.text: Imagine you saw a fictional community theatre production of a tragedy in 2025. In the final scene, the lead performer playing the protagonist discovers they have caused the death of someone they loved. As a performer in that role, explain the vocal and physical choices you would make to communicate the character's shock and guilt to the audience. Refer to specific vocal and physical skills.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (7-8): Names at least one precise vocal choice (e.g. voice drops to near-silence; all pace is stripped away so delivery becomes word by single word; a sharp intake of breath before speech begins) AND at least one precise physical choice (e.g. the body sinks from standing to crouching over the figure on the floor; hands reach out but stop short of touching; the face tilts up toward the audience then immediately turns away), both anchored clearly to this discovery moment; the effect on the audience is named and substantiated (e.g. the silence in the auditorium confirmed the audience was holding this moment with the performer); language is technically fluent throughout.
Secure (5-6): Names a vocal and a physical choice, generally anchored to the moment; audience effect explained for at least one choice; mostly specific but may contain one general descriptor.
Developing (3-4): Relevant choices present but described in general or emotional terms; little technical vocabulary; limited link to audience effect.
Emerging (1-2): Basic emotional description with no technical vocabulary and no specific moment or audience effect identified.

practice_questions.text: Analyse and evaluate the live theatre production you have seen. Focus specifically on the vocal and physical choices made by one performer in a key moment. Explain how those choices communicated meaning and evaluate how successfully they worked for the audience.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (25-32): Sustained analytical writing focused on a clearly named moment; at least two vocal choices and at least two physical choices are named with technical precision (not just 'louder' but 'projected from the diaphragm with the volume rising across the final three lines'); each choice is linked to a specific, named audience effect; an evaluative judgement is reached that is substantiated by the evidence given; terminology used accurately and fluently throughout.
Secure (17-24): At least one vocal and one physical choice named and explained with effect; some technical vocabulary; evaluative judgement present though may not be fully substantiated; generally anchored to a specific moment.
Developing (9-16): Choices identified but described in general emotional terms; some relevant vocabulary; some attempt at audience effect; limited evaluation.
Emerging (1-8): Largely descriptive or plot-based; minimal technical vocabulary; no evaluative judgement.

practice_questions.text: Name the profession of Fran Price.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for: nurse.

practice_questions.text: What is meant by the term 'proxemics' in drama?
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for a basic correct answer (e.g. the use of space or distance between performers); 1 mark for development explaining how proxemics communicates meaning (e.g. closeness suggests intimacy or confrontation; distance suggests emotional withdrawal or status difference).

practice_questions.text: Explain how the staging of the Price family's kitchen and rose garden can communicate the emotional difference between Fran and Bob as characters. How might a director use proxemics and set design to signal this difference?
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying each character's associated space (Fran/kitchen, Bob/garden); 1 mark for a specific set design choice that distinguishes the two spaces (e.g. a raised garden level, different floor texture, contrasting lighting quality); 1 mark for explaining a specific proxemics moment (e.g. Fran crossing into the garden as an unusual and significant gesture); 1 mark for linking the spatial choice to the effect it creates on the audience's understanding of the relationship.

practice_questions.text: As a performer playing Bob Price in the rose-garden scene where one of his children arrives with a difficult revelation, explain the vocal and physical choices you would make to communicate his emotional guardedness. Refer to a specific named moment in the play.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Specific vocal choices (e.g. slower pace, lower pitch, controlled volume, deliberate pauses before responding) and specific physical choices (e.g. continued engagement with the rose plants as a displacement activity, a slight turn of the body that creates a partial profile rather than full face-to-face contact, a tension in the shoulders that the performer releases slowly as they acknowledge the child's presence) anchored to a named moment (e.g. Ben's arrival in the autumn scene, or the moment a child approaches Bob while he is gardening). The effect of these choices on the audience is explained: the guardedness creates dramatic tension and prepares the audience for the revelation that his composure is concealing.

Secure: Both a vocal and a physical choice are named and linked to the character at the right moment. Explanation of effect is present but perhaps one choice is slightly generic.

Developing: A choice or choices are described without anchoring to a named moment, or the choices describe feeling rather than technique (e.g. 'I would act nervous' or 'I would seem distracted').

Emerging: Basic description of the character with little reference to specific performer skills; no named moment.

practice_questions.text: As a director bringing together the whole Price family on stage for the first time, explain how you would use blocking, proxemics and at least one design choice to communicate the family's internal tensions and hierarchies before any dialogue has been spoken.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A clear and specific staging vision addressing blocking (named positions for each character — e.g. Bob upstage in the garden area, Fran centre stage kitchen, each child placed in a spatial relationship that suggests their dynamic with the parents), proxemics (distances and angles that signal relationships), and at least one concrete design discipline (e.g. lighting: a warmer domestic glow on the kitchen side, a cooler exterior quality for the garden area, creating a visual split; costume: Bob in worn gardening clothes, Fran in a nurse's practical outfit, the children in clothes that signal their distance from home). Every choice is justified with a named effect on the audience.

Secure: Most elements present; at least one named design choice and clear proxemics thinking; audience effect generally addressed; one or two areas may be slightly generic.

Developing: Relevant staging ideas but descriptive rather than analytical; design elements mentioned without specificity (e.g. 'warm lighting for the house'); proxemics described without justification.

Emerging: Basic list of where characters might stand with little design thinking or reference to effect.

practice_questions.text: Identify the narrative role Rosie plays in the structure of Things I Know to Be True.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for: narrator (or narrator-figure / the character who delivers direct-address monologues to the audience).

practice_questions.text: Name the character in The Crucible who is pressed to death off stage rather than hanged.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for: Giles Corey.

practice_questions.text: What is meant by 'proxemics' in the context of staging a drama?
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for defining proxemics as the physical distances between performers on stage; 1 mark for development, e.g. noting that these distances communicate status, power, intimacy or threat to the audience, and that a director uses proxemics deliberately to create meaning (for example, Abigail placed at centre stage, always the centre of the group, signals her dominance before she speaks).

practice_questions.text: Explain how a costume designer could use fabric, colour and silhouette to distinguish Elizabeth Proctor from the court officials in The Crucible.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks: 1 mark for a specific costume detail with named element (e.g. a grey-blue linen dress with plain collar in contrast to the black wool of the court officials); 1 mark for the effect this creates on the audience (e.g. the softness of the fabric against the rigidity of the officials' dress signals Elizabeth's humanity within a dehumanising system); 1 mark for a second named costume choice (e.g. a small detail of warmth — a cream underskirt, a slightly draped collar — suggesting that her austerity is worn, not innate); 1 mark for linking both choices to Miller's intentions (communicating to the audience that Elizabeth is the moral heart of a play whose institutions have no compassion).

practice_questions.text: As a performer playing Abigail Williams in the courtroom scene of Act 3, explain the vocal and physical choices you would make to communicate her performance of possession to the audience. Refer to one specific moment in the scene.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: The response names specific vocal choices (e.g. beginning with a controlled, even delivery that shifts to a rising pitch and increasing volume as the performance of possession escalates, with sudden drops to a whispered stillness to create unease); names specific physical choices (e.g. a shift from upright, composed posture to sudden uncontrolled physical movement — arms raised, body twisting away from Mary Warren — then a return to stillness as Abigail reasserts control); anchors both choices to a named moment (e.g. the moment Abigail pretends to see Mary Warren's spirit descending on her); explains the effect on the audience (e.g. the switches create a vertiginous double awareness — the audience sees the performance within the performance, which heightens their frustration and dread); both vocal and physical choices are present.

Secure: Both vocal and physical choices named; at least one anchored to a named moment; generally accurate effect on audience described.

Developing: Describes feeling ('Abigail would seem frightened') without translating into specific vocal and physical skills; limited or no named moment.

Emerging: Basic description of what Abigail does rather than how a performer would make specific choices; no named moment.

practice_questions.text: Analyse how Miller uses the character of Reverend Hale to communicate his intentions about the relationship between individual conscience and institutional authority in The Crucible.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: The response analyses Hale's arc from confident expert to remorseful witness as Miller's demonstration that individuals can recognise institutional injustice — but that recognition comes too late to save the innocent. The candidate identifies Miller's allegorical purpose (the parallel with HUAC witnesses who eventually saw the hearings as unjust but had already named names) and shows how Hale performs the audience's own journey. Specific moments are named (Hale's initial authority in Act 1, his growing doubt in Act 3, his desperate pleading in Act 4). Staging implications are noted (e.g. a performer tracking Hale's declining physical authority as the play progresses). Judgement is substantiated.

Secure: Identifies Hale's arc and links it to Miller's intentions; at least one named moment; some reference to audience effect; limited staging reference.

Developing: Describes Hale's change without fully analysing why Miller includes it; limited reference to Miller's intentions or the allegory.

Emerging: Retells Hale's role in the plot with minimal analytical engagement.

practice_questions.text: You are a director staging the moment in Act 3 when Mary Warren turns on Proctor and accuses him of witchcraft, after failing to maintain her recantation under Abigail's pressure. Discuss how you would use performer positioning, levels, lighting and sound to communicate the audience's experience of witnessing an irreversible moment of injustice.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: The response offers a coherent, specific staging concept that communicates the turning point. Performer positioning is precise (e.g. Proctor isolated downstage centre, surrounded by accusers who have formed a semicircle behind him, blocking his exit routes; Mary Warren retreating upstage to join Abigail's group, her crossing of the stage tracked by audience as a physical betrayal); levels are discussed (e.g. Danforth on an elevated platform, Proctor on the floor, the physical height gap embodying the injustice); lighting choices are specific and named (e.g. a hard-edged profile lantern on Proctor sharpens his isolation; a broader flood on the accusers flattens them into an undifferentiated mass; a gradual dimming of the overall state as the accusation takes hold); sound choices are named (e.g. a rising, low-frequency sound cue — not music, but something sub-bass and almost physical — beginning under Mary Warren's accusation and building to a sustained drone under the blackout); every choice justified with reference to the audience's experience and Miller's intentions; substantiated judgement.

Secure: Most disciplines addressed; at least one named technical element per skill; performer positioning described with some precision; link to meaning; generally accurate.

Developing: Ideas present but generic across most disciplines; limited named technical detail; effect on audience asserted rather than developed.

Emerging: Basic list of ideas; one or more disciplines absent; no reference to the moment's significance or Miller's intentions.

practice_questions.text: Give the German term for Brecht's 'alienation effect'.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for: Verfremdungseffekt.

practice_questions.text: What is meant by 'gestus' in Brecht's epic theatre?
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying it as a physical attitude or gesture used by a performer; 1 mark for explaining that it reveals the character's social position or class relationship rather than their private inner feelings.

practice_questions.text: Analyse how the use of placards or title cards in a Brechtian production creates the V-effect for the audience.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks: 1 mark for naming placards as a Brechtian technique; 1 mark for explaining that they announce scenes or reveal outcomes before they occur; 1 mark for analytical development (e.g. this removes suspense and prevents emotional absorption by inviting the audience to ask 'why' rather than 'what next'); 1 mark for linking to Brecht's intention that theatre should produce critical thinking rather than passive emotional response.

practice_questions.text: As a lighting and set designer, explain how you would design the visual environment for a scene in which a figure of institutional authority interrogates a vulnerable character. Your design should reflect Brechtian staging principles. Refer to specific design choices and explain their effect on the audience.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (7-8): Specific, named design choices are made for both set and lighting that clearly reflect Brechtian principles. Set might include exposed scaffolding, visible backstage space, a raised platform for the authority figure to create levels, and visible rigging — communicating that this is constructed theatre, not a real room. Lighting might use unfiltered profile lanterns rigged in view, a hard-edged beam on the authority figure from directly above (high angle, creating harsh shadow), and a flat cold wash on the vulnerable character, with no soft naturalistic fill. The designer explains how these choices serve the V-effect: the audience is kept at a critical distance, reading the scene as a statement about institutional power rather than being absorbed in the individual emotional exchange. Effect on the audience is named.

Secure (5-6): Both set and lighting are addressed with reasonably specific choices. Brechtian principles are referenced. Effect on audience is mentioned.

Developing (3-4): Design choices are present but generic ('harsh lighting, bare set'). Limited connection to Brechtian intention.

Emerging (1-2): Very general design ideas with little or no reference to Brechtian techniques or effect on audience.

practice_questions.text: Analyse how Brecht's use of songs interrupting the action reveals his intentions for the audience. What is Brecht trying to make the audience think, feel or understand through this technique?
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (10-12): The response analyses how songs function as a V-effect device, breaking emotional absorption at the peak of a scene and returning the audience to a critical position. Brecht's didactic intention is clearly articulated: theatre is a tool for social change; the audience must be kept alert, judgement intact, in order to act differently in the world. The response may analyse how a song's lyrical content offers an ironic commentary on the dramatic situation, or how the shift in theatrical register (from dramatic scene to performed number) makes visible the constructed nature of what they are watching. Multiple functions of the technique are explored, not just one. The analysis connects the technique to Brecht's political philosophy.

Secure (7-9): Brecht's intentions are explained with reference to the V-effect and the idea of keeping the audience thinking. At least one function of songs is analysed with explanation of audience effect.

Developing (4-6): Songs are described as a technique but the analysis focuses on what they do to the story rather than what they do to the audience's critical relationship to the play.

Emerging (1-3): Songs are mentioned as a feature of Brecht's work but no analytical development of intention or audience effect.

practice_questions.text: You are directing a production that applies Brechtian staging principles throughout. Explain how you would stage a scene in which a character must make a moral choice under pressure from those in authority. In your answer, refer to: the staging configuration, the use of gestus by performers, at least two specific design disciplines (lighting, sound, set or costume), and the effect you intend on the audience.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (17-20): The response applies Brechtian principles consistently and specifically across multiple staging disciplines. The performer playing the authority figure demonstrates a clearly described gestus (e.g. slow, deliberate speech; a physical stillness that occupies space without moving; a costume that signals institutional role — uniform, wig, gown — over a plain underscore). The character under pressure has a contrasting gestus (e.g. contained, inward, reduced physical footprint). Staging configuration is chosen and justified (e.g. traverse staging so the audience sit on both sides, making them feel complicit in witnessing the interrogation). Set design is spare and Brechtian: visible structure, a raised platform for authority, a plain chair centre stage as the only furniture, meaning concentrated by absence. Lighting uses profile lanterns rigged visibly at end-on angles, a hard front-light on the authority figure and a cooler, lower-intensity beam on the character under pressure, with no naturalistic fill. Sound uses live percussion visible in the corner, building a rhythm under the interrogation that gets slower as pressure mounts, then stops entirely at the decision moment — the silence is as deliberate as any sound. A placard or projection announces the outcome of the scene before it begins. The response explains what the audience is intended to think and feel: the V-effect keeps them critical, the gestus signals systemic power rather than individual villainy.

Secure (13-16): Most Brechtian elements are present and staged with reasonable specificity. At least three design disciplines are addressed. Gestus is used for at least one performer. Audience effect is explained.

Developing (8-12): Relevant Brechtian ideas are applied but may be thin on specificity or miss one or more design disciplines. Gestus may be named but not fully demonstrated in practice.

Emerging (1-7): Some knowledge of Brecht is shown. Design choices are vague. Limited application of specific techniques.

practice_questions.text: Identify the term for the physical attitude or stance, associated with Brecht, that a performer uses to communicate a character's social status in a single image.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for: gestus.

practice_questions.text: What is meant by 'proxemics' as a staging tool?
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying that proxemics refers to distance between performers on stage; 1 mark for explaining that it is used intentionally to communicate relationship, status, power or intimacy between characters.

practice_questions.text: Explain how a designer might use costume to distinguish Fogg from the ensemble in Around the World in 80 Days. Refer to at least one specific costume choice and its effect on the audience.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks: identification of a specific costume item (e.g. Victorian frock coat, waistcoat, pocket watch as fixed constants throughout the journey) (1); explanation that Fogg's unchanged costume contrasts with the constantly shifting ensemble costumes around him (1); explanation of how this contrast reinforces his status as the still centre of the play (1); comment on the audience's experience — for example, that the fixed costume gives the audience a visual anchor in each new location as everything else transforms (1).

practice_questions.text: As a performer playing Jean Passepartout in the moment when Fogg announces that they must immediately depart for Yokohama despite a setback, explain the vocal and physical choices you would make. Refer to one specific staging choice.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: The response makes precise, concrete vocal choices (e.g. a rapidly rising pitch as Passepartout processes the news, followed by a mid-sentence break — a vocal pause that communicates stunned disbelief before the rush of anxious speech; volume rising slightly, pace increasing as panic builds). Physical choices are equally specific (e.g. an initial involuntary step backward at the announcement, shoulders rising toward the ears in a physical gesture of alarm; hands briefly raised before dropping as Passepartout visibly decides to comply). Staging choice is named and justified (e.g. Passepartout positioned downstage centre, closer to the audience than Fogg, so that his reaction is the audience's primary lens into the moment; turning briefly to face the audience before snapping back to Fogg communicates that Passepartout, like the audience, finds the plan absurd). The response explains how these choices create comedy and audience empathy.
Secure: Both vocal and physical choices are present and generally concrete; staging reference is included; the effect on the audience is described.
Developing: Relevant ideas but either vocal or physical choices are generic (e.g. 'I would look shocked'); staging choice absent or vague.
Emerging: Describes feeling without translating into specific performance choices.

practice_questions.text: Discuss how a director might stage the moment Aouda first appears, in the India scenes, to communicate her vulnerability and the play's moral stakes to the audience. Refer to proxemics, lighting and at least one performer choice.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: The response articulates a clear directorial vision for the moment. Proxemics are used with precision — for example, Aouda is placed centre stage, surrounded by the ensemble, whose physical mass and proximity communicate threat without any dialogue; Fogg and Passepartout are positioned upstage, initially outside the scene, so the audience perceives the danger before the protagonists do. Performer choices for Aouda are specific: a still, contained posture, arms close to the body, limited movement communicating constraint; voice initially silent or near-silent, communicating shock. Lighting is named and justified: a tight warm special on Aouda isolating her from a cooler, more diffuse wash on the ensemble around her, creating a visual focal point and generating audience sympathy for her position. The response connects these choices to the play's broader concern with what Fogg's adventure means for the people he encounters. Sound design might also be referenced (e.g. a soundscape mixing the ensemble's voices with distant music to create the atmosphere of the location, contrasting with silence around Aouda's moments of stillness). A directorial intention is clearly stated and the choices are weighed against each other.
Secure: At least three theatrical elements are addressed with mostly concrete choices; directorial intention is generally clear; proxemics, lighting and performer choices are all present.
Developing: Some staging ideas are present; fewer than three elements addressed in concrete detail; the connection to the play's moral stakes is implied rather than developed.
Emerging: Lists staging ideas without explaining how they work together or what effect they create for the audience.

practice_questions.text: Analyse how Eason constructs the relationship between Fogg and Passepartout to create comic effect and communicate meaning to the audience.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: The response analyses Fogg and Passepartout as a deliberately constructed double-act, explaining that Eason intends the contrast between Fogg's stillness and Passepartout's energy to be the primary comic mechanism. The analysis goes beyond description to consider what the playwright wants the audience to take from this dynamic: Fogg's calm in the face of chaos communicates Victorian stoicism and eccentricity as both admirable and absurd; Passepartout's panic functions as a realistic human mirror for the audience, who can laugh at what Fogg refuses to acknowledge. Concrete staging references are made — for example, how blocking choices that separate them spatially allow the audience to read both reactions simultaneously, with Fogg's stillness upstage amplifying Passepartout's movement downstage. A considered judgement is reached about how this character dynamic communicates something broader about the play's themes.
Secure: The double-act dynamic is identified and mostly analysed; at least one staging reference; the link to broader meaning is present.
Developing: The relationship is described with some relevant observation, but analysis is limited to surface description rather than playwright's intention.
Emerging: Describes the characters separately rather than analysing the relationship between them.

practice_questions.text: Name the twin who is raised by Mrs Johnstone in Blood Brothers.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for: Mickey / Mickey Johnstone.

practice_questions.text: What is meant by the term 'gestus' in performance?
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying gestus as a Brechtian performance concept involving physical and vocal choices; 1 mark for explaining that it communicates a character's social or political identity, not just their individual emotion.

practice_questions.text: Explain how a director might use proxemics and levels to communicate the power difference between Mrs Johnstone and Mrs Lyons in the deal scene.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks: naming a specific proxemics arrangement (e.g. Mrs Lyons stands, Mrs Johnstone seated; Mrs Lyons centre stage, Mrs Johnstone to the side) (1); naming a levels choice (e.g. Mrs Lyons on a raised step or platform) (1); explaining the effect of this arrangement on the audience's understanding of power (1); linking the staging to the play's class theme (1).

practice_questions.text: Analyse how Russell uses the character of Mrs Lyons to explore the theme of manipulation and power in Blood Brothers. What does Russell want the audience to understand about how the powerful use the powerless?
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks: identifying Mrs Lyons's use of superstition as a manipulation tool (1); explaining how this reflects a class power dynamic (employer over employee) (1); analysing what Russell intends the audience to understand about systemic manipulation (1); linking to at least one specific named moment in the play (1).

practice_questions.text: As a performer playing Mickey, explain the vocal and physical choices you would make in the moment Mickey confronts Edward during the final scene of Blood Brothers. Refer to at least one vocal choice and at least one physical choice, and explain the effect of each on the audience.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Names at least one specific vocal choice (e.g. raised volume, broken pitch, accelerating pace) AND one specific physical choice (e.g. advancing proxemics towards Edward, unstable posture, shaking hands gripping the gun) for the named moment. Explains the effect of each choice on the audience with clarity. Demonstrates awareness of the contrast between Mickey's emotional state and the class context. May reference the gestus of the moment.

Secure: One vocal and one physical choice identified with explanation of effect. Choices are generally concrete. Anchor to the named moment is present.

Developing: Relevant but generic (e.g. 'I would be angry'). Some physical or vocal idea mentioned but not named precisely. Effect on audience implied rather than stated.

Emerging: Describes how Mickey feels without translating into performer choices. Minimal or no reference to the specific moment.

practice_questions.text: As a director, discuss how you would stage the deal scene in which Mrs Johnstone agrees to give one twin to Mrs Lyons. In your answer, refer to performer positioning, a lighting choice, and one further design discipline. Explain how each choice communicates the relationship between the two women to the audience.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Treats the deal scene as a power-map between two women from different classes. Specifies performer positioning (e.g. Mrs Lyons standing and moving around a seated, still Mrs Johnstone; Mrs Lyons occupying centre stage throughout). Names a lighting choice with concrete detail (e.g. a warm overhead lighting special on Mrs Lyons drawing focus; a cooler, lower-intensity fill on Mrs Johnstone that visually diminishes her). Introduces a further design element with equal specificity (e.g. costume contrast: Mrs Lyons in structured wool, Mrs Johnstone in worn cotton; or sound: a quietening soundscape so each pause carries weight). Explains the effect of each choice on the audience and links to Russell's social argument. Reaches a directorial decision.

Secure: Covers positioning and two design disciplines with generally concrete choices. Class contrast communicated. Effect on audience addressed.

Developing: Some staging ideas but generic. Positioning mentioned without specifics. Design choices described in general terms (e.g. 'dark lighting for sadness').

Emerging: Basic ideas with no named detail. Little or no explanation of audience effect.

practice_questions.text: Name Hanako's older sister in The Great Wave.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for: Reiko.

practice_questions.text: What is meant by the term 'proxemics' in performance?
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying proxemics as the physical distance between performers; 1 mark for explaining that it communicates relationship, power or emotion between characters.

practice_questions.text: Explain how a costume designer could use fabric and silhouette to communicate Etsuko's ageing across the play. Refer to specific design choices and their effect on the audience.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks: identification of a specific costume approach for Etsuko (1); naming of a fabric, colour or silhouette choice for an early scene (1); description of how this changes in a later scene (1); explanation of what effect the visual progression creates for the audience (1).

practice_questions.text: Analyse how Turnly uses the character of Kum-Chol to present a morally complex view of complicity and institutional authority.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks: identification that Kum-Chol is complicit in a state crime but is not portrayed as simply villainous (1); analysis of the performative implication of this complexity, e.g. gestus choices that distinguish official role from individual moments (1); reference to a specific staging moment or scene (1); explanation of the effect this ambiguity creates for the audience (1).

practice_questions.text: As a performer playing Hanako in the first interrogation scene, explain how you would use vocal and physical choices to communicate the tension between outward submission and inward resistance. Refer to at least one specific vocal skill and one physical skill.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Both a concrete vocal skill (e.g. near-whispered volume with controlled, level intonation to imply disciplined suppression rather than passive fear; deliberate pauses before answering to suggest internal negotiation) and a concrete physical skill (e.g. upright but entirely still posture, hands flat on the table, maintaining eye contact with interrogators only when directly addressed) are named and justified with reference to this scene. The effect on the audience is specified: watching a young woman calculate her survival in real time. Secure: One concrete vocal and one physical choice with generally accurate effect; may be less specific about the moment. Developing: Describes what the character feels but translates this into generic choices (speaks quietly, looks scared) with no named moment. Emerging: Identifies the emotional state with no performance translation.

practice_questions.text: As a director, discuss how you would stage the teaching scenes between Hanako and Jung Sun to communicate the gradual shift in their relationship from coerced formality to reluctant human connection. Consider the use of proxemics, levels, blocking and at least one design element. Refer to specific moments within the scenes.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: A sustained, specific discussion of the teaching scenes as a choreographic arc. Proxemics choices are concrete and tracked across multiple scenes (starting distance named in metres or spatial terms, reducing across scenes). Levels are used deliberately (e.g. both seated at a table establishes equality of constraint; one standing mid-scene shifts power briefly). Blocking describes specific moves (e.g. Hanako begins each lesson by sitting on the far edge of the desk, Jung Sun facing her from across; by a later scene, she has shifted to the same side of the table to correct his pronunciation). At least one design element is specific: lighting (e.g. a neutral 4200K overhead state for the formal lessons, softening to a warmer, lower-intensity Fresnel as the relationship develops); or sound (the ambient propaganda music audible in earlier lessons gradually dropping in volume as the scenes progress, suggesting the gradual reduction of the state’s presence in the space between them). Effect on audience is specified at each stage. Substantiated judgement about what the staging is arguing about coercion and human connection. Secure: Two or three staging choices across the scenes, mostly concrete, at least one design element, generally accurate effect. Developing: Aware of the proxemic opportunity but describes changes in general terms; limited design detail. Emerging: Describes the scene as a classroom with limited staging analysis.

practice_questions.text: What is a gobo?
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for: a metal disc with a cut-out pattern inserted into a profile lantern to project a pattern of light and shadow onto the stage.

practice_questions.text: What is a soundscape in theatre design?
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying that a soundscape is a layered composition of multiple simultaneous sounds; 1 mark for explaining that it creates an immersive sonic environment that establishes location, atmosphere or mood.

practice_questions.text: Explain how a set designer might use levels to communicate the relationship between two characters to the audience.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks: 1 mark for naming levels as a set design tool (e.g. rostra, platform, ramp); 1 mark for explaining how elevated height signals status, power or authority; 1 mark for explaining how a lower-positioned character can appear vulnerable, submissive or trapped; 1 mark for linking the spatial relationship to a specific intended effect on the audience's understanding of the characters' dynamic.

practice_questions.text: As a lighting designer, explain how you would design the lighting for a tense confrontation between two characters at the climax of a play. Refer to specific lighting choices and explain their effect on the audience.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: at least two specific lighting choices named with precision (e.g. a tight hard-edged profile lantern above one character in cold blue-white at 80% intensity, cross-fading to a low warm side-light on the other; a slow fade to a near-blackout with a single special on the speaking character's face); each choice is anchored to the climax and linked to a named effect (e.g. 'the contrast isolates each character and prevents the audience from reading the other's reaction, creating suspense'); lantern type, colour and intensity are all specified.

Secure: at least one lighting choice with named elements (lantern type or colour); effect described with some specificity; linked to the moment.

Developing: general lighting ideas (bright on one, dark on other); lantern type or colour not specified; effect on audience generic ('creates tension').

Emerging: basic lighting reference (turn lights down) with no specification; effect not linked to the moment.

practice_questions.text: Analyse how a costume designer might use colour, silhouette and fabric to communicate the themes of power and vulnerability in a production. In your answer, refer to specific costume choices and their intended effect on the audience.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: sustained analysis of how specific costume elements (named colour, fabric texture, silhouette, accessories) communicate the theme of power for one character and vulnerability for another; choices are linked to what the designer intends the audience to understand (e.g. 'the gold brocade coat with padded shoulders signals authority and is read immediately by the audience as a costume of dominance, while the pale, undyed linen with a loose, unstructured silhouette communicates the other character's social fragility'); at least two distinct costume elements analysed with the theme in view throughout.

Secure: clear explanation of how at least two costume choices communicate character or theme; some specific vocabulary (colour, fabric, silhouette) used; theme identified and linked to most choices.

Developing: description of what characters might wear with limited analysis of meaning; theme named but not sustained; specificity low.

Emerging: simple costume descriptions with no thematic analysis; vague colour references without explanation.

practice_questions.text: As a designer working across two disciplines of your choice, explain how you would design a key scene to communicate the playwright's intentions to the audience. Refer to specific choices from each discipline and their combined effect.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: two design disciplines chosen and clearly identified; specific, named choices from each (e.g. a gobo projecting fragmented window-frame shadows in lighting; a worn Victorian wallpaper set with a split cyclorama showing a colourless sky beyond); choices are analysed in terms of the playwright's intended audience effect; the combination of disciplines is discussed (e.g. how the lighting interacts with the texture of the set); the staging logic is internally consistent and the answer is anchored to a specific scene or moment.

Secure: two disciplines identified; mostly specific choices with some named elements; audience effect described; some discussion of how the disciplines work together.

Developing: design ideas from two disciplines but limited specificity; general descriptors used; audience effect implied; no analysis of the interaction between disciplines.

Emerging: general staging description with little or no specification; discipline boundaries blurred; audience effect absent.

practice_questions.text: In which staging configuration does the audience sit on all four sides of the performance space?
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for: theatre in the round.

practice_questions.text: What is meant by the term 'proxemics' in theatre?
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying that proxemics refers to physical distance on stage; 1 mark for explaining that it concerns the distances between performers, and between performers and audience, and how those distances communicate power, intimacy or relationship.

practice_questions.text: Explain how a thrust stage affects the performer's use of the performance space compared to a proscenium arch stage.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks: 1 mark for correctly defining a thrust stage (performance area extends into the audience, audience on three sides); 1 mark for contrasting with proscenium (audience on one side only, frame separating stage and auditorium); 1 mark for explaining an implication for blocking (the performer must play to three sides; their back is always turned to some of the audience); 1 mark for explaining an implication for audience relationship (greater proximity, more visible physical detail, higher exposure for the performer).

practice_questions.text: Explain how staging a production in the round rather than using a proscenium arch might affect the audience's experience of the performance.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks: 1 mark for defining theatre in the round (audience surrounds the space on all sides); 1 mark for identifying a specific effect on audience experience (e.g. the audience feels implicated or immersed rather than distanced; they can see each other watching across the space, which emphasises shared community or shared guilt); 1 mark for identifying a limitation or challenge (sightlines cannot be guaranteed; every performer's back is turned to part of the audience); 1 mark for analytical development (e.g. this configuration suits a play that wants the audience to feel unable to escape their role as witness).

practice_questions.text: As a set designer, explain how you would design a set for a traverse stage production. In your answer, discuss how the configuration affects your design choices and what effect your set would have on the audience.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: specific understanding of traverse configuration (two audience banks facing each other across a long narrow space); at least two specific set design choices driven by the configuration (e.g. low-profile furniture so sightlines are maintained; a minimal, symbolic central set piece such as a bare table and two chairs to emphasise the confrontational symmetry of the space; floor materials used to define zones rather than walls that would block views); each choice linked to a precise audience effect (e.g. 'the audience on both sides watches the other group watching the performers, which creates a sense that everyone is under surveillance'); scale, shape and texture referenced.

Secure: traverse configuration understood; at least two design choices described with some specificity; audience effect generally described.

Developing: configuration recognised but design choices are generic and not driven by traverse's specific demands; audience effect implied.

Emerging: basic staging ideas with no specific understanding of traverse; little or no discussion of how the configuration shapes the design.

practice_questions.text: As a designer, compare two staging configurations and explain which you would choose for a production exploring themes of surveillance, power and control. Justify your choice with reference to specific design and staging possibilities each configuration offers or denies.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: two configurations clearly defined and contrasted; the chosen configuration is justified with reference to the theme (surveillance, power, control) and at least two specific staging/design possibilities it enables (e.g. traverse: the audience watches the action across a contested space, seeing each other watching, which mirrors the theme of mutual observation; in-the-round: the performers are surrounded and cannot escape, embodying the theme of constant scrutiny); specific design choices discussed (set, lighting or sound elements that work with the chosen configuration); the rejected configuration is discussed to strengthen the argument.

Secure: two configurations compared; chosen configuration justified with theme in view; at least one specific staging/design possibility named per configuration; some design vocabulary used.

Developing: two configurations described but comparison is superficial; theme mentioned but not sustained in the argument; design choices general.

Emerging: one or two configurations named with basic description; no clear justification for choice; theme not connected to configuration.

practice_questions.text: Name one theme explored in The Great Wave by Francis Turnly.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for any of: state authoritarianism / identity erasure / ambiguous loss / family endurance / complicity / diplomatic silence / abduction as state policy.

practice_questions.text: What is meant by the term 'soundscape' in theatre design?
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying a soundscape as a designed composition of layered sounds; 1 mark for explaining that it evokes place, atmosphere or emotional state using diegetic and/or non-diegetic elements.

practice_questions.text: Analyse how Turnly uses the theme of identity erasure in the teaching scenes of The Great Wave. Refer to one staging or performance choice a director might use to communicate this theme.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks: identification of the identity-erasure theme in the teaching scenes (1); analysis of how Hanako's own language becomes the instrument of the state (1); a named staging or performance choice, e.g. underscore, micro-pause, proxemics (1); explanation of the effect this creates for the audience (1).

practice_questions.text: Explain how a lighting designer might use a lighting special to communicate the theme of ambiguous loss in a scene where Etsuko is alone. Refer to specific lighting choices and their effect on the audience.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks: identification of a lighting special as a tightly focused beam on a single performer (1); a specific choice about colour temperature, intensity or lantern type for this special (1); description of how the rest of the stage is lit during this moment (1); explanation of the effect this contrast creates for the audience in terms of the ambiguous-loss theme (1).

practice_questions.text: Analyse how Turnly uses the theme of state power to communicate a political argument about the relationship between governments and individual citizens. Consider how a director might make this political argument visible to the audience through staging and design in the diplomatic or interrogation scenes.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Identifies Turnly's political intention as staging the gap between institutional procedure and individual human cost; analyses how the diplomatic/interrogation scenes make this gap visible through staging (not just through dialogue); discusses at least two concrete directorial or design choices — e.g. level asymmetry in the interrogation (official raised, Hanako at floor level), a neutral, controlled vocal delivery from officials contrasted against Hanako's constrained physicality, a cold white lighting state in official scenes vs the warmer domestic tones of the Japanese family — and explains the effect of each choice on the audience. Reaches a substantiated judgement about what political claim the play is making. Secure: Discusses the political theme with some design reference; generally concrete but may be less precise about specific scenes or effects. Developing: Describes the political content but treats it as background information rather than as a staged argument; design choices are generic. Emerging: Brief identification of the political theme with little analytical engagement.

practice_questions.text: As a director, discuss how you would stage the moments of diplomatic silence in The Great Wave to communicate the theme of state indifference to individual suffering. Consider lighting, sound, the physical arrangement of performers and at least one performer choice. Refer to specific moments of the play.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: A full discussion of how official silence is staged as an active form of violence rather than a neutral backdrop. Specific lighting choices: e.g. a cold, high-intensity overhead state (a 5600K profile wash from directly above) that flattens the faces of officials, making them look institutional rather than human; contrasted with the lower-key, warmer state used when families speak. Sound design: the absence of soundscape in diplomatic scenes — a deliberate silence after the sea sounds of the surrounding scenes — so that official silence becomes sonically total. Performer choices for officials: deliberate, measured vocal pace, no variation in pitch, eye contact only with documentation rather than with Hanako or her family — gestus of bureaucratic authority. The proxemic arrangement of diplomatic scenes: officials seated at a raised, wide table; Hanako or her family at a single chair facing them across a distance of at least four metres, downstage. Effect on the audience: the staging makes institutional indifference as visually uncomfortable as Hanako's captivity. Secure: Two or three strong choices with mostly accurate effects, at least one named moment. Developing: Identifies the thematic opportunity but staging is described in general terms. Emerging: Describes the diplomatic scenes as background information with limited staging analysis.

practice_questions.text: Name the convention of love that Romeo performs for Rosaline in Act One, characterised by idealised, distance-worshipping verse.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for: courtly love.

practice_questions.text: What is a gobo in theatre design?
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying what a gobo is (a plate placed in front of a lantern); 1 mark for explaining what it does (projects a pattern or shape of light onto the stage or a surface).

practice_questions.text: Analyse how a costume designer might use colour to communicate the theme of inherited conflict between the two families from the very first scene of the play.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks: identifying the specific costume strategy (colour coding per family) (1), naming specific colours or tonal contrasts and justifying the choice (1), linking the choice to the theme of inherited allegiance (1), describing the effect on the audience's reading of the feud before dialogue begins (1).

practice_questions.text: Explain how a lighting designer might use a gobo and lighting states to communicate the theme of fate across the whole production of Romeo and Juliet. Refer to two specific moments.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks: describing a specific gobo choice linked to the star imagery of fate (1), naming two specific moments where the lighting state shifts in response to the theme (1 for each moment up to 2), describing the effect on the audience at one of those moments (1).

practice_questions.text: Analyse how Shakespeare uses the theme of youth versus age to communicate his intentions about the society of Verona. Refer to at least two moments in the play.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: the student analyses how the generational gap is a structural feature of the tragedy, not just characterisation; they name two specific moments (e.g. the Nurse’s advice to accept Paris in Act Three; Capulet’s threats in Act Three Scene Five) and explain what Shakespeare wants the audience to understand about patriarchal authority; the analysis extends to staging choices (movement vocabulary, levels, proxemics) that physicalise the gap; judgement is sustained about what Shakespeare intends the audience to feel about the adults’ failure.

Secure: the student identifies the youth-versus-age theme, names two moments, and explains the audience’s likely response; staging reference may be present.

Developing: the student describes what adult characters do without fully analysing Shakespeare’s intentions; thematic identification without close examination.

Emerging: the student describes events without analysis of intentions; descriptive.

practice_questions.text: You are directing the opening brawl scene in Act One. Discuss how you would use costume, blocking, levels and sound to communicate both the theme of inherited conflict and the world of Verona to the audience. Refer to specific staging decisions throughout.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: the student designs the brawl scene with specific, justified choices across costume, blocking, levels and sound; costume specifies colour families for each household and justifies the choice with reference to audience reading; blocking describes specific spatial choices (e.g. the Montague servants entering from stage left, Capulet from stage right, converging at centre stage with the Prince upstage elevated) and justifies each with reference to power and theme; levels distinguish authority from servants; sound design names specific elements (diegetic city sounds, a non-diegetic underscore that cuts as the brawl becomes fatal) and justifies each; performer choices for at least one character are specified; every choice is anchored to a named effect on the audience and a thematic meaning.

Secure: the student covers most disciplines with generally concrete choices; at least one named element per discipline; justification present.

Developing: the student covers two or three disciplines with generic choices; staging ideas described without full justification.

Emerging: the student lists staging ideas without specificity; descriptive rather than analytical.

practice_questions.text: Name the theoretical concept Artaud used to describe his vision of theatre as a sensory, immersive experience.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for: Theatre of Cruelty.

practice_questions.text: What is meant by 'total theatre' in Artaud's work?
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying that total theatre uses every available sensory element as a primary language of communication; 1 mark for explaining that this includes light, sound, movement and spatial configuration, which are not subordinate to the written text but are equal or primary means of creating meaning.

practice_questions.text: Explain how a soundscape in an Artaudian production differs from naturalistic background sound, and the effect this difference has on the audience.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks: 1 mark for identifying that naturalistic sound illustrates the setting (birdsong, traffic) whereas an Artaudian soundscape is a dense, layered audio environment; 1 mark for describing a specific quality of that soundscape (e.g. layered voices, distorted percussion, sub-bass frequencies); 1 mark for explaining the effect on the audience (e.g. the audience is physically enveloped rather than simply hearing background sound); 1 mark for connecting this to Artaud's intention to overwhelm the senses and produce heightened awareness.

practice_questions.text: As a lighting and sound designer, explain how you would design the sensory environment for a scene in which a single performer depicts a community experiencing collective trauma. Your answer should reflect Artaud's principles of total theatre. Refer to specific design choices and their effect on the audience.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (7-8): The response makes specific, named design choices for both lighting and sound that reflect Artaudian immersion. Lighting might use a strobe at low frequency to fragment movement into stills, a series of floor-rigged birdies casting upward light that distorts the performer's face, and a sudden blackout at the scene's climax. Sound might use a subwoofer drone that the audience physically feels, layered with a processed vocal track of syllables rather than words, building in intensity and then cutting to silence. The designer explains how these choices produce a total sensory experience, engulfing the audience rather than providing illustration. The effect on the audience goes beyond 'unsettled' to articulate the Artaudian purpose: the audience is forced into heightened presence.

Secure (5-6): Specific design choices are made for both disciplines with reference to Artaudian immersion. Effect on audience is explained.

Developing (3-4): Design ideas are present but generic ('harsh lighting and loud sound'). Limited connection to total theatre or sensory immersion.

Emerging (1-2): Very general design ideas with little reference to Artaud's principles or effect on audience.

practice_questions.text: Analyse how Artaud's concept of total theatre reveals his intentions for the relationship between the audience and the theatrical experience. What is Artaud trying to achieve by making every element of design and performance a primary language?
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (10-12): The response analyses Artaud's philosophical intention: theatre as a ritual act that breaks down the safe, comfortable passivity of the conventional theatre-going experience. Total theatre is explained as a rejection of the text-as-hierarchy, replacing it with a sensory environment in which the audience cannot maintain critical distance. The response analyses how specific elements (soundscape density, spatial immersion, non-verbal movement, extreme lighting) each serve this intention. The distinction between surface effect (the audience is overwhelmed) and deeper purpose (the audience is woken, made fully present) is clearly made. Artaud's influence on subsequent practice may be referenced.

Secure (7-9): Artaud's intentions are clearly explained with reference to total theatre and audience immersion. At least two elements of total theatre are analysed. Effect on audience is articulated beyond surface description.

Developing (4-6): The response focuses on what Artaud's techniques do (shock, disturb) without fully analysing why or connecting to his deeper philosophical purpose.

Emerging (1-3): Basic description of Artaud's work with limited analysis of intention or audience effect.

practice_questions.text: You are directing an Artaudian production in which the audience is surrounded by the action in a promenade configuration. Explain how you would use performer movement, soundscape, lighting and set design to stage a scene in which characters are overwhelmed by an invisible but all-encompassing force. Refer to specific staging choices and explain the effect you intend on the audience at each stage of the scene.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (17-20): The response demonstrates sustained, detailed application of Artaudian principles across all four staging disciplines. Promenade configuration is justified (audience surrounded, cannot maintain safe distance; performers move through and around them). Performer movement begins with a ritual pattern — slow, deliberate, bodies at full extension — before fragmenting into increasingly urgent, physical sequences as the invisible force intensifies. Tableau is used at the climax: all performers simultaneously freeze in positions of strain or submission, held for an uncomfortable duration. Soundscape builds from a barely audible sub-bass drone to a multi-layered wall of processed sound, then cuts to silence at the tableau. Lighting uses moving lights that sweep the space and the audience, floor-rigged birdies creating upward shadows, a strobe at the peak of intensity, and a slow fade to a single tight lighting special on one performer at the end. Set design is minimal — no representational furniture; the floor is textured (sand, a different surface from the surrounding space) to create a defined ritual space. Costume is abstract (wrapped cloth, no contemporary clothing) to remove naturalistic context. Every choice is connected to Artaudian total theatre: the experience is the meaning.

Secure (13-16): All four disciplines are addressed with specific choices. Promenade configuration is used. Performer movement includes tableau and non-naturalistic sequences. Effect on audience is explained.

Developing (8-12): Relevant Artaudian ideas are applied but coverage of disciplines may be uneven. Movement may be naturalistically conceived. Effect on audience is noted but not deeply explored.

Emerging (1-7): Some knowledge of Artaud is shown. Design choices are vague or generic. Limited coherent staging strategy.

practice_questions.text: Name one theatrical device Russell uses to communicate the theme of fate in Blood Brothers.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for any one of: the Narrator / circular structure / the shoes-on-the-table superstition / the prologue tableau / the Narrator's recurring warnings.

practice_questions.text: What is meant by the term 'blocking' in theatre?
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying blocking as the arrangement of performers on stage; 1 mark for explaining that it shapes focus, meaning and the relationship between characters in performance.

practice_questions.text: Explain how a set designer might communicate the class divide between the Johnstone and Lyons households through the use of stage space and levels.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks: describing a specific use of space for the Johnstone household (e.g. bare, crowded, limited furniture, performers close together) (1); contrasting with a specific use of space for the Lyons household (e.g. more space, raised level, structured furniture) (1); naming a levels choice with effect (1); explaining what this spatial contrast communicates to the audience about the two families' social positions (1).

practice_questions.text: Analyse how Russell uses the nature-versus-nurture theme to make a political argument about class in Blood Brothers. What does Russell want the audience to understand about the role of social circumstances in shaping a life?
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks: identifying that Mickey and Edward share identical biology but different upbringings (1); explaining that the divergence of their lives is Russell's argument about nurture (1); analysing what Russell wants the audience to conclude (that the class system, not individual character, determines outcome) (1); anchoring to a specific named moment or design choice that makes this argument concrete (1).

practice_questions.text: Analyse Russell's intentions in presenting fate as something the audience knows about from the very start of Blood Brothers. How does Russell use structure, the Narrator and theatrical devices to create a sense of inevitable tragedy throughout the play?
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sustained analysis of Russell's use of circular structure, the Narrator's role and the superstition device as interlocking theatrical arguments about fate. Explains that Russell's intention is not simply to create suspense but to implicate the audience in the watching of an unjust system. Discusses how the Narrator's commentary prevents emotional escape (Brechtian alienation). References at least two specific moments and explains the intended audience effect of each. Reaches a substantiated conclusion about what Russell wants the audience to feel and think by the final tableau.

Secure: Clear identification of at least two structural or theatrical devices used to communicate fate. Good explanation of Russell's intentions. At least one named moment. Effect on audience addressed.

Developing: Relevant points but plot-led. Describes the circular structure or the Narrator rather than analysing why Russell made these choices. Effect on audience implied.

Emerging: Basic description of the ending or the Narrator's role. Little or no analysis of Russell's intentions.

practice_questions.text: As a director, discuss how you would stage the moment Mickey learns he has lost his job in Blood Brothers. In your answer, refer to performer choices (vocal and physical) and two design disciplines, explaining how each communicates the play's themes of class and fate to the audience.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Treats this moment as a pivot in the class-and-fate argument. Specifies performer choices (e.g. initial stillness and flat vocal delivery transitioning to heavy, slow movement; reduced eye contact and sunken posture). Names two design disciplines with concrete choices (e.g. lighting: shift from warm work-light wash to a cooler, narrowing state that isolates Mickey; sound: industrial soundscape cutting to silence or a minor-key underscore). Explains the effect of each choice on the audience and links to the themes of class and fate. Reaches a directorial judgement about the scene's purpose in the play as a whole.

Secure: Covers performer choices and two design disciplines with generally concrete ideas. Thematic link to class and/or fate made. Effect on audience addressed.

Developing: Some staging ideas but generic. Performer choices described in emotional terms without translating into specific vocal or physical detail. Design choices vague.

Emerging: Basic ideas. No named design detail. Little or no link to theme.

practice_questions.text: Name one of the invented vocabulary terms Blackman coined to describe the racial groups in Noughts and Crosses.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for any one of: Cross (the ruling Black group), nought (the second-class white group), or blanker (the slur for a nought). Accept any correctly identified invented term from the play.

practice_questions.text: Define the term 'non-diegetic sound' and give one example of how it is used in Noughts and Crosses.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for a correct definition (non-diegetic sound originates from outside the fictional world and is heard by the audience but not the characters); 1 mark for a relevant example from the play (e.g. news bulletins or broadcast voiceovers representing the state's voice intruding on the intimate story).

practice_questions.text: Analyse how a director might use levels and blocking in the school integration scenes to communicate the theme of segregation without dialogue.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks: identification of a blocking or level choice for the Cross students (e.g. elevated central positions) (1); contrasting choice for the nought students (e.g. lower level, edge of stage, physically isolated) (1); explanation of what this communicates to the audience about the hierarchy (1); link to a named staging configuration or a specific moment in the scene (1).

practice_questions.text: Explain how a sound designer might use non-diegetic sound to communicate the theme of state power in Noughts and Crosses. Refer to a specific sound choice and its effect on the audience.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks: identification of a specific non-diegetic sound (e.g. broadcast news bulletin as a state voiceover) (1); explanation of where and how it is delivered in the performance space (e.g. from high, wide offstage speakers to create a sense of ambient authority surrounding the stage) (1); explanation of the effect on the audience (e.g. makes the state feel inescapable, ever-present) (1); link to how this reinforces the theme of systemic power over the intimate story (1).

practice_questions.text: Analyse how Cooke uses the theme of love across enforced lines to communicate the personal cost of systemic racism to the audience. Refer to at least two moments in the play.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Argues that the relationship between Sephy and Callum is constructed as the play's emotional measure of what the system destroys; analyses how Cooke stages the arc of the relationship (from childhood ease, through the increasing danger of proximity, to the brief hope of the hostage scene, and the ultimate separation); connects each stage to staging choices (proxemics, lighting state, blocking) that make the cost physical and visible to the audience; references at least two named moments; reaches a judgement about what Cooke intends the audience to carry out of the theatre.

Secure: Identifies the relationship as central to the play's emotional argument; references at least two moments; explains at least one staging implication; reaches a general judgement.

Developing: Describes the relationship and what happens to it rather than analysing Cooke's intentions; staging references are generic or absent.

Emerging: Summarises the love story without addressing the playwright's purpose or the staging implications.

practice_questions.text: As a director staging the execution sequence in Noughts and Crosses, discuss how you would use staging configuration, lighting, sound and performer positioning to communicate the theme of state power and implicate the audience as witnesses. Refer to specific choices across at least two design disciplines.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Presents a coherent directorial concept for the execution sequence; specifies a staging configuration and justifies it in relation to audience implication (e.g. centre stage facing the house, or a thrust that places the audience close to the action); names specific lighting choices (e.g. a single overhead profile lantern, harsh white with no colour, creating a clinical spotlight on the executed performer; the rest of the stage in near-blackout); names specific sound choices (e.g. silence or a sustained low-frequency underscore building to silence at the moment of execution; crowd voiceover from speakers around the auditorium to make the audience feel inside the crowd); explains how performer positioning (levels, proxemics) reinforces the political argument; explains the effect of each choice on the audience and links to the play's themes; response is anchored to the specific moment rather than generalised.

Secure: Addresses the execution sequence with mostly concrete choices; at least one named lighting and one sound element; staging configuration is specified; effect on audience is explained.

Developing: Addresses the sequence in general terms; design choices are sometimes vague or generic; effect on audience is implied.

Emerging: Identifies the execution as important without specifying design choices or explaining audience effect.

practice_questions.text: Identify one type of lantern used in stage lighting.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for any one of: Fresnel / profile / flood / moving light / birdie / strobe. Accept any legitimate lantern type from theatrical practice.

practice_questions.text: What is meant by the term 'soundscape'?
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying that a soundscape is made up of multiple sound layers; 1 mark for explaining that the layers are combined to create an immersive sonic environment that establishes location, period or mood for the audience.

practice_questions.text: Explain how a lighting designer's use of a gobo can communicate meaning to the audience at a specific moment in a production.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks: 1 mark for accurately defining a gobo as a shaped template inside a lantern that projects a pattern of light; 1 mark for naming or describing a specific pattern (e.g. bar gobo suggesting imprisonment, leaf gobo suggesting a natural environment, window-frame gobo placing the action inside a building); 1 mark for explaining the effect on the audience's reading of the scene (e.g. the bars reinforce the theme of confinement visually even as the dialogue speaks of freedom); 1 mark for a developed evaluative statement or link to directorial intention.

practice_questions.text: In the live production you have seen, explain how one lighting choice and one sound choice worked together at a specific moment to create meaning for the audience.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (10-12): Identifies a specific moment in the production; names a precise lighting choice (lantern type, colour, direction, intensity or effect) and a precise sound choice (type, texture, placement, diegetic or non-diegetic status); analyses how the two choices worked in combination to create a specific audience effect; makes an analytical statement about what the director was trying to communicate through this design combination; language is technically fluent and uses accurate terminology throughout.
Secure (7-9): Both a lighting and a sound choice are named and explained with reasonable specificity; audience effect is identified; some analysis of intention present; mostly accurate terminology.
Developing (4-6): Lighting and sound choices identified but described generally; limited technical vocabulary; some attempt at effect or intention but not developed.
Emerging (1-3): General descriptions only; no technical vocabulary; no analysis of intention or audience effect.

practice_questions.text: Imagine you are a lighting designer working on a fictional production of a ghost story at a hypothetical studio theatre. In the scene where the protagonist first sees the ghost, design the lighting state you would use. Refer to specific lighting choices and explain their intended effect on the audience.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (7-8): Names at least two specific lighting elements (e.g. a cold profile special at steep angle from above stage right for the ghost; a Fresnel wash in a deep blue-green gel across the full stage; a bar gobo projected across the protagonist suggesting entrapment); each choice is justified with reference to its intended audience effect (e.g. the steep top-light creates deep shadows on the ghost's face that deny the audience a clear identity for the figure, creating unease); language is technically fluent.
Secure (5-6): At least two lighting choices named and justified; audience effect explained for at least one; generally specific but may have one general descriptor.
Developing (3-4): Relevant lighting ideas present but described in general terms (e.g. 'I would make the lighting dark and spooky'); limited technical vocabulary; effect mentioned but not developed.
Emerging (1-2): One or two general lighting ideas with no technical vocabulary and no link to audience effect or design intention.

practice_questions.text: Analyse and evaluate the live theatre production you have seen. In your answer, focus on how the design choices (in at least two design disciplines) communicated meaning to the audience. Reach a substantiated evaluative judgement about how successfully the design realised the directorial concept.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (25-32): Detailed, sustained analysis of at least two design disciplines; every design choice is named with technical specificity (lantern type, gobo, gel colour, fabric, soundscape texture); every choice is anchored to a named moment and linked to a stated audience effect; the response evaluates the overall success of the design in realising the directorial concept with substantiated judgement; fluent technical language throughout.
Secure (17-24): At least two design disciplines addressed with reasonable specificity; audience effect identified for most choices; an evaluative judgement present; some technical language.
Developing (9-16): Design choices identified but described generally; limited technical vocabulary; some attempt at audience effect; limited or absent evaluative judgement.
Emerging (1-8): Largely descriptive; one discipline only or very general across both; no technical vocabulary; no evaluative judgement.

practice_questions.text: Identify one technique a sound designer might use to physicalise the theme of time throughout Around the World in 80 Days.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for any clearly relevant technique, e.g.: a ticking clock soundscape / a metronome effect built into the underscore / a countdown rhythm that grows louder as the play progresses.

practice_questions.text: What is meant by 'soundscape' as a design technique?
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying that a soundscape is a layered composition of sounds; 1 mark for explaining that it creates atmosphere or sense of place, either built in real time or from recordings.

practice_questions.text: Analyse how a director might use a tableau at the moment of the date line revelation in the London ending to communicate the play's themes to the audience.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks: identification of tableau as a static visual image (1); explanation of how the stillness of a tableau contrasts with the play's physical energy, giving the moment weight (1); specific description of what the image might contain (e.g. the full ensemble frozen in the positions of their final characters, with Fogg at the centre, looking at the clock) (1); comment on how this communicates the themes of time and adventure to the audience (1).

practice_questions.text: Explain how a designer might use costume and soundscape to represent a non-European location in Around the World in 80 Days with cultural specificity rather than as a generic exotic backdrop. Refer to one specific design choice.
