practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks: identification of a specific design choice (e.g. a tabla rhythm and sitar melody in the soundscape for the Indian marketplace, or researched Indian costume fabrics for ensemble members) (1); explanation that this communicates the production's engagement with the real culture rather than a stereotype (1); explanation of how this affects the audience's reading of the scene (1); link to the colonial theme and the production's responsibility towards the cultures Fogg passes through (1).

practice_questions.text: Analyse how Eason and a production team might use staging and design to communicate the theme of time to the audience across the whole play, with particular attention to the play's final scenes.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: The response analyses the theme of time as central to Eason's structural and design intentions, explaining that the countdown is not just narrative information but the emotional engine of the audience's experience. The response analyses specific staging choices: the ticking clock soundscape growing in volume across the play, the mechanical precision of ensemble physical sequences, and the tonal pivot of the final scenes as specific design moments that serve the theme. The London ending is analysed as the culmination of the time theme: the apparent failure represents time run out; the date line revelation reverses this, suggesting that the Victorian mastery of industrial time is both triumphant and absurd. A blackout and return of light are discussed as the staging of this reversal. A substantiated judgement is made about how effectively the production communicates the theme.
Secure: Most points present; at least two staging or design choices discussed concretely; the final scenes are referenced; link to playwright's intention is generally clear.
Developing: Relevant observations about the theme but staging implications are generic or incomplete; the final scenes may not be discussed.
Emerging: Describes the theme without connecting it to specific staging or design choices.

practice_questions.text: You are directing Around the World in 80 Days. Discuss how you would use lighting, sound, costume and the ensemble's physical performance to stage a non-European location scene in a way that engages meaningfully with both the adventure genre and the play's colonial themes. Refer to specific design and performance choices.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: The response selects a specific scene (e.g. the Indian marketplace or the Yokohama acrobat sequence) and makes detailed choices across multiple theatrical elements. Lighting choices are named and justified (e.g. a warm amber wash with specific directional uplighting to suggest sunlight at a different latitude, contrasting with the cool grey of the English scenes). Sound design is specific (e.g. live tabla rhythm, a specific raga mode, ambient street sounds that ground the scene in a real cultural context). Costume choices for ensemble members are researched and particular (e.g. specific Indian garments rather than generic 'Eastern' costume). The ensemble's physical performance choices are described (e.g. a gestus for each character that communicates social function precisely — a merchant's expansive trading gesture, a servant's contained deference — rather than caricature). The response explicitly connects these choices to the colonial theme, explaining how they give the location a sense of genuine inhabited reality. Fogg's physicality and proximity within the scene are discussed. A directorial intention is clearly stated and the choices cohere into a unified vision.
Secure: At least three elements covered with concrete choices; the colonial theme is addressed; a directorial intention is present.
Developing: Some concrete choices are made; fewer than three elements covered; the colonial theme is mentioned but not addressed through specific staging choices.
Emerging: General ideas about staging without concrete choices; colonial theme not addressed.

practice_questions.text: Name one theme of Things I Know to Be True related to family relationships.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for any one of: conditional/unconditional love; family secrets; parental expectation; the distance between generations; what holds a family together.

practice_questions.text: What is meant by the term 'dramatic irony'?
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for a basic correct answer (e.g. when the audience knows something a character does not); 1 mark for development explaining how this creates tension or affects audience engagement (e.g. the audience's awareness of Bob's concealed secret makes every scene where he appears carry an additional layer of dramatic tension).

practice_questions.text: Analyse how Bovell uses the rose garden as a symbol to communicate the play's themes of concealment and truth.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks: identification of the garden as a symbol (1); explanation of what it represents (Bob's emotional life, the work required to maintain appearances) (1); reference to the garden's seasonal change and how it mirrors the structural arc (1); a specific staging or design observation about how the symbol can be made visible (e.g. bare winter stems, a single cut rose as a prop) (1).

practice_questions.text: Explain how a lighting designer could use changes in lighting state across the four seasons to communicate the play's themes of truth and concealment. Refer to specific lighting choices.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying a specific seasonal lighting quality (e.g. warm amber wash for spring / summer; cool, stripped-back state for winter); 1 mark for explaining how the change in lighting state tracks the emotional arc of the play; 1 mark for a specific technical choice (e.g. a cross-fade between states, a suddenly harsher profile lantern for the revelation moment); 1 mark for explaining the effect of that choice on the audience's understanding of the themes.

practice_questions.text: Analyse how Bovell uses the play's structure and dramatic methods to explore the theme of conditional and unconditional parental love. Consider what the playwright intends the audience to question about the Price family by the end of the play.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Detailed analysis of Bovell's intentions across the seasonal structure, with specific reference to how different revelations test parental love in different ways. The student explains what Bovell wants the audience to question (whether any love is truly unconditional; whether the family's stability was ever real), with reference to dramatic methods (the withholding of Bob's secret, the direct-address passages that create dramatic irony, the Frantic Assembly movement sequences as moments of emotional truth). No plot summary.

Secure: Identifies the key revelations and their relation to parental love; makes some analytical comment about Bovell's intentions; references at least one dramatic method. Mostly analytical.

Developing: Describes what happens across the seasons without sustained analysis of Bovell's intentions or the effect on the audience.

Emerging: Retells the plot with little thematic analysis.

practice_questions.text: As a director, explain how you would stage the moment when the family reunites after a revelation that has tested their bonds. Using proxemics, lighting and costume, show how your staging communicates whether the family's love is conditional or unconditional. Refer to specific named choices and their effects.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A specific staging vision for a named reunion or confrontation moment. Proxemics: precise distances and angles for each character, with justification (e.g. Bob remains at an upstage distance but Fran crosses to her child downstage centre, the gap between the parents communicating their different responses); lighting: named state change or quality (e.g. a cross-fade into a warmer shared wash as acceptance is communicated); costume: specific choice for each character that signals their emotional position (e.g. a parent's everyday domestic costume contrasting with the returning child's travel-worn appearance). Every choice anchored to the named moment with audience effect explained.

Secure: Most disciplines addressed; at least one named lighting choice and clear proxemics thinking; audience effect generally stated; one area may be somewhat generic.

Developing: Relevant ideas; descriptive rather than analytical; limited technical specificity.

Emerging: Basic list of staging ideas without design specificity or thematic justification.

practice_questions.text: Name the Brechtian technique in which a performer embodies a character's social position in a single crystallised gesture.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for: gestus.

practice_questions.text: What is meant by the term 'gestus' in the context of set-play performance?
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying gestus as a technique associated with Brecht; 1 mark for explaining that it is a physical gesture or attitude that makes a character's social position or social relationship visible to the audience.

practice_questions.text: Analyse how a designer might use set design to communicate the theme of class and poverty in A Taste of Honey without stating the theme explicitly.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks: identification of a specific set element that communicates poverty (1), explanation of how that element makes the class theme visible (1), identification of a second set element or prop as symbol that reinforces the theme (1), explanation of the cumulative effect on the audience's understanding of Jo and Helen's circumstances (1).

practice_questions.text: Explain how a director might use lighting to communicate the equality and warmth of Jo and the Boy's relationship in the canal scenes, in contrast to other relationships in the play.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks: identification of a specific lighting choice for the canal scenes that signals equality (1), explanation of how that lighting choice communicates warmth or tenderness (1), identification of a contrasting lighting state used elsewhere in the play (1), explanation of the contrast and its effect on the audience's understanding of the relationship's significance (1).

practice_questions.text: Analyse how Delaney uses the theme of motherhood and the structural irony of the play's ending to communicate her intentions about cycles of poverty and neglect. Refer to specific moments in the play.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Perceptive analysis of the structural irony in the ending (Jo at the same point Helen was when she had Jo); identifies that Delaney's intention is not to condemn Helen but to make an argument about social and economic cycles; discusses at least two specific structural moments (e.g. Helen's departure and return, the final tableau); explains the intended effect on the audience with precision; may include directorial or design insight.

Secure: Clear analysis of the motherhood theme with at least two moments referenced; understands Delaney's intention is an argument about cycles; generally accurate effect on audience.

Developing: Relevant points but mainly descriptive; identifies that Jo may repeat Helen's mistakes but does not develop this as an intentional structural argument; effect on audience vague.

Emerging: Basic description of Helen as a bad mother; little or no analysis of Delaney's structural intentions.

practice_questions.text: As a director staging A Taste of Honey, explain how you would use staging, lighting, sound and costume to communicate the themes of class, race and queer friendship to a contemporary audience. Refer to specific moments in the play.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: All four design areas addressed (lighting, sound, set/staging, costume) with specific, concrete choices for each; every choice anchored to a named moment (e.g. the canal scenes, Geof and Jo making a home, Peter's scenes in the flat); each choice clearly communicates a specific theme to the audience; shows awareness of historical context and how contemporary staging can honour it; all choices are specific (gel colours, fabric textures, sound cues named as diegetic or non-diegetic, set materials).

Secure: Three or more design areas covered; at least one named moment per area; generally concrete choices; themes clearly addressed; some engagement with historical context.

Developing: Two design areas covered; choices are relevant but generic; limited named moments; themes identified but not communicated with design precision.

Emerging: Basic listing of staging ideas with little thematic justification; no named moments; descriptive.

practice_questions.text: Name one theatrical technique a director could use in Act 3 to make mass hysteria physically visible to the audience.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for any one of: tableau (freezing the ensemble at a single signal), use of a soundscape that builds under the accusations, proxemic arrangement of the accusers as a unified group, ensemble movement that lacks individual distinction. Accept other valid staging responses.

practice_questions.text: What is meant by the term 'gestus'?
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying gestus as a term from Brecht's theatre practice referring to a combination of gesture and posture; 1 mark for development, e.g. noting that gestus reveals a character's social attitude or function in a single visible image, making it useful for showing how characters in The Crucible perform their institutional roles (e.g. Danforth turning to face the public gallery when pronouncing judgement, playing his authority to a crowd).

practice_questions.text: How might a lighting designer use contrasting lighting states to communicate the difference between the institutional world of the court and the private world of the Proctor household in The Crucible?
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks: 1 mark for a specific court lighting choice with named technical detail (e.g. a cold, blue-white wash using Fresnel lanterns providing flat, even coverage that flattens faces and removes shadow); 1 mark for the effect on audience (e.g. the light of official proceedings that judges and exposes, making the space feel inhuman and clinical); 1 mark for a specific domestic lighting choice with named technical detail (e.g. a warm amber side-light from a single profile lantern positioned at a low angle, creating shadow and warmth); 1 mark for linking the contrast to Miller's thematic intentions (the design makes the institutional world feel dehumanising and the private world feel human, visually encoding the play's argument about what the court destroys).

practice_questions.text: Analyse how Miller uses the theme of reputation to build dramatic tension in Act 4 of The Crucible. In your answer, refer to a specific staging moment.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks: 1 mark for identifying the central reputation conflict in Act 4 (Proctor must sign or refuse — his name will be either a public lie or a private truth); 1 mark for a specific moment (e.g. the moment the signed confession is presented to him, or the tearing of the paper); 1 mark for an analysis of how Miller uses this to build tension (e.g. the audience, knowing the truth, watches Proctor approach his decision in real time — the tension is produced by proximity to a choice we cannot make for him); 1 mark for a staging observation (e.g. a performer using long physical stillness before the tear so that the act of tearing becomes the release of accumulated tension, not an impulsive gesture).

practice_questions.text: How does Miller use the theme of conscience to communicate his intentions about individual integrity and the costs of living under an unjust authority? Refer to specific moments and the play's broader context.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: The response analyses Miller's use of conscience as both a personal and political theme. The candidate identifies the McCarthy parallel explicitly: Miller wrote this play while HUAC was demanding that Americans name their friends as communist sympathisers. Proctor's refusal to sign mirrors the real refusal to name names. The response anchors this to specific moments (the linen scene, where private conscience and public reputation are in conflict; the Act 4 confession scene, where the signed paper is both evidence and symbol). Staging implications are noted (e.g. the tearing scene's use of physical stillness and a narrowing lighting state to isolate Proctor at the moment of choice). Effect on audience is analysed (Miller wants the audience to feel both the nobility and the cost of Proctor's refusal, so that they leave the theatre understanding what is at stake when institutions demand public lies). Judgement is substantiated.

Secure: Identifies Miller's intentions around conscience; links to at least one specific moment; some reference to the McCarthy context; generally accurate analysis of audience effect.

Developing: Describes the events of Act 4 rather than analysing Miller's intentions; limited reference to context or audience effect.

Emerging: Basic summary with minimal analytical engagement; little or no reference to staging, context or Miller's purpose.

practice_questions.text: You are a director staging the play's final moments of Act 4: from the point where Proctor signs the confession to the moment he tears it up and the play ends. Using set, lighting, sound and performer choices, explain how you would communicate the themes of conscience and reputation to the audience in this sequence.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A sustained, coherent staging concept across all disciplines, anchored to the themes of conscience and reputation. Set is described specifically (e.g. a bare stone-flagged floor, a single table, two chairs — the prison stripped of everything except the paper on the table, which becomes the visual focus of the scene; perhaps a small high window letting in cold dawn light); lighting is specific and named (e.g. opening with a dim, cold Fresnel wash that flattens the cell; a gradual narrowing during the signing sequence until a single tight profile special falls on Proctor's hands as he signs; a held pause at the tear; then a slow fade to black after Elizabeth's final line, the stage light leaving as if the world itself is extinguishing); sound is named and purposeful (e.g. near-total silence; the faint sound of the congregation praying outside as a diegetic intrusion — the community Proctor is dying for — then silence at the tear, then a single tolling bell as the blackout completes); performer choices are precise (Proctor's slow, controlled movement throughout; absolute stillness from Hale and Danforth; Elizabeth not moving but holding eye contact with Proctor; the tear slow and quiet; the body held upright after it as a final physical statement); every choice is justified with reference to the themes. Substantiated directorial judgement.

Secure: All disciplines addressed with mostly concrete choices; both themes engaged; generally accurate effect on audience; some named technical detail.

Developing: Generic choices across most disciplines ('dim lighting', 'quiet music'); limited named technical detail; themes named but not developed in relation to staging choices.

Emerging: Basic list of ideas; one or more disciplines absent; themes mentioned but staging choices not connected to them.

practice_questions.text: Name one language other than English spoken in The Empress that signals the play's theme of identity.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for: Bengali OR Hindustani (either accepted).

practice_questions.text: What is meant by the term 'props as symbols' in theatre design?
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying that a prop is an object used on stage; 1 mark for explaining that when used symbolically its meaning exceeds its practical function, standing in for a theme, a character's history or an idea (accept equivalent explanation).

practice_questions.text: Explain how a lighting designer could use contrasting lighting states to make the theme of Empire visible in The Empress. Refer to specific lighting choices.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks: identification of a specific Windsor lighting choice (1) e.g. a deep amber or gold wash with directional warmth to signal Imperial wealth; identification of a contrasting East End lighting choice (1) e.g. a cooler white or blue-grey wash suggesting London weather and working-class austerity; explanation of how the contrast makes inequality immediately legible to the audience (1); link to the specific theme of Empire and its unequal distribution of comfort and privilege (1).

practice_questions.text: Analyse how Gupta uses blocking and proxemics in the court conspiracy scenes to communicate the theme of racial hierarchy without relying on dialogue.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks: identification of a specific blocking choice (1) e.g. the English court figures arranged in a closed circle from which Abdul is spatially excluded; explanation of how this spatial exclusion communicates racial hierarchy without dialogue (1); analysis of the contrast when Abdul enters Victoria's private space with more open blocking (1); link to the theme of racial hierarchy as something enforced through physical social arrangements, not just spoken prejudice (1).

practice_questions.text: Analyse Gupta's intentions in using bilingual exchanges between Abdul and Victoria in the Hindustani lesson scenes. What does she want the audience to understand about language, power and identity at these moments?
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (10–12): Detailed analysis of Gupta's multiple intentions: to dramatise a genuine crossing of cultural barriers (Victoria choosing to learn Hindustani signals personal respect that transgresses Imperial norms); to make the audience feel the political charge of language as power (what does it mean that the Empress of India does not speak the language of India until a servant teaches her?); to reveal the court's hostility to Victoria's Indian connection as a form of racial policing. Candidate links each intention to a specific dramatic method (the scenes' intimate staging, the shift in tone from formal court English to the informality of a lesson, the sound of Hindustani on an English stage) and explains the audience effect. Substantiated judgement.

Secure (7–9): Two intentions clearly articulated with some reference to dramatic method; audience effect identified though not fully developed for both.

Developing (4–6): One intention identified with limited reference to how Gupta achieves it; audience effect implied.

Emerging (1–3): Describes what happens in the Hindustani lesson scene rather than analysing Gupta's purpose.

practice_questions.text: You are directing the scenes in The Empress set in the Ayahs' Home in Hackney, which show Rani building community with other stranded Indian women. How would you stage these scenes to communicate the theme of solidarity to the audience? Refer to set design, lighting, sound, costume and at least one performer's choices.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (17–20): Specific, justified choices across all five areas. Set design: a configuration that places the performers in a community arrangement (circle or modified thrust) using domestic objects from India as props-as-symbols (worn sari cloth, cooking vessels, a child's toy). Lighting: a warm Fresnel wash in amber distinguishable from the Windsor gold by its lower intensity and informality, suggesting lamplight rather than opulence. Sound: Hindustani or Bengali song as underscore, transitioning to live voice when the community sings together, the acoustic shift from amplified to live marking a move from isolation to belonging. Costume: the worn, travel-stained garments of the ayahs carrying both the beauty of their Indian fabrics and the signs of a long journey. Performer (Rani): the specific physical unclenching of her body as she enters the community — hands opening, breath deepening, posture widening from the contracted docks silhouette — and the vocal shift from guarded English register to free Bengali. All choices justified with reference to the solidarity theme and the intended audience effect.

Secure (11–16): Most design areas covered with concrete choices; at least one named performer choice; effect on audience identified.

Developing (6–10): Some relevant ideas but generic; limited justification; one or more areas missing.

Emerging (1–5): Basic listing; no named performer choices; descriptive.

practice_questions.text: Name the director who led Theatre Workshop and premiered A Taste of Honey in 1958.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for: Joan Littlewood.

practice_questions.text: What is meant by the term 'diegetic sound' in theatre design?
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying that diegetic sound exists within the world of the play; 1 mark for explaining that characters can hear it as well as the audience, as opposed to non-diegetic sound such as underscore that only the audience hears.

practice_questions.text: Explain how a sound designer might use diegetic sound to locate A Taste of Honey in its specific 1958 Salford context.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks: identification of a specific diegetic sound from the Salford context (1), explanation of how it anchors the play in its specific location rather than a generic setting (1), identification of a second sound detail or the use of off-stage diegetic sound (1), explanation of the cumulative effect on the audience's understanding of the play's world (1).

practice_questions.text: Analyse how the collaborative devised origins of A Taste of Honey — the contribution of Theatre Workshop alongside Delaney's script — shape the play's hybrid form.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks: identification of at least one specific feature of the play attributed to Theatre Workshop rather than Delaney alone (1), explanation of how this feature creates a hybrid between naturalism and Brechtian presentation (1), identification of a second feature that contributes to this hybrid form (1), explanation of the combined effect on the audience's experience of the play (1).

practice_questions.text: Analyse how Delaney uses the specific social context of 1958 Salford to communicate her intentions about working-class women's lives to the audience. Refer to specific moments and design possibilities in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Perceptive analysis of at least two specific contextual details (post-war poverty, Salford's distinct identity, the Lord Chamberlain's censorship, the Notting Hill riots) and how they shape Delaney's intentions; connects context to specific staging possibilities (set design details, costume, diegetic sound); analyses what Delaney wants the audience to understand about working-class women's lives; may discuss Theatre Workshop's collaborative contribution.

Secure: Clear analysis with at least two contextual details; connects context to staging or intentions; generally accurate effect on audience.

Developing: Relevant context noted but mainly descriptive; limited connection to staging or intentions; effect on audience implied not stated.

Emerging: Basic facts about the play's context without analysis of Delaney's intentions.

practice_questions.text: As a designer working on a contemporary production of A Taste of Honey, explain how you would use set design, costume and sound to communicate the specific social, economic and theatrical context of 1958 Salford to a contemporary audience. Refer to specific moments in the play.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: All three design disciplines addressed with concrete, historically specific choices; set choices draw on specific 1958 Salford detail (named materials, levels, damp-staining, practical window); costume choices reference period utility fashion with specific fabric or colour detail; sound design includes named diegetic sound cues and their effect; each choice is anchored to a named moment; shows clear directorial intention connecting context to audience experience; engages with the Brechtian-naturalistic hybrid form.

Secure: All three areas covered; at least one named moment per discipline; generally concrete choices; context clearly referenced; effect on audience identified.

Developing: Two design areas covered; some historical specificity but partly generic; limited named moments; context referenced but not analysed.

Emerging: Basic listing of set, costume and sound ideas; minimal historical specificity; no named moments; descriptive.

practice_questions.text: In which year did Things I Know to Be True receive its world premiere?
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for: 2016.

practice_questions.text: What is meant by the term 'physical theatre'?
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for a basic correct answer (e.g. a style of theatre in which physical movement and the body are central to performance); 1 mark for development (e.g. physical theatre often integrates devised movement, contact work and gesture with or instead of spoken text, as seen in Frantic Assembly's chair duets and partner lifts).

practice_questions.text: Explain how the contemporary Adelaide setting shapes the play's themes and how a set designer might communicate this setting on stage. Refer to specific design choices.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying the Adelaide setting as suburban, middle-class and contemporary; 1 mark for explaining how this setting creates expectations that the revelations then undercut; 1 mark for a specific set design choice (e.g. rose bushes, warm earth-coloured floor cloth, kitchen visible through gauze partition); 1 mark for explaining the effect of that choice on the audience's understanding of the play's context.

practice_questions.text: Analyse how the co-development with Frantic Assembly shapes the form and style of Things I Know to Be True. What does the integration of physical theatre sequences mean for a performer preparing the role?
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks: identification of the hybrid form (naturalistic dialogue + Frantic Assembly movement) (1); explanation that the movement sequences are structural, not optional (1); specific reference to Frantic Assembly's vocabulary (chair duets, contact lifts, round-by-through-under) (1); analysis of what this means for a performer (must be trained in both Stanislavskian interior work and physical theatre technique, must be able to shift between modes) (1).

practice_questions.text: Analyse how Bovell's theatrical context — the co-development with Frantic Assembly and the contemporary Australian setting — shapes the meaning a 21st-century audience derives from the play. Consider how the playwright uses the collision between naturalism and physical theatre to communicate his intentions.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Detailed analysis of how the Frantic Assembly co-development shapes the play's form at a structural level: the hybrid form means that Bovell can communicate family dynamics naturalistically in dialogue while using movement to access emotional depths the dialogue cannot reach. The student analyses what this collision of styles does for the audience: the interruption of naturalism by physical theatre creates moments of heightened intensity. Reference to the Adelaide setting as a context that is both specific and universal. The student analyses Bovell's intentions (to tell a recognisably human story about family that crosses cultural contexts, using movement as an additional expressive language).

Secure: Identifies the hybrid form and the Adelaide setting; makes some analytical comment about Bovell's intentions; references at least one aspect of Frantic Assembly's practice. Mostly analytical rather than descriptive.

Developing: Describes the Frantic Assembly involvement and the setting without sustained analysis of what this means for the play's meaning or audience effect.

Emerging: Basic factual points about Bovell or Frantic Assembly with little analytical development.

practice_questions.text: As a designer working on a production of Things I Know to Be True, explain how you would design the set and costume to communicate the play's contemporary Australian suburban context. For the Frantic Assembly movement sequences, explain how your set design would accommodate the physical demands of the sequences. Refer to specific choices and their effects.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Set: specific design choices for the garden and kitchen (e.g. a warm earth-tone floor cloth, three rose bushes planted in stage-right garden area, a kitchen unit with practical work surface on stage left, gauze partition between the two spaces that can be lit differently to suggest interior/exterior); explanation of how the garden changes across the seasons (progressive stripping back of foliage). Costume: specific choices for each character (e.g. Bob in worn, practical gardening clothes in muted olive/tan tones; Fran in a nurse's uniform for some scenes, domestic but precise clothing otherwise; each child in clothing that signals their distance from home). Physical theatre accommodation: a clear, open upstage space for the movement sequences, without set furniture that would obstruct contact work; explanation of how lighting changes between the naturalistic scenes (warmer, more directional) and the movement sequences (a broader, more even wash, or a stark spot on the couple in a chair duet). Every choice anchored to a named design intention and audience effect.

Secure: Most areas covered; at least one named costume choice and one named set choice with justification; movement sequence space acknowledged; audience effect addressed.

Developing: Relevant ideas; descriptive without full specificity; movement sequences mentioned but not addressed in design terms.

Emerging: Basic list of design ideas without justification or reference to Frantic Assembly's physical demands.

practice_questions.text: Name the author of the 1562 narrative poem that Shakespeare used as his primary source for Romeo and Juliet.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for: Arthur Brooke.

practice_questions.text: What is meant by the term 'fourth wall' in theatre?
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying the fourth wall as the imaginary boundary between the stage and the audience; 1 mark for explaining what 'breaking the fourth wall' means (performers acknowledge or address the audience directly, as if removing the barrier).

practice_questions.text: Explain how a designer might use a lighting wash to communicate the Elizabethan shared-light convention to a modern audience and its effect on their experience of the play.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks: identifying the specific lighting choice (a wash that covers stage and part of the auditorium) (1), explaining how this connects to the Elizabethan context (shared light, no fourth wall) (1), describing the effect on the audience (they feel implicated in the world of Verona) (1), linking the choice to a specific moment of the play where direct address is enhanced (1).

practice_questions.text: As a lighting designer, explain how you would design the lighting for the scene in Act Three where Lord Capulet confronts Juliet in her bedroom. Refer to specific lighting choices and their contextual justification.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: the student specifies at least two distinct lighting choices for the scene, naming lantern types, directions, colours and intensities; the choices are justified with reference to Elizabethan patriarchal context (Capulet’s authority being institutionally supported) and to character (Juliet in softer, warmer light to communicate vulnerability; Capulet in harsh top-light to communicate institutional power); the contrast between lighting states is described; effect on the audience is named.

Secure: the student makes concrete lighting choices, names at least one lantern direction or colour, and links the choices to the context and character with some justification; effect on audience present.

Developing: the student suggests lighting changes but in generic terms (dark, threatening lighting; warm romantic lighting for Juliet); contextual reference present but not linked to staging consequence.

Emerging: the student describes mood without naming specific lighting elements; descriptive rather than analytical.

practice_questions.text: Analyse how Shakespeare uses the Elizabethan convention of soliloquy to communicate his intentions about Juliet's isolation and agency. Refer to at least two moments in the play.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: the student analyses how soliloquy in the Elizabethan shared-light context is not just a literary device but a staging one (the audience is directly addressed, implicated in Juliet’s decision-making); they name two specific soliloquy moments (the balcony scene’s extended musings; the potion soliloquy in Act Four) and explain what Shakespeare intends the audience to understand about Juliet’s isolation and agency; the analysis connects Elizabethan convention to modern staging choices; judgement sustained.

Secure: the student identifies soliloquy’s function, names two moments, explains the audience’s response to Juliet’s isolation; contextual link to Elizabethan staging may be present.

Developing: the student describes what happens in soliloquy scenes without analysing Shakespeare’s intentions; context mentioned but not connected to staging.

Emerging: the student describes the scenes without analysis; minimal awareness of Shakespeare’s intentions or the audience’s experience.

practice_questions.text: You are directing a production of Romeo and Juliet in a thrust stage configuration, drawing on the Elizabethan shared-light convention. Discuss how you would use set design, staging configuration, performer choices and sound to communicate the world of Verona and the tragedy of the feud to the audience. Refer to specific staging decisions throughout.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: the student designs a coherent production in a named thrust configuration, making specific choices about set design (e.g. minimal furniture representing both Montague and Capulet spaces through symbolic props rather than elaborate builds), staging configuration (the thrust bringing the audience into Verona’s streets), performer choices (direct address to the audience for soliloquies, using the audience proximity established by the thrust), and sound (a diegetic city soundscape that surrounds the audience, building the world of Verona beyond the stage edges); every choice is justified with reference to Elizabethan context and audience effect; a directorial throughline is evident; contextual knowledge is applied rather than listed.

Secure: the student makes concrete choices across most disciplines, links them to context and audience effect; some disciplines may lack full development.

Developing: the student mentions thrust staging and some design ideas but does not fully justify choices with contextual reasoning; context described rather than applied.

Emerging: the student lists staging ideas without contextual connection; descriptive rather than analytical.

practice_questions.text: In which year did The Crucible premiere on Broadway?
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for: 1953.

practice_questions.text: What is meant by 'allegory' in the context of The Crucible?
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for defining allegory as a work in which the literal story is designed to be read as a parallel to a different situation; 1 mark for development, e.g. noting that in The Crucible the literal story of Salem 1692 is a parallel for McCarthyite America 1953, with Miller using the historical distance to help audiences recognise the pattern of unjust accusation without defending the contemporary version.

practice_questions.text: Explain how a set designer could use the choice between a historically specific colonial interior and an abstract, timeless set to communicate different readings of The Crucible's allegorical purpose.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks: 1 mark for describing the historically specific choice with a concrete element (e.g. rough wooden beams, clay floors, period furniture that grounds the audience in 1692); 1 mark for the effect on the audience (e.g. the specific material reality of 17th-century New England makes the suffering concrete but risks encouraging historical distance — 'this is their problem, not ours'); 1 mark for describing the abstract choice with a concrete element (e.g. a bare stage with a single raised platform for the court and a back wall of bare stone that reads as any institution of power); 1 mark for the contrasting effect (e.g. the abstract design allows the allegory to resonate across time — the audience cannot dismiss it as historical — and directly communicates Miller's intention that the pattern is universal).

practice_questions.text: How does the Puritan belief in collective moral responsibility help explain why the Salem community believed the witch trials were justified? Refer to the historical and social context.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks: 1 mark for explaining the core Puritan belief (the community's prosperity depends on the moral purity of all its members — one sinner endangers the whole); 1 mark for how this makes private behaviour a legitimate public concern (if a neighbour sins, the community is at risk, so surveillance is theologically justified); 1 mark for connecting this to how the trials operated (accusation without reliable evidence is possible because the fear is genuine, not merely cynical); 1 mark for linking this to Miller's dramaturgical purpose (by making the logic coherent from within the community's own beliefs, Miller shows the audience how institutional injustice does not require obvious malice — it only requires a sufficiently frightened community).

practice_questions.text: How does Miller use the parallel between Salem 1692 and McCarthyite America to communicate his intentions about the relationship between institutional power and individual conscience? Refer to specific aspects of the play's context.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: The response analyses the allegorical structure precisely: Salem 1692 is the literal story; HUAC 1950-54 is the intended parallel. The candidate identifies specific structural parallels (accusation without reliable evidence; the demand to name names; blacklisting as social death vs hanging as literal death; the rewarding of confession and naming over refusal and silence). Miller's personal position is noted (his own HUAC subpoena in 1956, his refusal to name names, his identification with Proctor). The response analyses what Miller wants the audience to understand — not just that McCarthyism was unjust, but that the same machinery of fear can operate in any society that prioritises institutional self-preservation over individual due process. Staging implications are noted (e.g. how abstract staging choices let the allegory breathe across time). Judgement is substantiated and shows understanding of the play as a political act.

Secure: Identifies the Salem-McCarthy parallel accurately; notes Miller's own position; analyses at least two specific structural parallels; some reference to audience effect; limited staging reference.

Developing: Describes the historical context without analysing Miller's allegorical purpose; limited connection between the two timescales; audience effect asserted rather than developed.

Emerging: Basic description of one historical context with minimal analytical engagement; allegory not addressed.

practice_questions.text: You are a director making a production of The Crucible for a contemporary audience. Discuss how you would use performer-audience configuration, set and costume to communicate the play's allegorical purpose — that the pattern of unjust accusation belongs to every age, not only to 1692 Salem.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: The response offers a coherent directorial concept that prioritises the allegorical over the historically specific. Performer-audience configuration is argued and justified (e.g. in the round — the audience is surrounded by and implicated in the community; or a thrust stage that pushes the court scene into the audience's space, making them uncomfortable observers; the choice is explicitly argued, not merely stated); set design is specific and abstract (e.g. a bare raised platform for the court that could be any century's dock; a single wooden table for the domestic scenes; the set stripped of period ornament so that its austerity resonates universally; perhaps a back wall that begins as rough stone and is progressively lit to suggest different institutional spaces — courtroom, committee room, prison); costume is specific and argued (e.g. court officials in severe monochrome that deliberately avoids period specificity — the black is contemporary bureaucracy as much as Puritan severity; the accused in undyed, rough natural fabrics that give them warmth and individuality against the officials' uniformity; Tituba's costume in warmer earth tones that mark her as doubly marginalised — the first accused because she is the easiest to sacrifice); every choice is justified with reference to the allegorical purpose; substantiated directorial judgement about what the audience should understand and feel as they leave the theatre.

Secure: All three disciplines addressed with mostly concrete choices; allegorical purpose engaged; performer-audience configuration chosen and defended; generally accurate effect on audience.

Developing: Ideas present but generic; limited named technical detail; allegorical purpose mentioned but staging choices not fully connected to it.

Emerging: Basic list of ideas; one or more disciplines absent; historical context described but allegorical staging not addressed.

practice_questions.text: Name one vocal skill a performer might use to communicate a character's nervousness.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for any of: raised pitch; rapid pace; a stammer or fragmented phrasing; reduced volume (quieter delivery); a prolonged pause before answering; a tremor in the voice.

practice_questions.text: What is meant by 'projection' as a vocal skill?
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying that projection is the ability to carry the voice so it is heard clearly by the audience; 1 mark for clarifying that projection is not simply loudness but involves breath support, resonance and forward placement of the voice to reach the back of the auditorium.

practice_questions.text: Explain how a performer might use stillness and pace to communicate a character's shock at hearing unexpected news.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks: 1 mark for correctly identifying stillness as a deliberate physical choice (absence of movement at a moment of intensity); 1 mark for explaining how stillness signals shock to the audience (the sudden stop draws focus and signals something of significance); 1 mark for identifying pace as a vocal choice (slowing to almost nothing, or an abrupt stop); 1 mark for explaining the combined effect on the audience (the audience reads the performer's frozen body and near-silent voice as the outward sign of an inner world that has been overturned).

practice_questions.text: As a performer playing a character who is trying to appear confident while concealing fear, explain in detail the vocal and physical choices you would make. Anchor your answer to a specific type of scene or moment.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: both vocal and physical choices are named with precise detail; vocal: e.g. a steady, lowered pitch and measured pace to project surface confidence, but a fractional rise in pitch on specific words that betray anxiety, and controlled breathing to prevent a tremor; physical: e.g. upright posture with shoulders deliberately set back, head held at eye level, but fingers interlaced behind the back or a hand pressed lightly against the thigh to manage micro-tremors invisible to the other character but visible to the audience; proxemics: standing in a fixed position rather than moving, because movement might betray instability; choices anchored to a specific moment type (e.g. a job interview, a confrontation with a parent, a public speech).

Secure: both vocal and physical choices present with some specificity; anchored to a moment; effect on audience generally described.

Developing: one category (vocal or physical) described with more detail than the other; limited specificity; effect on audience implied rather than stated.

Emerging: states emotion ('confident but scared') without translating into specific skill choices; no anchoring to a moment.

practice_questions.text: Analyse how a director might use performers' vocal and physical skills to communicate a theme of power and powerlessness in a key scene. Refer to at least two specific skills and their intended effect on the audience.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: the theme of power/powerlessness is the sustained lens throughout; at least two specific skills named for each end of the power relationship (e.g. the powerful character: slow, low-pitched deliberate speech; full-front posture with weight planted; minimal gesture; the powerless character: fragmented phrasing, rising pitch; curled posture; retreating proxemics moving away toward the edge of the stage); each choice is analysed for its intended effect on the audience's understanding of the theme (e.g. 'the contrast in posture makes the power differential immediately legible before either character speaks, positioning the audience as witness to a dynamic they recognise'); choices are connected to directorial intention.

Secure: theme identified; at least two skills discussed with some specificity; effect on audience described; directorial intention present.

Developing: relevant skills described but analysis of their thematic function is limited; audience effect implied.

Emerging: skills named without analysis; theme not sustained; audience effect absent.

practice_questions.text: As a performer and a lighting designer working on the same climactic scene, explain how you would use performer skills and lighting design to communicate the scene's emotional turning point to the audience. Refer to specific choices from both disciplines.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: a clearly defined emotional turning point; specific, named performer choices (vocal: pitch, pace, pause with precise detail; physical: posture change, proxemics movement, gesture anchored to the turning point); specific, named lighting choices (lighting state, lantern type, colour, intensity, direction — all changing to reflect the turning point); the interaction between performance and lighting is discussed (e.g. 'the performer's physical stillness makes the slow cross-fade in lighting more visible — the change in the world around them mirrors the internal shift'); the combined effect on the audience is precisely stated.

Secure: turning point identified; at least two performer skills and two lighting choices with some specificity; effect on audience described; some discussion of how the disciplines interact.

Developing: one discipline stronger than the other; design or performance choices are general; turning point described rather than analysed; little discussion of discipline interaction.

Emerging: basic performance or design ideas; turning point not clearly defined; audience effect absent; no interaction between disciplines.

practice_questions.text: In which year was Queen Victoria formally declared Empress of India?
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for: 1876.

practice_questions.text: What is a gauze in theatre design?
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying that a gauze is a fabric or material stretched across a stage space; 1 mark for explaining that it can create translucent or dissolving effects when lit from behind, used for backdrops or to suggest depth and distance (accept equivalent explanation).

practice_questions.text: Explain how a set designer could use the collision of English missionary furnishings and Indian domestic objects in the Ayahs' Home scenes to communicate the theme of cultural displacement.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks: identification of a specific English furnishing element (1) e.g. plain wooden mission-hall chairs or a Christian print on the wall; identification of a contrasting Indian object (1) e.g. a sari cloth folded on a chair, a brass cooking vessel or a child's toy from India; explanation of the contrast's effect on the audience (1) the cultural in-between world is made visible before a word is spoken; link to the theme of displacement (1) the women cannot fully belong to either world, and the set embodies that liminality.

practice_questions.text: Analyse how Gupta uses the historical erasure of Abdul Karim's papers after Victoria's death as dramatic material. What staging choices could make this moment of erasure powerful for the audience?
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks: identification of the historical fact (Abdul's papers were burned by the royal household after Victoria's death in 1901) (1); identification of a specific staging choice for this moment (1) e.g. a slow fade to black on the Windsor set space while the rest of the stage remains lit; analysis of how this design choice makes historical destruction physically visible (1); link to Gupta's broader purpose: that the play itself is the recovery of a story that was deliberately destroyed (1).

practice_questions.text: Analyse Gupta's intentions in choosing to set The Empress in 1887 — the year of the Golden Jubilee — and in staging the public spectacle of Empire alongside the private abandonment of Rani at the docks. What does she want the audience to think and feel about Victorian Britain?
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (10–12): Detailed analysis of at least three distinct intentions, each linked to a specific dramatic method: the Jubilee as ironic framing (Gupta wants the audience to feel the gap between official Imperial celebration and individual human cost); the choice to place Rani's abandonment in the same year as Abdul's arrival (the two characters are simultaneously products of the same Imperial system, one ascending and one discarded); the use of real institutions (the Ayahs' Home, the Lascar community) to give the play historical authority and make the audience feel they are being shown something true, not invented. Each intention linked to specific staging/dialogue/structural method and the intended audience effect. Substantiated judgement.

Secure (7–9): Two intentions clearly articulated with some reference to dramatic method and audience effect.

Developing (4–6): One intention identified; limited reference to method; audience effect implied.

Emerging (1–3): Describes the historical setting rather than analysing Gupta's dramaturgical purpose.

practice_questions.text: You are designing the production of The Empress for a large proscenium arch theatre. How would you use set design, lighting, sound and costume to communicate the contrast between the Golden Jubilee world of Windsor and the hidden world of the Lascar community and the Ayahs' Home to the audience? Refer to specific design choices for both worlds.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (17–20): Specific, justified choices across all four design disciplines applied to both worlds, with clear contrast between them. Windsor set design: raised levels, heavy drape or gauze backcloth in crimson and gold, a formal chair or dais for Victoria, sightlines that place the court in a hierarchy legible from every seat. Lascar/Ayahs' Home set design: lower, warmer space at stage level, maritime and domestic objects as props-as-symbols, no raised platform. Windsor lighting: deep gold and amber wash with a profile lantern special on Victoria's seat; profile lanterns for the court to create a sense of official illumination. East End lighting: warm low-level Fresnel wash, no specials, the suggestion of lamplight rather than stage light. Windsor sound: minimal, perhaps a formal orchestral underscore hinting at Victorian ceremony. East End sound: a diegetic soundscape with Bengali or Hindustani song from within the scene. Windsor costume: deep crimson and gilt for Victoria, black formal English tailoring for the court, Abdul's court livery marking him as different. Ayahs' Home costume: worn sari fabrics in blues and greens, suggesting the beauty of original garments after a long journey. All choices justified with reference to the historical context and the intended audience effect. Substantiated directorial judgement about how the contrast communicates the play's argument.

Secure (11–16): Most design areas covered for both worlds with concrete choices; contrast between the two worlds clearly established; effect on audience identified.

Developing (6–10): Some relevant choices but one or more areas missing or generic; contrast between worlds present but underdeveloped.

Emerging (1–5): Basic listing of choices with minimal justification; little sense of the designed contrast between worlds.

practice_questions.text: In which city was Blood Brothers first performed in 1983?
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for: Liverpool / Liverpool Playhouse.

practice_questions.text: What is meant by 'deindustrialisation' in the context of Blood Brothers?
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying deindustrialisation as the closure or decline of factories, docks and industrial employers; 1 mark for explaining that in Liverpool this process caused mass unemployment in the 1970s and 1980s, which forms the economic backdrop to Mickey's job loss and imprisonment in Act Two.

practice_questions.text: Explain how a costume designer might use period-specific clothing to communicate the historical context of Blood Brothers and its relevance to the class divide theme.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks: naming a specific period costume choice for the Johnstone family (e.g. faded cotton, shell suit, worn trainers) with a link to the economic context (1); naming a contrasting period costume for the Lyons family (e.g. structured wool, well-cut professional clothes) (1); explaining what this costume contrast communicates to the audience about class and opportunity (1); linking the period-specific choices to the play's social argument about deindustrialisation or Thatcher-era inequality (1).

practice_questions.text: Analyse how Russell uses his own working-class background and the historical context of 1980s Liverpool to shape the argument of Blood Brothers. What does this context reveal about Russell's theatrical intentions?
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks: identifying Russell's Merseyside, working-class background and career path (1); explaining how his background gives him insight into Mickey's world that a middle-class playwright might not have (1); linking the historical context of deindustrialisation and Thatcher-era unemployment to specific plot events (1); analysing Russell's theatrical intention to argue that social injustice, not personal failure, shapes lives (1).

practice_questions.text: Analyse Russell's intentions in setting Blood Brothers in Liverpool during the period of deindustrialisation. How does the historical context shape what Russell wants the audience to understand about class, opportunity and injustice?
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sustained analysis of how the Liverpool deindustrialisation context is not decoration but argument. Explains that Russell wants the audience to understand Mickey's fate as structurally caused — by unemployment, lack of opportunity and the Thatcher-era withdrawal of support from working-class communities — not as personal weakness. Discusses how Russell uses Edward's contrasting trajectory to make this argument precise: same biology, different social infrastructure, different outcome. References at least two specific named moments or design contexts and analyses the intended audience effect. Reaches a substantiated judgement about Russell's social and theatrical purpose.

Secure: Clear identification of the historical context and Russell's political intention. Good explanation of how context shapes character arcs. At least one named moment. Audience effect addressed.

Developing: Context described rather than analysed. Some link to Mickey's fate made but the political intention is not clearly articulated. Mostly descriptive.

Emerging: Basic facts about Liverpool or Thatcher with little or no analysis of Russell's theatrical intentions.

practice_questions.text: As a director, discuss how you would use set design, costume and lighting to communicate the historical context of 1980s Liverpool in Blood Brothers. In your answer, explain how these design choices would help a contemporary audience understand the social and political forces shaping the characters' lives.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Coherent directorial vision that treats the 1980s Liverpool context as an active argument rather than decoration. Set design: names a specific choice (e.g. a terraced-street platform that gradually acquires signs of economic decline — boarded-up windows, broken street lamps — across Act Two). Costume: names period-specific choices for Johnstone and Lyons families with contrasting fabric and condition, explaining the class argument embedded in each. Lighting: names a specific shift (e.g. warm tungsten domesticity in childhood scenes transitioning to cold, industrial fluorescent quality in the unemployment and prison scenes), linking colour temperature to the political climate. Explains the intended effect on a contemporary audience and reaches a directorial judgement about how the historical context serves Russell's social purpose.

Secure: Covers three design disciplines with generally concrete choices. Historical context linked to at least one design decision. Effect on contemporary audience addressed.

Developing: Some historical context mentioned but design choices are generic. Little named detail. The link between context and design choice is asserted rather than explained.

Emerging: Basic staging ideas with no named detail. Historical context barely referenced or only mentioned in passing.

before.exam_tip_html: For questions asking you to use context to inform staging choices, the examiner is looking for specificity: not “I would use 1980s costumes to show the period,” but “I would dress Mickey in a faded shell suit and worn trainers by Act Two to signal the economic decline of working-class Liverpool in the early 1980s, contrasting with Edward’s well-cut professional suit.” Context should be the reason for a design choice, not a label attached to it. For the 12-mark playwright’s intentions question on context, always explain what Russell wants the audience to understand about the society he is depicting, not just what that society was like. Use phrases such as: “Russell wants a contemporary audience to recognise that what happened to Mickey was not personal failure but structural injustice.”

practice_questions.text: In which year did the Pyongyang Declaration, acknowledging the North Korean abductions of Japanese citizens, take place?
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for: 2002.

practice_questions.text: What is meant by the term 'documentary theatre'?
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying documentary theatre as theatre rooted in factual events or testimonies; 1 mark for explaining that it draws on historical sources, interviews or documented evidence to create dramatic meaning.

practice_questions.text: Explain how a lighting designer could use colour temperature to communicate the contrast between Japan and North Korea in The Great Wave. Refer to specific design choices and their effect on the audience.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks: identification of contrasting colour temperatures for the two locations (1); a specific warm colour choice for Japan (e.g. amber, 3200K warm white Fresnel wash) (1); a specific cool or neutral colour choice for North Korea (e.g. cold blue gel, 5600K overhead profile) (1); explanation of the effect these contrasts create for the audience in terms of the geographic or political divide (1).

practice_questions.text: Analyse how Turnly's decision to root The Great Wave in the documented DPRK abduction programme shapes the audience's experience of the play. Refer to one specific staging or performance choice that draws on this context.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks: identification of the play's documentary roots (the real DPRK abductions, 1977-1983) (1); analysis of how audience knowledge of these events changes the theatrical experience (1); reference to a specific staging or performance choice, e.g. the minimal institutional set of the interrogation scenes, the precision of historical dates signalled through design (1); explanation of the effect this creates for the audience (1).

practice_questions.text: Analyse how Turnly uses the historical context of the DPRK abduction programme and the 2002 Pyongyang Declaration to communicate a political argument about the relationship between state power and individual life. Consider how a director might use staging to make this argument vivid for a contemporary audience.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Demonstrates specific knowledge of the historical context (abductions 1977-1983, Megumi Yokota, Pyongyang Declaration 2002); analyses Turnly's intention as using documented history to make an argument in the present tense about state accountability; discusses at least two concrete directorial choices that use historical context, e.g. the minimal institutional set signalling real bureaucratic systems, the sound design using diegetic North Korean propaganda music rooted in documented recordings, the staging of the Declaration scene as confirmation rather than resolution; explains the effect of each choice on a contemporary audience; reaches a substantiated judgement about what political argument the historical context allows Turnly to make. Secure: Demonstrates sound historical knowledge and links it to staging choices; generally concrete, at least one named moment, generally accurate audience effect. Developing: Describes the historical situation but does not connect it to specific staging choices; staging references are generic. Emerging: Brief mention of North Korea and Japan with little historical specificity or staging analysis.

practice_questions.text: As a director, discuss how you would stage the scene in which the Tanaka family learns of the Pyongyang Declaration. Consider how the staging should communicate both the significance of the official acknowledgement and the incompleteness of its resolution. Refer to lighting, sound, performer choices and proxemics.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: A full discussion of a specific, historicised staging of the Declaration scene. Lighting: the scene might begin in the domestic amber of the Japan sequences, then shift — at the moment of the announcement — to a cooler, more neutral state that neither celebrates nor mourns, held in an ambiguous middle register; this choice communicates that what the family has received is not a happy ending. Sound: the announcement might arrive via a radio (diegetic sound) whose volume is controlled by the performer; a soundscape that includes distant sea waves throughout the scene roots the moment in the play's controlling metaphor. Performer choices: Reiko receives the news with a controlled, quiet voice — a reduced volume that communicates shock rather than relief; her body stills completely, hands visible to the audience. Etsuko might move toward Reiko but stop at arm's length — a proxemic choice that communicates two people unable to fully comfort each other because what they have confirmed is not return, only evidence. Proxemics: the family arranged in a triangle downstage, facing toward the audience at an angle that gives the audience access to all three faces. Effect on audience: the staging communicates that confirmation is not reunion — the historical incompleteness is made emotionally immediate. Secure: Two or three strong choices, mostly concrete, at least one named design element, generally accurate effect. Developing: Aware of the emotional weight of the scene but staging is generic; limited historical specificity. Emerging: Describes what happens in the scene rather than analysing how it would be staged.

practice_questions.text: Give one word that describes language used to make a judgement about the effectiveness of a theatrical choice.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for any one of: evaluative / analytical / critical / judgement-based. Accept any precise term that accurately names language expressing a reasoned assessment of effectiveness.

practice_questions.text: What is meant by 'subtext' in the context of live theatre analysis?
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying that subtext is unstated meaning beneath the surface action; 1 mark for explaining that it is communicated through theatrical choices (performer, staging or design) rather than through explicit dialogue.

practice_questions.text: Explain how a director might use the positioning of a performer on stage after other performers have exited to communicate subtext to the audience.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks: 1 mark for identifying that the lingering performer attracts focus because they are the only figure on stage; 1 mark for explaining the staging choice (e.g. the performer remains centre stage, or moves to a specific position that carries symbolic weight in the production); 1 mark for the audience effect (e.g. the audience reads isolation, guilt, unresolved conflict or the weight of a decision on the character); 1 mark for a link to subtext, directorial concept or a broader theme of the production.

practice_questions.text: Analyse how one specific moment in the live production you have seen communicated a theme of the production to the audience. Refer to both a performer choice and a design choice in your answer.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks: 1 mark for identifying a named moment and a theme; 1 mark for naming a specific performer choice at that moment and briefly explaining how it communicated the theme; 1 mark for naming a specific design choice at that moment and briefly explaining how it communicated the theme; 1 mark for an analytical statement about how the two choices worked together or for an evaluative comment on the effectiveness of the communication.

practice_questions.text: Analyse how the director of the live production you have seen communicated the production's central theme to the audience. Refer to specific theatrical choices and their effect on the audience.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (10-12): Identifies a clear directorial concept or central theme; names at least two specific theatrical choices (from performance and/or design) that communicate this theme; analyses how each choice serves the directorial intention rather than just describing it; evaluates how successfully the theme was communicated overall with a substantiated judgement; technically fluent language throughout.
Secure (7-9): Directorial concept identified; at least two choices named and linked to theme; some evaluative language; generally specific but may be uneven in technical detail.
Developing (4-6): Relevant choices identified but analysis stays at surface level; theme identified but choices not clearly linked to it; limited technical vocabulary.
Emerging (1-3): Description of plot or general impressions; no identifiable directorial concept; no analysis of intention or audience effect.

practice_questions.text: Analyse and evaluate the live theatre production you have seen. In your answer, explain how the director communicated meaning through specific performer and design choices. Reach a substantiated evaluative judgement about how successfully the production communicated its central themes to the audience.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (25-32): Sustained analytical writing that moves consistently between description of specific choices and evaluation of their effect; at least two performer choices (one vocal, one physical) and at least two design choices (across at least two disciplines) are named with technical precision; each choice is anchored to a named moment; directorial concept is identified and choices are evaluated against it; a clear, substantiated evaluative judgement about overall success is reached, supported by specific evidence including audience response; technically fluent throughout.
Secure (17-24): Performer and design choices present and mostly specific; audience effect identified; some evaluation of directorial concept; a judgement reached though not always fully substantiated; technical vocabulary mostly accurate.
Developing (9-16): Relevant choices identified; some attempt at linking to audience effect or theme; evaluation attempted but often unsubstantiated opinion; limited technical vocabulary.
Emerging (1-8): Largely plot summary or description; no evaluative judgement; minimal technical vocabulary; choices listed without analysis.

practice_questions.text: In which year was Jules Verne's novel Around the World in 80 Days first published?
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for: 1872.

practice_questions.text: What is meant by 'physical theatre' as a theatrical tradition?
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying that physical theatre emphasises storytelling through physical movement, ensemble creation or imagination; 1 mark for explaining that it typically foregrounds the performer's body as the primary storytelling tool, often with minimal set and visible transformation.

practice_questions.text: Explain how the in-the-round staging configuration at the New Vic shapes the demands placed on the performers in Around the World in 80 Days.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks: identification that in-the-round means the audience surrounds the performance area on all sides (1); explanation that there is no 'upstage' as a place of exit or concealment and no wing space (1); a specific staging demand that follows from this (e.g. every physical transformation must be visible and legible from every angle; costume changes must be made in full view; blocking must constantly work from multiple directions) (1); explanation of how this connects to the play's physical-theatre ensemble form (1).

practice_questions.text: Analyse how knowledge of Verne's 1872 historical context might shape a director's choices for staging a non-European location in Around the World in 80 Days.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks: identification of the relevant historical context (Victorian colonial gaze; non-European locations presented as exotic backdrop in Verne's novel) (1); explanation that a modern director is aware this framing is now problematic (1); a specific staging or design choice that responds to this context (e.g. using researched costume elements to give characters cultural specificity; building a soundscape from authentic musical textures for each location) (1); explanation of how this choice communicates something different to a modern audience than Verne's original framing intended (1).

practice_questions.text: Analyse how the 2013 New Vic production of Eason’s adaptation uses the physical-theatre tradition to both celebrate Verne’s adventure story and create a production that a modern audience can engage with critically.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: The response analyses Eason's use of physical theatre (ensemble multi-roling, object transformation, visible storytelling) as a deliberate formal choice that serves two purposes simultaneously: it honours the adventure genre's energy and pace, keeping every episode kinetic and theatrical, while the visible construction of the world (performers explicitly becoming objects, locations and minor characters) invites the audience to watch the storytelling as storytelling rather than being absorbed unquestioningly into the colonial adventure narrative. The alienation effect created by visible transformation is connected to Brecht's tradition of making theatre's mechanics visible. The response analyses specific staging moments (e.g. the ensemble physically creating the steam engine) as both thrilling spectacle and implicit reminder that this is a constructed story. A judgment is made about whether Eason achieves both goals successfully.
Secure: The dual function of physical theatre is identified and mostly analysed; at least one specific staging moment referenced; the connection to both adventure and modern audience engagement is generally clear.
Developing: Physical theatre is described but its function in relation to the colonial theme is not analysed; the staging moment may be general rather than specific.
Emerging: Describes physical theatre without connecting it to Eason's intentions or the audience's critical engagement.

practice_questions.text: You are directing Around the World in 80 Days for a contemporary audience. Discuss how you would use staging configuration, physical theatre, lighting and costume to communicate both the Victorian context and a modern perspective on the story. Refer to specific design and performance choices in at least two scenes.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: The response makes clear directorial choices grounded in both historical contexts. For the Victorian context: costume choices (e.g. Fogg's fixed Victorian frock coat and pocket watch as the anchoring symbol of industrial time; Reform Club gentlemen in identical black with top hats, moving in synchronised tableau to communicate their conformity and social rigidity). For the modern perspective: physical-theatre choices that make the construction visible (e.g. the ensemble visibly preparing each location before Fogg arrives, signalling to the audience that the world is being made, not simply inhabited); in a specific non-European scene, researched costume elements and a culturally specific soundscape that give the location genuine texture. Lighting choices for both Victorian and non-European scenes are named (e.g. cool, sharp profile lantern for the Reform Club; a warmer, wider wash with more directional side-light for the Indian scenes to suggest a different quality of light without caricature). The in-the-round configuration is discussed with reference to sightlines and the impact on blocking. A unified directorial vision is clearly stated and sustained.
Secure: At least three elements covered with concrete choices; both historical contexts are referenced; two scenes addressed; a directorial intention is present.
Developing: Some concrete choices; fewer than three elements in detail; one or both historical contexts may not be addressed through specific staging choices.
Emerging: General ideas about staging and context without concrete choices or connection between the two.

practice_questions.text: In which year was Malorie Blackman's novel Noughts and Crosses first published?
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for: 2001.

practice_questions.text: Define the term 'Verfremdungseffekt' and explain how it applies to the staging of Noughts and Crosses.
