practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for a correct definition (Brecht's technique of making the familiar seem strange so the audience looks at it afresh rather than accepting it as natural; also called the alienation effect); 1 mark for a relevant application to the play (e.g. the racial reversal makes a recognisable hierarchy strange so the audience questions it rather than accepting it; the direct address and minimal staging maintain critical distance).

practice_questions.text: Explain how knowledge of the Macpherson Report (1999) might influence a set designer's choices for the state institutions — schools, courts, prison — in Noughts and Crosses.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks: identification of what the Macpherson Report found (institutional racism as a structural problem) (1); explanation of how this context justifies a design choice that makes the state's spaces feel imposing and institutional rather than individual (e.g. elevated platforms, rigid architectural lines, harsh institutional lighting, uniforms with status markings) (1); explanation of the effect on the audience (the state feels systemic and impersonal, reinforcing the play's political argument) (1); link to a specific named space or moment in the play (1).

practice_questions.text: Analyse how Cooke's choice to use speculative fiction — an alternate Britain with a reversed racial hierarchy — shapes what a contemporary audience understands about racial privilege.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks: identification of what speculative fiction allows (distance from any single historical event; audience does the work of translation) (1); explanation of how the reversal makes privilege visible (those at the top do not see the system as a system) (1); reference to how this connects to the Verfremdungseffekt — making the familiar strange (1); link to a staging implication (e.g. contemporary design references keeping the world recognisably close rather than fantasy-remote) (1).

practice_questions.text: Analyse how Cooke uses the historical and social context of the play to make the audience engage with questions about racial inequality in contemporary Britain. Refer to at least two specific contextual factors and at least one staging or design choice.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Identifies at least two specific contextual factors (Macpherson Report and institutional racism, US civil rights school segregation, apartheid South Africa, Black British theatre tradition) and connects each to a specific staging or design choice that makes the context legible in the production; analyses how Cooke uses the alternate world to create Brechtian distance while maintaining emotional engagement through the intimate scenes; discusses the dual role of the play as both a young adult story and a political intervention; reaches a judgement about what Cooke ultimately wants the audience to take away from the theatre.

Secure: Identifies at least two contexts; connects them to at least one staging choice; explains the intended audience response; reaches a general judgement.

Developing: Lists historical contexts without connecting them to staging or directorial choices; response is mostly background information rather than analysis of intention.

Emerging: Identifies one context with little analysis of how it shapes the play's theatrical meaning.

practice_questions.text: As a director staging Noughts and Crosses for a contemporary audience, discuss how you would use the play's speculative fiction setting to influence your design choices for costume, set and lighting. Refer to the historical and social contexts of the play and explain how your choices would communicate the themes of racial inequality and privilege to your audience.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Presents a coherent directorial concept that uses the alternate-world setting as a design principle rather than a fantasy backdrop; specifies costume choices that communicate Cross privilege and nought marginalisation through recognisable contemporary markers (tailored versus worn, institutional uniform versus individual) rather than a simple black/white binary; names specific set elements that make state institutions feel imposing (raised levels, rigid lines, institutional materials such as steel or concrete for Cross spaces; lower, warmer, more worn materials for nought spaces); names specific lighting choices (e.g. warm directional light for Cross domestic spaces, harsher institutional fluorescent quality for state buildings); connects each choice to at least one historical or social context; explains the effect of each choice on the audience's understanding of privilege and inequality; response covers at least two design disciplines in depth and is anchored to named moments of the play.

Secure: Addresses multiple design disciplines; choices are mostly concrete; at least one historical context is connected to at least one design decision; effect on audience is explained.

Developing: Design choices are sometimes vague; historical context is mentioned but not connected to specific creative decisions; effect on audience is implied rather than argued.

Emerging: Identifies some design ideas without connecting them to context or explaining effects; response is largely descriptive.

practice_questions.text: Name one physical theatre company that co-developed a GCSE Drama set play with the playwright.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for: Frantic Assembly (who co-developed Things I Know to Be True with Andrew Bovell).

practice_questions.text: What is meant by 'multi-roling' in physical theatre performance?
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying that multi-roling means a performer plays more than one role in a production; 1 mark for explaining that the shift between roles is signalled through physical, vocal or costume changes rather than requiring separate actors.

practice_questions.text: Explain how a Frantic Assembly chair duet communicates the emotional relationship between two characters to the audience.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks: 1 mark for identifying a chair duet as a physical theatre technique using chairs as props in a movement sequence; 1 mark for naming a specific physical quality of the technique (e.g. the proximity and movement of the two performers around the chairs, their weight and resistance); 1 mark for explaining how a specific physical quality communicates an emotional state (e.g. one performer circling the other while the other remains still communicates power imbalance or emotional withdrawal); 1 mark for explaining the effect on the audience (e.g. the audience reads the relationship through bodies rather than words, making the emotional state feel immediate and physical).

practice_questions.text: As a performer in a physical theatre production, explain how you would use physical theatre techniques — including at least one Frantic Assembly method — to stage the moment when a character realises they have lost someone they depended on. Refer to specific physical choices and explain their effect on the audience.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (7-8): The response identifies a named physical theatre technique (e.g. a lift in which the other performer's weight is suddenly absent; a chair duet that ends with the performer alone; a tableau in which the ensemble turns their backs while the central performer faces the audience). Both physical qualities (specific weight, height, speed, spatial positioning) and the effect on the audience are described precisely. The response demonstrates understanding that physical theatre communicates through the body rather than through verbal announcement of emotion. At least one Frantic Assembly method is named and applied.

Secure (5-6): A named technique is used and a named moment is referenced. Physical choices are described with some specificity. Effect on audience is explained.

Developing (3-4): Physical choices are mentioned but described vaguely ('I would move slowly and show sadness'). Limited specific technique reference.

Emerging (1-2): Basic description of movement with no named technique and no explanation of audience effect.

practice_questions.text: Analyse how physical theatre companies like Frantic Assembly use the ensemble to communicate themes and social relationships that individual characters alone cannot express. What do directors of physical theatre intend the audience to understand through ensemble movement?
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (10-12): The response analyses how the ensemble functions as a collective body that can represent community, social force or shared experience. The director's intention is clearly articulated: by synchronising or fragmenting the ensemble's movement, the audience reads social relationships (unity, division, coercion, solidarity) in a way individual performances cannot achieve. The response may analyse how the ensemble mirrors central relationships (a chair duet framed by ensemble members repeating the same physical tension in miniature), how multi-roling within the ensemble allows social types to be embodied and challenged, and how the physical collective makes visible the social structures that surround individual characters. The connection to theatrical intention is sustained throughout.

Secure (7-9): The ensemble's functions are explained with some analytical development. At least two functions of ensemble work are explored. Effect on audience is analysed.

Developing (4-6): The ensemble is described correctly but analysis focuses on what it looks like rather than what it communicates or why the director uses it.

Emerging (1-3): Basic description of ensemble as a group of performers with limited analysis of its communicative function.

practice_questions.text: You are directing a physical theatre production of a play in which a family gradually fractures under the weight of unspoken truths. Explain how you would use physical theatre techniques — including ensemble movement, lifts or chair duets, and tableau — alongside specific design choices in lighting and sound to stage the moment when the central truth is finally revealed. Refer to specific staging choices and explain the effect on the audience at each stage.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (17-20): The response demonstrates sustained, detailed application of physical theatre techniques alongside specific design choices. The build to the revelation is staged physically: the ensemble begins in a configuration of apparent domestic normality before performing a Frantic Assembly-influenced sequence that reveals the physical tensions beneath the surface (bodies beginning to resist, orbits contracting, a lift that fails or is withdrawn at the critical moment). The tableau at the revelation is precisely described — the physical positions of every performer, the spatial relationship between them, the use of levels (one performer on a raised platform, the others at floor level). Lighting uses a gobo pattern that fragments the stage during the ensemble sequence, then narrows to a single lighting special on the central figure at the tableau, with the surrounding performers in dim fill. Sound uses an overlapping soundscape of spoken fragments that collapses to silence at the revelation, or a sound cue that cuts abruptly. Costume, set or staging configuration may be addressed. Every choice is connected to physical theatre's communicative intention: the audience reads the family's fracture through bodies and space.

Secure (13-16): Physical theatre techniques are applied with reasonable specificity across ensemble, lifts or chair duets, and tableau. At least two design disciplines are addressed. Effect on audience is explained.

Developing (8-12): Physical theatre ideas are present but staging may be thin on specificity or miss design disciplines. Tableau may be noted but not precisely described.

Emerging (1-7): Some knowledge of physical theatre is shown. Design choices are vague. Limited coherent staging strategy.

practice_questions.text: Name the dramatic method Gupta uses when a character steps forward and speaks directly to the audience.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for: direct address.

practice_questions.text: What is meant by code-switching in the context of The Empress?
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying that it involves moving between two or more languages; 1 mark for explaining its purpose — to signal power, identity, exclusion or cultural difference within a scene.

practice_questions.text: Analyse how Gupta uses a Hindi song as a dramatic method to shape the audience's response to the Indian characters' situation.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks: identification that songs interrupt the naturalistic action (1); explanation that this creates a Brechtian distancing effect, preventing simple emotional absorption (1); reference to a named song moment in the play (1); explanation of how the audience is invited to reflect politically rather than just feel (1).

practice_questions.text: Explain the effect on the audience when Rani moves from speaking English with Mrs Wormwood to speaking Bengali with Mr Das in the Lascar lodging-house scenes.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks: identification that the language shift signals a change in status and safety (1); explanation that English-speaking audience members experience Rani's exclusion from within the docks scene and then her inclusion in Bengali community (1); reference to how a performer could physically mark this shift (1); explanation of the political meaning this creates for the audience watching Victorian race and power dynamics (1).

practice_questions.text: Analyse the playwright's intentions in making Rani's letters home a central dramatic device in The Empress. Consider what Gupta wants the audience to understand about belonging, voice and the Indian experience in Victorian Britain.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Candidate analyses multiple intentions behind the letter device (private testimony made public; the fragility of connection across empire; the contrast between official history and personal voice); anchors analysis to named moments of the play; explains the audience's likely emotional and political response; weighs how the staging of letters (direct address, design choices) amplifies Gupta's intentions; sustained throughout.

Secure: Candidate identifies two or more intentions and explains how the letter device serves them; refers to at least one named moment; some reference to staging or performer effect; generally accurate.

Developing: Candidate describes what letters show about Rani rather than analysing what Gupta intends the audience to think or feel; may retell elements of plot; intentions identified but not explored.

Emerging: Brief description of letters as a plot device; little or no analysis of playwright's purpose or audience effect.

practice_questions.text: You are directing The Empress for a GCSE Drama production. Discuss how you would stage the opening scene at Tilbury Docks, making specific choices about sound, lighting, costume and at least one performer, to communicate to the audience both the historical setting and the political situation Rani finds herself in. Refer to at least two design disciplines and one performer in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Detailed, specific choices across two or more design disciplines (named sound cues with texture and source, lantern types with colour and direction, costume fabrics with cultural and class signals) and at least one performer (vocal quality, posture, proxemics, gesture at a named moment); every choice is justified with reference to what it communicates to the audience about the historical and political situation; staging choices are consistent and create a coherent directorial vision; reference to the contrast between Indian and English visual/aural registers on stage.

Secure: Choices made across at least two disciplines and one performer; generally specific (e.g. names a fabric or a sound type); most choices are justified; staging is mostly coherent.

Developing: Some design and performer choices offered but generic (e.g. 'period costumes', 'sad music'); limited justification; staging lacks coherent directorial vision.

Emerging: Lists ideas with little specificity or justification; description rather than analysis of staging effect.

practice_questions.text: What is the first stage of a professional theatre rehearsal process called?
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for: read-through.

practice_questions.text: What is blocking in the context of theatre rehearsal?
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying that blocking is the pattern of movement a performer makes around the stage; 1 mark for explaining that blocking is set by the director during rehearsals and recorded in the prompt copy.

practice_questions.text: Explain the difference between a technical rehearsal and a dress rehearsal, and what each stage contributes to the production.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks: 1 mark for accurately describing the technical rehearsal (first run in the theatre with all technical elements, stop-start to fix cues); 1 mark for accurately describing the dress rehearsal (full continuous run in performance conditions, as close to opening night as possible); 1 mark for explaining what the tech contributes (co-ordination of all technical departments, refinement of cue timings); 1 mark for explaining what the dress rehearsal contributes (stamina and confidence for the company; final check that transitions are smooth; a director's last chance for major notes before the audience arrives).

practice_questions.text: Explain how a production meeting contributes to the success of a production, and what the stage manager's role is within it.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks: 1 mark for explaining that a production meeting brings director and all design/technical departments together to co-ordinate; 1 mark for giving a specific example of what is discussed or resolved (e.g. the director clarifies where a lighting special must fall; the set designer confirms the delivery date for a piece of scenery; a costume quick-change problem is identified and solved); 1 mark for the stage manager's role (records all decisions in the production notes, which feed into the prompt copy; circulates action points to departments); 1 mark for linking the production meeting to the audience's eventual experience (if departments are not aligned, the production fails technically in front of an audience — production meetings prevent this).

practice_questions.text: Analyse how the collaboration between a director and a sound designer during the rehearsal process might shape the audience's experience of a specific scene. In your answer, refer to at least one stage of the rehearsal process and specific sound design choices.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: the collaboration between director and sound designer is analysed through at least one named rehearsal stage (e.g. production meeting where director establishes the emotional intention of a scene; tech rehearsal where the sound cue is placed precisely at the moment a character makes a turning-point decision); specific sound choices named (e.g. a low-frequency drone building under a confrontation scene; a sudden sharp silence on the word of revelation; a diegetic sound cue of distant traffic that is gradually removed to create isolation); the intended effect on the audience is precisely stated and connected to the director's intention.

Secure: collaboration described through at least one rehearsal stage; specific sound choices present; audience effect described; directorial intention generally linked.

Developing: rehearsal process referenced but not used analytically; sound choices are generic; audience effect implied.

Emerging: basic description of sound design with no rehearsal process reference; audience effect absent.

practice_questions.text: As a director, describe the decisions you would make during rehearsals to stage a key scene that involves a sudden reversal of power between two characters. Refer to specific choices from at least two disciplines (performer and one design role) and explain how you would develop these choices through the rehearsal process.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: a clearly defined power reversal; specific performer choices developed through named rehearsal stages (e.g. in blocking the powerful character begins downstage centre with the other character upstage; as rehearsals progress the reversal is staged as a physical crossing — the characters swap spatial positions — timed to a specific line); specific design choices from one discipline (e.g. lighting: a cross-fade from a warm state favouring one character to a cold state favouring the other, refined during tech rehearsal); the rehearsal process is used meaningfully (choices are developed and changed during rehearsals, not simply presented as final); the combined effect of performance and design is discussed.

Secure: power reversal identified; performer and design choices present with some specificity; at least one rehearsal stage referenced; audience effect described.

Developing: staging ideas described but limited connection to rehearsal process; design or performance choices are general; audience effect implied.

Emerging: basic staging description with no rehearsal process vocabulary; power reversal not clearly staged; audience effect absent.

practice_questions.text: Name the dramatic term for when the audience knows something that the characters on stage do not.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for: dramatic irony.

practice_questions.text: What is subtext in drama?
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying that subtext refers to what is implied or felt but not directly spoken; 1 mark for explaining its effect, e.g. it creates tension between what characters say and what the audience understands they mean, particularly in scenes of restraint or conflict.

practice_questions.text: Analyse how Miller uses his heightened Puritan idiom to communicate the society of Salem to a theatre audience.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying a feature of the idiom (e.g. thee/thou, inverted syntax, formal sentence structures); 1 mark for linking this to Puritan society (e.g. a culture of control, religious authority, suppression of individual feeling); 1 mark for explaining the effect on a performer (e.g. requires careful breath planning and deliberate phrasing); 1 mark for explaining the audience effect (e.g. the formality of the language makes emotional outbursts feel more explosive by contrast).

practice_questions.text: Explain the effect of the heightened Puritan language on the dramatic tension in the domestic scenes between John and Elizabeth Proctor.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying the restraint or formality of the language in the domestic scenes; 1 mark for linking this to the subtext of guilt and suspicion between the characters; 1 mark for explaining how a performer might use this formality (e.g. long pauses within formal sentences, controlled vocal delivery, physical distance suggesting emotional coldness); 1 mark for explaining the audience effect (e.g. the audience can feel the unspoken weight of John's infidelity and Elizabeth's distrust through what neither character directly says).

practice_questions.text: Analyse Miller's intentions in staging the courtroom confrontation in Act 3. Consider how the playwright uses structure, staging configuration, dramatic irony and the scale of the ensemble scene to make the audience feel the injustice of the proceedings.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Clearly articulates Miller's intention (e.g. to position the audience as helpless witnesses who know the truth the court denies). Analyses at least two dramatic methods with concrete staging specifics anchored to named moments of the scene. Explains audience effect precisely, including the political allegory (McCarthyism / mass hysteria). Uses stagecraft vocabulary accurately throughout (blocking, proxemics, levels, dramatic irony, ensemble, sightlines). Reaches a substantiated judgement about which method most powerfully communicates Miller's intentions.

Secure: States Miller's intentions and analyses at least two methods. Generally concrete, with at least one named staging choice. Links to context (Salem / McCarthyism) at least once. Effect on audience explained.

Developing: Identifies Miller's themes but does not consistently explain how staging communicates them. Tends toward literary analysis rather than drama analysis. Generic references to 'dark staging' or 'powerful scenes' without specifics.

Emerging: Retells what happens in Act 3 without analysing intentions. Little or no staging vocabulary. No distinction between literary analysis and performance analysis.

practice_questions.text: You are directing the courtroom scene in Act 3, from the moment Proctor first challenges Abigail's accusations through to Mary Warren's collapse. Discuss how you would stage this extract, covering set design, staging configuration, blocking and proxemics, lighting, and the vocal and physical choices for both Proctor and Abigail. Explain how your choices communicate Miller's intentions to the audience.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Every choice is concrete and named (e.g. profile spot on Danforth to emphasise judicial authority, Proctor advancing downstage into the audience space on a thrust stage to make his appeal directly to the house, Abigail stage right controlling the other girls through a tight proxemic cluster, Mary Warren isolated downstage left as she retreats). Both vocal and physical choices for at least two characters are specified with named effects. Design choices across at least two disciplines are detailed (lighting state, set configuration, costume palette). Miller's allegorical intention is explicitly connected to staging choices. A substantiated directorial judgement is reached.

Secure: Covers most skill areas. Choices are generally concrete. Both performer and design perspectives present. Miller's intentions connected to most choices.

Developing: Addresses some skills but not all. Choices are generic in places (e.g. 'dark lighting to show the danger'). Performer and design perspectives not always both present in same answer.

Emerging: Describes the scene rather than directing it. Few or no named staging choices. No connection to Miller's intentions.

practice_questions.text: Name the structural technique Turnly uses to move between scenes set in Japan and scenes set in North Korea.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for: cross-cutting (accept: intercutting, parallel editing, alternating scenes).

practice_questions.text: What is a soundscape in theatre design?
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying that a soundscape uses layered sound to create atmosphere; 1 mark for explaining that it combines multiple audio elements (recorded, live, music, effects) simultaneously to suggest a place or emotional state.

practice_questions.text: Explain how Turnly uses stage directions about the sea to create meaning in The Great Wave. Refer to a specific moment or technique.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks: identification of the sea as a recurring stage direction (1); explanation that it connects the two locations through a shared presence (1); analysis of what this means for the audience (creates dramatic irony — Hanako is near a sea she cannot cross back; 1); reference to how this could be realised in performance — soundscape, lighting, or design (1).

practice_questions.text: Explain how a sound designer might use the sound of the sea to mark transitions between scenes in The Great Wave. Refer to specific sound choices and their effect on the audience.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks: identification of wave sound as a transition cue (1); specific sound choice (e.g. volume swell, stereo positioning, recorded or live sound, reverb added for the North Korean scenes to signal distance; 1); effect on the audience (connects both storylines through a shared auditory image, building unease; 1); link to playwright’s intention (the sea as the site of loss and the barrier between worlds; 1).

practice_questions.text: Analyse Turnly's intentions in using cross-cutting between the Japan scenes and the North Korea scenes throughout the play. What does he want the audience to understand and feel as a result of this structural choice?
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: the response analyses multiple intentions simultaneously — the creation of dramatic irony (the audience knows Hanako is alive before the family does), the political argument that both lives are destroyed by the same state act, and the moral pressure on the audience generated by knowing more than the characters. Choices are anchored to named moments (e.g. the interrogation scenes cutting back to Reiko’s grief) and the analysis explains why Turnly wants that specific emotional effect. The response shows awareness of the play’s documentary roots: the cross-cutting insists that this is not fiction but a real, structural injustice.

Secure: identifies dramatic irony and the political argument; generally accurate about effect on audience; at least one named moment.

Developing: describes the cross-cutting technique and notes that it creates tension; limited analysis of intention; effect on audience is implied rather than stated.

Emerging: lists what cross-cutting is without explaining what Turnly intends the audience to think or feel.

practice_questions.text: You are directing The Great Wave. Discuss how you would stage the transitions between the Japan and North Korea scenes to communicate the passage of time and the ongoing separation of the family. Refer to set, lighting, sound and performer choices in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: the response proposes a coherent design vocabulary for transitions — e.g. a wave soundscape that swells and fades, a shifting blue-grey lighting state on the cyclorama, gobo water-patterns that persist in both locations, and performer choices (changed posture, pace, costume additions) that show ageing. Every choice is anchored to a named moment and explained in terms of its effect on the audience. The response shows directorial intention — the wave image is the controlling metaphor, realised consistently across all design disciplines. Structural awareness: the wave-rhythm builds towards the Pyongyang Declaration scenes.

Secure: at least three design disciplines addressed; generally concrete choices; at least one named moment; effect on audience present.

Developing: relevant ideas about lighting and sound but choices are generic (“dark lighting,” “sad music”); few named moments; limited performer choices.

Emerging: describes the transitions in general terms without specific design or performer choices; no named moments; little directorial intention shown.

practice_questions.text: Name the type of verse in which noble characters in Romeo and Juliet predominantly speak.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for: iambic pentameter (accept blank verse).

practice_questions.text: What is a soliloquy?
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying it as a speech in which a character speaks their private thoughts aloud; 1 mark for specifying it is addressed to the audience or spoken as if others cannot hear.

practice_questions.text: Analyse how the shared sonnet structure at the Capulet feast could shape a director's blocking choices for the moment Romeo and Juliet first meet.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks: identification of the sonnet's fourteen-line division between the two characters (1); explanation that the form creates physical and rhythmic coupling between them before any touch (1); reference to a specific blocking or proxemics decision (e.g. Romeo moving downstage toward Juliet as the sonnet progresses) (1); link to the effect on the audience at that moment (e.g. the audience understands the union is inevitable, sealed in form before it is sealed in action) (1).

practice_questions.text: Explain how a lighting designer could respond to the shift from verse to prose (and back again) to signal changes in character status and emotional register across the play.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for naming a lighting choice for verse scenes (e.g. warm amber wash for the feast); 1 mark for naming a contrasting lighting choice for comic prose scenes (e.g. brighter, more even state for the Nurse's scenes); 1 mark for explaining the effect of each on how the audience reads the character's status or mood; 1 mark for referencing a specific named moment (e.g. the Nurse's verse in Act 4 and a corresponding design shift to cooler pale blue).

practice_questions.text: Analyse the playwright's intentions in having Romeo and Juliet share a sonnet at their first meeting rather than speaking in ordinary verse exchange. What is the audience meant to think and feel at this moment, and how might a director and performer bring those intentions to life?
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: The response analyses what the shared sonnet form is designed to communicate to the audience at this moment (a sense of perfect union, of two people already completing each other rhythmically before they complete each other narratively). The student explains both a performer choice (e.g. Romeo's vocal pace tightening to match Juliet's answering rhythm as the exchange progresses; a dropped gaze on the first kiss that lands on the couplet's final beat) and a design choice (e.g. a lighting special narrowing around the pair, the feast soundscape fading beneath them) with a clear effect on the audience named (wonder, inevitability, a tightening of focus). A substantiated judgement is offered about why this formal choice is dramatically more powerful than a simple exchange.

Secure: The student identifies the sonnet structure and links it to a sense of romantic union, names at least one performer choice and one design choice anchored to the scene, with a generally accurate effect on the audience.

Developing: The student identifies the sonnet and says it shows love, but the analysis is general and no concrete staging choices are named; effect on audience is implied rather than stated.

Emerging: The student identifies the scene and makes basic observations about love or poetry without linking to performance or design.

practice_questions.text: You are directing Romeo and Juliet. Discuss how you would stage Juliet's soliloquy in Act 3 Scene 2, in which she awaits news of the duel. Refer to your decisions about staging configuration, lighting, sound, costume and Juliet's vocal and physical performance, explaining the effect of each choice on the audience.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: The response covers staging configuration (e.g. a thrust stage or in-the-round to bring Juliet into the audience's shared space, honouring the Elizabethan direct-address tradition); a specific lighting design (e.g. a tight Fresnel special from above and slightly in front of Juliet, warming her face, the rest of the stage in a dim blue wash to isolate her emotionally); a sound design (e.g. distant, non-diegetic underscore of low strings giving way to silence as she begins speaking, the audience's attention pulled inward); a costume choice with justification (e.g. Juliet still in the white of her wedding gown, carrying symbolic purity and vulnerability, contrasting with the news she is about to receive); and specific vocal and physical choices for the performer (e.g. opening the soliloquy facing outward at centre stage, pace hurried and pitch high, then slowing and dropping as the language shifts from impatience to grief, hands opening and closing in the costume's fabric). Every choice is anchored to a named moment and a named audience effect.

Secure: The student covers most areas with at least one concrete design element and at least one named performer choice; effects on audience are generally accurate.

Developing: The student identifies some design elements but keeps them generic (warm lighting, quiet music); performer choices are described in emotional terms (she would seem nervous) without vocal/physical translation.

Emerging: The student lists staging ideas without justifying them; no named elements and no named moment.

practice_questions.text: Name the physical theatre company whose techniques Bovell incorporated into Things I Know to Be True.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for: Frantic Assembly.

practice_questions.text: What is meant by the term 'subtext' in drama?
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for a basic correct answer (e.g. the meaning beneath the surface of the dialogue, what is implied rather than stated); 1 mark for development showing understanding of how subtext functions in performance (e.g. what characters feel but cannot say, communicated through pause, physicality or the gap between words and action).

practice_questions.text: Analyse how Bovell uses Rosie's direct-address monologues to position the audience differently from the other characters on stage.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks: identification of Rosie as the narrator-figure who speaks directly to the audience (1); explanation of the temporal complexity of her monologues (partial foreknowledge, dual time frame) (1); explanation of how this creates dramatic irony for the audience (1); reference to the effect this has on the audience's emotional experience of the revelations as they arrive (1).

practice_questions.text: Explain the effect of using a Frantic Assembly movement sequence in place of naturalistic dialogue at a moment of high emotional intensity. How might a lighting designer enhance this effect?
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying that movement sequences externalise subtext or feelings that words cannot contain; 1 mark for a specific lighting choice (e.g. removing the general wash and using a single moving light to follow the performers, or allowing a soundscape to carry the scene while lighting dims to near-blackout); 1 mark for explaining the effect of that choice on the audience at that moment; 1 mark for linking the choice to the emotional content of the specific scene.

practice_questions.text: Analyse how Bovell uses direct-address monologue and physical movement as dramatic methods to communicate meaning that naturalistic dialogue alone cannot achieve. Consider what each method allows the playwright to do and what effect it creates for the audience.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sustained analysis of Bovell's intentions in using both direct address and physical movement, explaining that each serves a different but complementary purpose. Direct address: positions the audience as confidant, creates dramatic irony, allows temporal complexity. Movement: externalises subtext, communicates what words cannot. Both are read as deliberate alternatives to naturalism, not incidental features. The student makes clear what the playwright wants the audience to feel at these heightened moments. No plot summary.

Secure: Identifies both direct address and movement sequences, explains the function of each with some reference to audience effect. May not fully explore the temporal complexity of the monologues but shows clear understanding that these methods serve the play's emotional architecture.

Developing: Describes what direct address and movement sequences look like rather than analysing what Bovell intends them to achieve. Some audience effect mentioned but largely descriptive.

Emerging: Names one or both techniques with little or no analysis of playwright intention or audience effect.

practice_questions.text: As a director staging a Frantic Assembly movement sequence during a moment when two members of the Price family are unable to speak to each other directly, explain how you would use the movement itself, the soundscape, and a lighting choice to communicate the emotional content of the moment to the audience. Refer to specific staging decisions and their intended effects.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Specific movement vocabulary described (e.g. a contact-improvised lift that expresses the effort of holding a relationship together, or a chair duet in which one performer pursues and the other retreats); soundscape: named texture (e.g. a low, non-diegetic underscore that builds in volume and then cuts to silence at the peak of the sequence); lighting: specific choice (e.g. a slow cross-fade from a warm amber wash to a cooler blue as the sequence intensifies, using a gobo to project fractured light across the stage). Every choice anchored to the emotional content with a clear explanation of intended audience effect.

Secure: Most disciplines addressed; at least one named lighting choice and one specific description of the movement; soundscape present but possibly generic; audience effect mostly addressed.

Developing: Relevant ideas but described in general terms (e.g. 'dramatic music', 'slow movement'); limited reference to named staging elements; effect on audience implied rather than explained.

Emerging: List of ideas without justification; no reference to specific staging choices; mostly descriptive.

practice_questions.text: Name one structural device used to narrate events in Noughts and Crosses.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for any one of: dual narration / alternating monologues / direct address / news broadcasts / letters / voiceovers / episodic structure.

practice_questions.text: What is meant by 'direct address' as a dramatic technique?
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for stating that the performer speaks to the audience directly; 1 mark for explaining that this breaks the boundary between the dramatic world and the audience (e.g. 'the character steps outside the scene to speak to the audience, breaking the fictional frame').

practice_questions.text: Analyse how the use of alternating monologues by Sephy and Callum shapes an audience's response to the world of the play.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks: identification of the device (1), explanation of how it creates two competing perspectives (1), analysis of how this prevents simple identification with one side (1), reference to a named moment or scene in which one narrator's account contrasts with the other's (1).

practice_questions.text: Explain the effect of using news bulletins and broadcast voiceovers as a staging device in Noughts and Crosses. In your answer, refer to a specific moment when this device is used and explain the effect on the audience.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks: identifying the device as representing the voice of the Cross state (1), explaining how the authoritative broadcast tone contrasts with the intimate narrators (1), explaining the effect of this contrast on the audience's understanding of power and bias (1), reference to a specific moment or scene in the play (1).

practice_questions.text: Analyse the playwright's intentions in structuring Noughts and Crosses around dual narration, with both Sephy and Callum addressing the audience directly. What do you think Cooke wants the audience to think, feel and question as a result of this choice?
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (10-12): sustained analysis of Cooke's intentions with both political and emotional dimensions; argues that dual narration forces the audience to interrogate which perspective they instinctively trust and why, connecting this to the play's racial reversal; at least one named moment from the play; discussion of Brechtian witness function and how it shapes audience complicity; substantiated judgement about the overall effect of the device.
Secure (7-9): clear analysis of intentions with some reference to political effect; at least one named moment; some awareness of Brechtian dimension or audience positioning; generally accurate effect identified.
Developing (4-6): relevant points but mostly descriptive; may retell what happens rather than analysing intention; limited named moments; effect on audience implied rather than argued.
Emerging (1-3): basic identification of the device with little or no analysis of intention; largely plot-based response.

practice_questions.text: Discuss how you would stage the moments of direct address narration in Noughts and Crosses. In your answer, consider the performer's positioning and physical choices, the lighting design for these moments, and how the staging of narration differs from the staging of scenes. Refer to specific moments in the play.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (17-20): detailed staging vision covering performer positioning (named stage area, body orientation, proxemics relative to rest of cast), specific lighting choices for narration moments (named lantern type, gobo or wash, colour, intensity, cross-fade timing), sound design for news bulletins or transitions (broadcast texture, volume contrast, fading cue), and clear explanation of how each choice communicates the Brechtian political intent of the narrators; all choices anchored to named moments in the play; coherent directorial vision with justified conclusions.
Secure (12-16): most areas covered; at least one specific lighting choice and one performer choice; generally accurate staging logic; named moments referenced; some justification of choices in terms of audience effect.
Developing (7-11): relevant ideas but generic terminology ('spotlight', 'character moves forward'); limited justification; few named moments; effects on audience implied not argued.
Emerging (1-6): basic staging suggestions with little technical vocabulary or justification; may describe plot rather than staging choices.

before.exam_tip_html:
For the 12-mark Analyse Intentions question, the most frequent error is describing what happens in the scene instead of analysing what the playwright and director want the audience to think or feel at that moment. When writing about the dual narration device, do not retell who says what — instead argue: what does giving each character equal narrative authority force the audience to do? What does that make them feel? Why might Cooke have chosen this over a single-narrator approach? Every paragraph of your answer should contain a word like ‘suggests’, ‘implies’, ‘forces the audience to’, or ‘creates discomfort because’ — these are the phrases that show you are analysing intention, not retelling plot.

For extended-response staging questions, remember that the narration device has concrete staging implications. Do not just say “the characters speak to the audience.” Specify: where on stage does the narrator stand? What lighting state isolates them? What happens to the other performers and the set during narration? Examiners reward decisions that are specific and justified — ‘a tight Fresnel special from front-of-house picking out the narrator downstage centre while the rest of the stage dims to a cool blue wash’ is a Mastering-level design choice; ‘a spotlight’ is not.

practice_questions.text: Name the dramatic method in which one actor plays more than one character during a performance.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for: multi-roling (accept multi-role playing or role-doubling).

practice_questions.text: Define the term 'direct address' as used in theatrical performance.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying that direct address involves the performer speaking to the audience; 1 mark for explaining that it breaks or acknowledges the fourth wall, stepping outside the dramatic fiction.

practice_questions.text: Analyse how Eason uses mime to create the sense of an elephant in this play. Refer to specific physical choices the ensemble might make.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks: identification of mime as a technique (1); explanation of specific physical choices (low posture, synchronised rhythm, collective sway) (1); reference to the specific moment of the Indian journey (1); analysis of the effect on the audience (creates the creature through imagination, demonstrates physical theatre skill, makes the transformation visible and exciting) (1).

practice_questions.text: Explain the effect of the base-layer-plus-accessories costume strategy on the audience during rapid multi-roling transitions. Give a specific example from the play.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks: naming the costume strategy and how it works (1); a specific example of a role transition in the play (e.g. Reform Club gentleman to customs official) (1); explanation of the effect on pace (transitions are instant, energy is maintained) (1); explanation of the effect on the audience (sense of theatrical magic, admiration for skill, delight in the visible act of transformation) (1).

practice_questions.text: Analyse the playwright's intentions in using narration and direct address throughout the play. What is the audience meant to understand about their role in the storytelling?
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Full analysis of Eason's intentions across multiple narrative functions of direct address. Identifies that the audience is consciously recruited as a fellow traveller; that narration replaces scene-change transitions to maintain pace; that the technique self-reflexively celebrates storytelling as a theatrical act. Every point anchored to a named moment of the play with a named effect on audience understanding or emotion. Awareness of the Complicite/physical-theatre tradition behind this technique.

Secure: Identifies at least two purposes of narration and direct address with generally accurate effect on audience. At least one named moment. Some awareness of the theatrical tradition.

Developing: Identifies that direct address breaks the fourth wall and that narration updates the audience on the journey. Generic effect stated rather than analysed. Little reference to specific moments.

Emerging: Basic description of what narration does (tells the audience what is happening). No analysis of intention or audience effect.

practice_questions.text: As a director, explain how you would stage the moment when the ensemble represents a moving train during the crossing of the American plains. Discuss set, lighting, sound and performer choices you would make, and explain the effect of each choice on the audience.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Full directorial vision integrating set, lighting, sound and performer choices, all anchored to this specific moment. Set: specific use of chairs arranged in rows, minimal additional furniture, positioning on stage (upstage to downstage for sense of travel). Lighting: choice of lantern type and colour to suggest landscape (cool, wide wash; possible gobo for prairie light), transition cues as the train accelerates. Sound: specific soundscape elements named (steam whistle, rhythmic wheel click, wind, the attack sequence building from distance). Performer: specific physical vocabulary for collective sway, synchronised arm-and-body rhythms, the stillness of Fogg against the animated ensemble. Every choice is given a named effect on the audience. Substantiated directorial judgement about the overall intended experience.

Secure: Most design disciplines covered, generally concrete choices. At least one named design element and one performer choice with effects. The moment is correctly identified and the staging is coherent.

Developing: Some design disciplines covered but choices are generic (e.g. 'exciting lighting', 'train sound effects'). Effects are implied rather than stated. Limited performer detail.

Emerging: Basic listing of design ideas with little or no effect. Largely descriptive rather than directorial.

practice_questions.text: Identify one dramatic method Willy Russell uses to remind the audience that the ending of Blood Brothers is inevitable.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for any valid answer such as: the Narrator, direct address, the circular structure / prologue tableau showing the twins dead, the recurring superstition motif, the songs as commentary.

practice_questions.text: What is meant by the term "direct address" in drama?
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying that the performer speaks to the audience; 1 mark for stating that it breaks out of the fictional world of the play (or equivalent: acknowledges the audience, breaks the fourth wall).

practice_questions.text: Analyse how Russell uses the recurring Marilyn Monroe motif to create meaning across Blood Brothers.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks: identification of the motif (1); explanation of its first appearance and what it establishes (1); analysis of how its return in a later context shifts or deepens its meaning (1); reference to how a sound or staging choice could reinforce the motif for the audience (1).

practice_questions.text: Explain how a sound designer and a lighting designer might work together to create the effect of fate and inevitability during the Narrator's first appearance in the prologue of Blood Brothers.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for a specific sound choice (e.g. low underscore, a recurring musical theme, silence); 1 mark for explaining its effect on the audience; 1 mark for a specific lighting choice (e.g. tight profile spot, cold gel, isolated beam); 1 mark for explaining how together these choices communicate the Narrator's threatening, fate-laden function.

practice_questions.text: Analyse Russell's intentions in using the Narrator as a Brechtian commentator throughout Blood Brothers. What does Russell want the audience to think or feel each time the Narrator addresses them directly?
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sustained analysis of Russell's intent across multiple appearances of the Narrator; clear articulation of the Brechtian purpose (preventing emotional absorption, maintaining critical distance, implicating the audience in the class critique); reference to at least two named moments in the play; consideration of at least one design or performance choice that reinforces Russell's intention; substantiated judgement about the cumulative effect on the audience.

Secure: Clear analysis of Russell's intent with Narrator; reference to Brechtian technique explained (not just named); at least one named moment; some reference to how staging or performance supports the intention; effect on audience stated.

Developing: Relevant points about the Narrator's role; Russell's intent partially addressed; description of what the Narrator does rather than analysis of why; limited reference to named moments; effect on audience implied not explained.

Emerging: Basic identification of the Narrator's role with little analysis of intention; descriptive rather than analytical; no reference to named moments or design/performance choices.

practice_questions.text: A director is staging the scene in Blood Brothers where the Narrator confronts Mrs Johnstone with the consequences of the deal she has made with Mrs Lyons. As a director, explain how you would use staging, lighting and sound to communicate the Narrator's function as a moral force and the emotional impact on Mrs Johnstone. Refer to specific choices across all three areas.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Full range of staging, lighting and sound choices all concrete and named (e.g. proxemics — Narrator placed directly downstage of Mrs Johnstone cutting off her exit; lighting — a tight profile spot in cold blue-white on the Narrator, a warmer but dimming Fresnel wash on Mrs Johnstone; sound — a low, atonal underscore building beneath the dialogue, cutting to silence on the key accusatory line); all choices anchored to a specific moment with a named effect on the audience; directorial intention clearly stated; consideration of performer choices for Mrs Johnstone (collapsing physical energy, eyes downcast, voice breaking); substantiated overall judgement.

Secure: Most design areas covered with generally concrete choices; at least one named lighting type and one sound idea; proxemics or blocking addressed; Mrs Johnstone's performer response considered; effect on audience stated.

Developing: Relevant staging ideas but described generically ("dark lighting", "tense music"); few specific named choices; effect on audience implied; performer choices for Mrs Johnstone limited.

Emerging: Basic listing of staging ideas with little justification; no named design elements; descriptive rather than directorial.

practice_questions.text: Name the theatrical company that originally produced A Taste of Honey in 1958.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for: Theatre Workshop (also accept Joan Littlewood's Theatre Workshop / Theatre Royal Stratford East).

practice_questions.text: What is meant by the term 'direct address' in drama?
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying that a character speaks to/looks at the audience; 1 mark for explaining that this breaks the fourth wall or creates a direct relationship between performer and audience.

practice_questions.text: Analyse how Delaney's use of tonal swings between comedy and pain creates a particular effect on the audience in A Taste of Honey.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks: identification of tonal swings as a dramatic method (1); explanation of how comedy functions as a mask or defence mechanism for Jo and Helen (1); reference to a named moment of tonal shift in the play (1); explanation of audience effect — unease, emotional vulnerability, greater impact when pain surfaces (1).

practice_questions.text: Explain how a sound designer might use the live jazz musicians to communicate the play's hybrid naturalistic-presentational style at two different moments in A Taste of Honey. Refer to specific sound choices and their effect on the audience.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks: identification of a specific moment and a named sound quality (e.g. muted trumpet, slow blues phrase) for the first moment (1); explanation of effect on audience at that moment (1); identification of a contrasting second moment with a named sound quality (e.g. brighter, up-tempo brass underscoring a comic exchange) (1); explanation of how the contrast signals the play's shifts between emotional registers (1).

practice_questions.text: Analyse what Delaney intends the audience to understand about the relationship between Jo and Helen through the direct address moments in the play. Consider how the theatrical form contributes to this intention.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sustained analysis of how direct address functions theatrically (breaks fourth wall, creates audience complicity, allows the characters to share what they cannot say to each other), linked to Delaney's thematic intention — the gap between what is performed and what is felt in a mother-daughter relationship built on performance and survival. Named moments referenced without reproducing dialogue. Analysis of how the hybrid naturalistic/Brechtian form amplifies this — audience positioned as witnesses rather than voyeurs. Substantiated directorial judgement.

Secure: Clear analysis of direct address as a device; link to the characters' emotional concealment; some reference to theatrical form and audience effect; generally accurate.

Developing: Relevant points about direct address and the mother-daughter relationship but generic; effect on audience implied rather than stated; little engagement with theatrical form.

Emerging: Basic description of what direct address is; limited link to Delaney's intentions; mostly descriptive.

practice_questions.text: As a director, discuss how you would stage the opening scene of A Taste of Honey to communicate the play's hybrid form — both naturalistic kitchen-sink drama and Brechtian theatre event. Refer to set design, lighting, sound and performer choices.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Full directorial vision across all four design disciplines plus performer choices; staging configuration choice named and justified (e.g. end-on proscenium or thrust); set design specific (e.g. peeling wallpaper, practical gas ring, deliberately cramped but with jazz musicians visible upstage); lighting state for naturalistic scene contrasted with lighting special for direct address moments; sound design names instrument, quality, tempo, and function (underscore vs diegetic); costume signals character before dialogue (Helen's fur vs Jo's plain dress); performer choices include vocal quality (Salford vowels, pace, comic timing) and physical staging (proxemics between Jo and Helen); all choices linked to the hybrid naturalistic-Brechtian form and the play's themes. Substantiated directorial intention throughout.

Secure: Most design disciplines addressed with some concrete choices; staging configuration referenced; some link to theme; at least one specific performer choice alongside design choices.

Developing: Two or three design areas mentioned but described in general terms; limited specificity ("dark lighting", "jazz in the background"); performer choice present but thin.

Emerging: Listing of a few staging ideas with little justification or link to the play's form; no named design elements.

practice_questions.text: Name the lighting term for a metal or glass plate inserted into a lantern to project a pattern onto the stage.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for: gobo.

practice_questions.text: What is a soundscape in theatre design?
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying that a soundscape is a layered combination of ambient and specific sounds; 1 mark for explaining its effect, e.g. it builds an immersive audio environment that communicates the world of the play to the audience before or beyond what the set alone can show.

practice_questions.text: Explain the effect of using a harsh top light in the courtroom scene of The Crucible.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for describing the lighting choice (top light from profile lanterns rigged above the stage, creating downward shadows); 1 mark for linking to the scene's context (the courtroom is a place of interrogation and exposure); 1 mark for explaining the effect on the performers (every figure looks isolated, uncomfortable and guilty); 1 mark for explaining the audience effect (the cold, judicial quality of the light positions the audience as witnesses to a show trial, reinforcing Miller's allegory).

practice_questions.text: As a lighting designer, explain how you would design the lighting for the moment in Act 4 when Proctor makes his final decision about the signed confession. Refer to specific lighting choices and their effect on the audience.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Names specific lantern types, gel colours, angles and intensities anchored to the Act 4 jail setting. Describes at least two distinct lighting states (e.g. opening cold blue wash, shifting to a focused white special at the moment of decision). Explains how each state communicates something specific to the audience (e.g. the desaturated blue creates institutional bleakness; the upward shift to white creates a sense of moral clarity as Proctor chooses integrity over survival). Names effects such as a gobo to suggest bars or shadow. Links lighting to Miller's intentions explicitly.

Secure: At least two named lighting choices with generally accurate effect descriptions. Links to the scene's meaning at least once. Generally concrete, even if not fully specified.

Developing: Refers to lighting changing but in generic terms ('dark at the start, bright when he decides'). No named lantern types or colours. Effect on audience implied but not explained.

Emerging: States 'I would use dramatic lighting' without specification. No named elements. Little or no link to meaning or effect.

practice_questions.text: Analyse Miller's intentions in the contrast between the domestic world of the Proctor household and the courtroom in Act 3. Consider how a designer might use set, lighting and costume to make this contrast visible and meaningful to the audience.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: States Miller's intention clearly (e.g. to show the invasion of public hysteria into private life, or the way an institution of supposed justice becomes a machinery of persecution). Analyses the contrast through specific design choices in at least two disciplines (e.g. set: domestic hearth replaced by bare raised platform; lighting: warm amber of Acts 1-2 replaced by cold white interrogation lighting; costume: the grey linen of the townsfolk made more austere in the courtroom where judges wear pure black). Every choice is anchored to a named moment. Audience effect is explained. Connection to McCarthyism allegory present. Substantiated judgement reached.

Secure: States Miller's intentions. Analyses contrast through two design areas, generally concrete. At least one named staging choice per discipline. Effect on audience present.

Developing: Describes the domestic and courtroom scenes in general terms. Design references are generic. Miller's intentions stated but not analysed.

Emerging: Retells what happens in both scenes. No specific design choices. Descriptive rather than analytical.

practice_questions.text: You are the lead designer for a new production of The Crucible. Discuss how you would use set design, lighting, sound and costume to stage the courtroom scene in Act 3. Cover the staging configuration, the key design choices for each discipline and the performer choices for Danforth and Proctor. Explain how your overall design communicates Miller's intentions about power, justice and hysteria.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Covers all four design disciplines with named, specific choices (e.g. thrust configuration for the courtroom to make the audience feel enclosed; a raised platform for Danforth with a heavy oak table as his only furniture; cold white profile spots at steep angles with no gel to flatten and expose every face; the sound of the congregation murmuring as underscore building to silence when Proctor speaks; Danforth in dense black wool with a stiff white collar, Proctor in earth-toned linen roughened by outdoor work). Performer choices for at least two characters are specified with named vocal and physical choices. Miller's intentions about power and hysteria are directly connected to every design decision. A coherent directorial vision is articulated and justified.

Secure: Covers at least three design disciplines with generally concrete choices. Performer choices present for at least one character. Miller's intentions connected to the staging. Mostly specific, not fully sustained.

Developing: Addresses some design areas but not all. Generic choices ('a big set to show the power of the court'). Performer choices present but vague. Miller's intentions mentioned but not consistently linked to specific design decisions.

Emerging: Describes the courtroom generally. Few specific design choices. No named lantern types, fabrics or sound cues. No connection to Miller's intentions.

practice_questions.text: Name one staging configuration suitable for Romeo and Juliet's balcony scene that would allow the audience close proximity to both performers.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for any of: thrust stage, theatre in the round, traverse, end-on (accept any valid configuration with a brief justification if required).

practice_questions.text: What is a gobo in stage lighting?
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying it as a metal plate or insert placed inside a profile lantern; 1 mark for explaining that it projects a cut-out pattern, shape or texture onto the stage.

practice_questions.text: Explain how a sound designer could use contrasting soundscapes to signal the shift in mood between the Capulet feast scene and the tomb scene.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for a specific feast soundscape (e.g. Renaissance dance music or contemporary club music at a full, warm level); 1 mark for a specific tomb soundscape (e.g. near-silence with distant echo, or low string underscore fading to nothing); 1 mark for explaining the emotional effect of the feast sound on the audience (festivity, warmth, sensory noise Romeo must cut through); 1 mark for explaining the effect of the tomb sound on the audience (finality, isolation, the warmth of the earlier world gone).

practice_questions.text: As a lighting designer, explain how you would design the lighting for the balcony scene in Act 2 Scene 2 of Romeo and Juliet. Refer to specific lighting choices and explain the effect of each on the audience.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: The response names specific lantern types (e.g. a Fresnel for the garden wash, a profile spot for the tight special on the lovers), specific colours or gel choices (e.g. warm amber 204 gel for the garden, a cooler open white isolating the characters as the scene deepens), direction (from above and slightly front, creating natural moonlight angles), and explains the effect on the audience at named moments (the transition from the warm feast state to the private garden special signals to the audience that the scene has shifted from public to intimate; the narrowing pool of light as the sonnet is completed creates physical proximity even at a distance). The response also considers the rest of the stage (darkness beyond the lit area suggesting the dangers of Verona just out of sight) and justifies the choices with reference to the scene's dramatic purpose.

Secure: The student names at least one specific lighting choice with a colour or lantern type and explains its effect on the audience; references the scene's mood and a named moment.

Developing: The student gives general lighting ideas (warm and romantic, moonlight effect) without naming specific elements; the effect on audience is implied rather than stated.

Emerging: The student describes a basic lighting idea (bright for the feast, dark for outside) with no specific elements and no audience effect.

practice_questions.text: Analyse the playwright's intentions in the contrast between the warmth of the Capulet feast and the cold of the tomb. How might a designer use lighting and sound to communicate these contrasting intentions to the audience?
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: The response analyses what the contrast between feast warmth and tomb coldness is designed to make the audience feel: the play is structured so the audience is pulled into a world of life, colour and celebration, then has that warmth catastrophically withdrawn. The student names specific design choices for each location (e.g. amber wash, lutes-and-drums soundscape for the feast; cold blue-white profile special, near-silence or low underscore for the tomb), explains the dramaturgical function of each (the feast design creates investment in the lovers' world so the tomb design's coldness is more devastating), and makes a substantiated judgement about the directorial intention (the design arc from warmth to cold is the emotional argument of the play made physical).

Secure: The student identifies the contrast and links it to specific design choices for both locations with generally accurate effects on audience.

Developing: The student identifies the contrast in general terms and mentions lighting or sound without naming specific elements.

Emerging: The student describes the contrast between love and death without connecting it to design choices.

practice_questions.text: You are designing Romeo and Juliet for a thrust stage. Discuss your set, lighting, sound and costume choices for the production, focusing on how each design decision serves the play's exploration of the conflict between the two families and the lovers caught between them.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: The response is anchored to the thrust stage configuration, considering sightlines and audience proximity throughout. Set design is specific: a central revolve or multi-level platform with two architectural flanking structures for each family, allowing rapid transitions between public and private spaces without blackouts. Lighting design is described with named lanterns and gel colours: warm gold (Lee 102) wash for Capulet's domain, cool silver (Lee 201) for Montague's, with a neutral state (open white, open flat lighting) for street scenes where the feud is public; a tight profile special for shared private moments between the lovers. Sound design distinguishes the feast (warm, layered Renaissance or contemporary music) from the duel (percussive soundscape, sudden silence at the moment of death) from the tomb (absolute near-silence broken by echo). Costume uses family colour coding (red and gold Capulet, blue and silver Montague) with Romeo in a neutral grey and Juliet in white, both visually separated from their families. Each choice is justified with reference to a named moment and a named effect on the audience.

Secure: The student covers most design departments with at least one concrete element each, and at least one choice is anchored to a named scene with an audience effect.

Developing: The student addresses most departments but keeps choices generic; production concept is mentioned but not consistently applied across departments.

Emerging: The student lists design ideas with little justification and no named moments; the thrust stage configuration is mentioned but not used to shape any specific choice.

practice_questions.text: Name one type of lantern a lighting designer might use to create a soft, warm domestic atmosphere in A Taste of Honey.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for any of: Fresnel lantern / flood / PAR can. (Profile/ellipsoidal is also acceptable if the student explains it produces a focused effect rather than soft wash — credit the explanation.)

practice_questions.text: What is a gobo in lighting design?
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying it as a metal (or glass) plate inserted into a profile lantern; 1 mark for explaining that it projects a pattern or texture onto the stage/set.

practice_questions.text: Explain how a costume designer might use Helen's fur coat to communicate her character and social position in A Taste of Honey. Refer to specific costume choices.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks: identification of the fur coat as a costume choice (1); explanation of its fabric/silhouette/condition (slightly worn, aspirational) and what this communicates about Helen's social position (1); link to character — Helen performs worldliness and independence (1); effect on the audience — they read her character before she speaks (1).

practice_questions.text: As a lighting designer, explain how you would design the lighting for a moment when Jo and the Boy share their brief winter intimacy inside the flat. Refer to specific lighting choices and their effect on the audience.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Specific lighting state named with lantern type (e.g. Fresnel with amber gel from a low, warm angle); justification of why this quality of light evokes warmth and candlelight in the cold flat; contrast with the flat's base lighting state (bare overhead bulb, cooler wash) so the audience feels the shift; explanation of what this communicates about the characters' relationship; possible use of a gobo to suggest firelight flicker or shadows; effect on audience named (intimacy, fragility, the sense that this warmth is temporary). All choices anchored to the named moment.

Secure: Named lighting choice with some justification; at least one specific design element (gel, lantern, intensity); link to character relationship and audience effect; generally concrete.

Developing: General lighting described (warm, soft) without naming lantern or gel; effect on audience stated but not developed; little link to the moment's meaning.

Emerging: Basic description (bright or dim lights) with no design specifics; no link to meaning or audience effect.

practice_questions.text: Analyse what Delaney intends the audience to understand about class and aspiration through the design of the flat and its contrast with the world outside in A Taste of Honey.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sustained analysis of how the flat's design communicates class — the gap between the domestic interior and the industrial Salford outside; how props-as-symbols (Helen's fashion magazines, Jo's drawings) reveal character aspiration against limited circumstance; how the sound of the world outside (trams, canal, chimneys) presses in on the flat; analysis of Delaney's intention to make the audience feel the weight of limited options on these women, not judge them; specific reference to design choices and their effect at named moments. Substantiated critical judgement.

Secure: Clear analysis of flat as a symbol of class; design choices referenced (set, sound or costume); link to Delaney's intentions; some engagement with audience effect.

Developing: Relevant points about the flat's squalor; some reference to design; limited analysis of intention; effect implied not stated.

Emerging: Descriptive account of the flat's appearance; little analysis of why Delaney constructs it this way.

practice_questions.text: As a director, discuss how you would use set design, lighting, sound and costume to bring the opening scene of A Taste of Honey to life for a contemporary audience. Your answer should communicate the play's social context and the relationship between Jo and Helen.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Full directorial vision; staging configuration named and justified (e.g. end-on proscenium with sight of jazz musicians upstage); set design specific (peeling wallpaper, practical bare bulb, cramped furniture, industrial backdrop or projected chimney shadow using gobo); lighting state for the opening (cool, flat overhead wash establishing austerity; transition to warmer state when characters' dynamic shifts); sound design specific (tram bells off-stage left, jazz musicians launching into an up-tempo tune as Helen and Jo arrive, soundscape of the city pressing in); costume choices with named fabrics and silhouettes (Helen's worn camel fur coat vs Jo's school-coat with buttons missing); performer choices including vocal register (Salford accents, Helen's breezy pace vs Jo's sharper responses) and physical staging (Helen taking the centre stage, Jo circling the edges); all choices linked to class, aspiration and the play's social context. Substantiated and convincing.

Secure: Most design areas addressed with some concrete choices; staging configuration referenced; character relationship communicated through design; at least one specific design detail per discipline.

Developing: Two or three design areas mentioned; some specifics but patchily; performer choices thin; limited link to social context.

Emerging: Listing of basic staging ideas; few or no specific design elements; social context not engaged.

practice_questions.text: Name one staging configuration that would suit Noughts and Crosses and briefly state why.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for any one named configuration (end-on / proscenium arch / thrust / in-the-round / traverse) with a brief justification (e.g. 'end-on because it allows projection onto a back wall and focuses the audience on the two narrators at downstage centre').

practice_questions.text: What is meant by 'Verfremdungseffekt' in the context of theatre design?
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for stating that it means making familiar things strange or creating a sense of estrangement; 1 mark for explaining that this is associated with Brecht and is used to provoke critical thinking rather than emotional immersion in the audience.
