practice_questions.text: Explain the effect of using projection in Noughts and Crosses. In your answer, refer to a specific moment when this design element could be used and explain how it affects the audience.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks: identifying projection as a world-building device on a bare stage (1), explaining that it can communicate news, authority or location without physical set (1), explaining the specific effect on the audience at a named moment (e.g. fragmented newspaper headlines during the school scene suggesting Cross media bias) (1), explaining how this projection choice reinforces the play's political message (1).

practice_questions.text: As a lighting designer, explain how you would design the lighting for two contrasting scenes in Noughts and Crosses: the beach scene in which Sephy and Callum meet as children and the interrogation scene. For each scene, name specific lighting elements and explain their effect on the audience.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (7-8): both scenes addressed with specific, named lighting elements for each; beach scene: named warm colour (e.g. Lee 103 straw or amber gel), broad wash, possibly a ripple gobo suggesting water, spacious positioning of lanterns to suggest openness; interrogation scene: hard-edged profile lantern, cold white or blue gel, tight pool isolating a single chair, high contrast to create claustrophobia; for each scene, a clear explanation of the effect on the audience (warmth and freedom vs surveillance and confinement); choices are concrete (lantern type, gel colour or number, angle, spread).
Secure (5-6): both scenes addressed with generally appropriate choices; at least one specific element per scene; effect on audience identified if not fully developed.
Developing (3-4): relevant ideas but generic (warm light for beach, dark for prison); limited specificity; effect on audience implied.
Emerging (1-2): basic identification of lighting with little or no justification; may describe only one scene.

practice_questions.text: Analyse the playwright's and director's intentions in choosing a largely bare stage for Noughts and Crosses. What do you think this staging choice communicates to the audience about the world of the play?
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (10-12): sustained analysis linking the bare stage to the play's Brechtian intent and thought-experiment quality; argues that a naturalistic set would anchor the play too firmly in a recognisable world, undermining its estrangement effect; at least two named scenes discussed with specific staging implications; considers how different elements (levels, symbolic props, projection) take over from physical set; substantiated judgement about the cumulative effect on the audience's critical engagement.
Secure (7-9): clear analysis of intentions with reference to the play's political or Brechtian dimension; at least one named scene; generally accurate effect identified; some specific staging elements discussed.
Developing (4-6): relevant but largely descriptive; may explain that bare stage is practical rather than political; limited named moments; effect on audience implied.
Emerging (1-3): basic point that the stage is bare with little or no analysis of why or what this communicates.

practice_questions.text: Discuss how you would design the set, lighting and costume for the Cross school scene in Noughts and Crosses, in which Callum arrives on his first day. Explain how each design choice communicates the power dynamics between Callum as a nought student and the Cross school environment, and what effect you want these choices to have on the audience.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (17-20): detailed and coherent design vision covering set (how the space is configured to make Callum physically smaller or more exposed; use of levels; institutional furniture), lighting (named lanterns and gels, hard-edged surveillance quality, colour contrast with earlier warm scenes), and costume (specific fabric and fit details for Callum's uniform vs Cross students' uniforms, communicating exclusion through material quality and fit); every choice anchored to the named scene and justified by its effect on the audience; consistent directorial vision; substantiated conclusions about cumulative audience response to the design as a whole.
Secure (12-16): all three design areas addressed with at least one specific choice per area; generally accurate staging logic; named moment referenced; some justification of choices in terms of audience effect.
Developing (7-11): relevant ideas across at least two design areas; generic terminology in places; limited justification; effects implied.
Emerging (1-6): basic design suggestions with little technical vocabulary; may drift into plot retelling rather than design analysis.

before.exam_tip_html:
For the 8-mark Interpret as Designer question, the single most common error is giving one design idea per discipline (a dark blue light, a sound effect, a plain set) without justifying the choice with reference to what it communicates to the audience at that specific moment. The mark scheme at Mastering level requires concrete, named elements: not ‘dark lighting’ but ‘a 10-degree profile lantern from front-of-house, gelled in a cold Lee 201 full CT blue, picking out the interrogation chair with a hard-edged pool’. Not ‘period costume’ but ‘a charcoal wool blazer, stiff and over-pressed, signalling institutional authority through the rigidity of its fabric’. Every design choice must carry a ‘because’ — what does it make the audience think or feel?

For extended staging questions, avoid trying to design every scene of the play. Focus on one or two named moments in detail — the beach opening, the school scene, the interrogation, the execution — and demonstrate a coherent design language across those moments. Examiners reward a clear and consistent directorial vision, not a list of ideas.

practice_questions.text: Identify one stage configuration that would allow an audience to see both the Johnstone and Lyons households simultaneously in Blood Brothers.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for any valid staging configuration that allows simultaneous viewing, such as: split stage (end-on or proscenium with divided acting area), traverse staging, thrust staging with areas on either side.

practice_questions.text: What is meant by a "gobo" in lighting design?
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying that a gobo is a thin metal plate inserted into a lantern; 1 mark for explaining that it projects a pattern of light (texture, shapes, foliage, window frames) onto the stage or set.

practice_questions.text: Explain how a costume designer could use colour and condition of clothing to signal the class difference between Mickey Johnstone and Edward Lyons.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for a specific choice for Mickey (e.g. faded colours, worn natural fibres, ill-fitting silhouette); 1 mark for explaining its effect on the audience; 1 mark for a contrasting choice for Edward (e.g. structured fabrics, cleaner palette, well-fitted blazer); 1 mark for explaining how the contrast communicates the class divide immediately to the audience.

practice_questions.text: As a lighting designer, explain how you would design the lighting for the moment Mickey receives news of the factory closure in Blood Brothers. Refer to specific lighting choices and their effect on the audience.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Fully concrete lighting design with named lantern type (e.g. Fresnel, profile spot), direction (e.g. top light from slightly stage right), colour (e.g. shift from warm straw to cold neutral white or desaturated blue), intensity (e.g. gradual dimming of surrounding wash, leaving Mickey in a tight pool), and a named gobo or absence of texture; every choice anchored to the moment and its effect on the audience named precisely (e.g. the removal of warmth isolates Mickey, making the audience feel his abandonment by the social world).

Secure: Most lighting areas covered with generally concrete choices; named lantern type and colour present; direction addressed; effect on audience stated for at least one choice.

Developing: Relevant lighting ideas but described generically ("dark lighting", "spotlight on Mickey"); few named elements; effect on audience implied.

Emerging: Basic mention of lighting with little specification; descriptive rather than analytical; no effect on audience.

practice_questions.text: Analyse Russell's intentions in contrasting the physical environments of the two households in Blood Brothers. What does he want the audience to understand about class and environment through the design of these two worlds?
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sustained analysis of Russell's class-critique intention across multiple design disciplines; analysis of how the contrast is not just realistic but political (same biology, different environments); specific reference to at least two design disciplines (set, lighting, sound, costume) with concrete examples; reference to named moments; consideration of how design choices make the audience interrogate their own assumptions about class; substantiated judgement.

Secure: Clear analysis of Russell's intent; reference to at least two design disciplines with some specificity; named moment referenced; effect on audience stated.

Developing: Relevant points about class contrast; intent partially addressed; general design observations rather than analysis of intention; effect on audience implied.

Emerging: Basic description of the two households with little analysis of Russell's purpose.

practice_questions.text: A director is staging the opening scene of Blood Brothers, where the Narrator introduces both households and the audience sees the two worlds of the play for the first time. Discuss how you would use set design, lighting and sound to establish the contrast between the Johnstone and Lyons worlds, and explain what effect these choices would have on the audience's understanding of the play's central themes.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Full set, lighting and sound design with concrete, named choices across all three areas; split stage clearly described with specific materials, textures and condition for each household; lighting states named with lantern types, colour gels and directions for each world; sound design with specific diegetic ambient sounds for each household and an underscore strategy for the Narrator's first appearance; all choices anchored to the moment and to the play's themes of class and fate; directorial intention clearly articulated; consideration of performer choices for the Narrator in this opening; substantiated overall judgement about the cumulative effect.

Secure: Most design areas covered with generally concrete choices; split stage addressed; lighting and sound choices present with some specificity; themes addressed; effect on audience stated.

Developing: Relevant staging ideas described generally; few named elements; themes mentioned but not interrogated; effect on audience implied.

Emerging: Basic listing of design ideas with no specificity; thematic connection limited or absent.

practice_questions.text: What term describes a staging arrangement where two separate areas of the stage are lit simultaneously to show two locations at once?
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for: split staging.

practice_questions.text: What is a gobo in lighting design?
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying it as a template placed inside a lantern; 1 mark for explaining that it projects a pattern or image of light onto a stage surface or backdrop.

practice_questions.text: Explain the effect on the audience of using a cold blue-grey lighting state for the Tilbury Docks scenes in contrast to a warm amber wash for the Windsor Castle scenes.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks: identification that colour contrast signals the two worlds visually (1); explanation of the specific emotional or symbolic effect of the cold dock lighting (industrial exposure, poverty, vulnerability) (1); explanation of the ironic effect of the warm Windsor lighting (wealth used against the Indian characters within it) (1); link to the play's political argument about imperial inequality (1).

practice_questions.text: As a costume designer working on The Empress, explain how you would design Abdul Karim's costume across the play to communicate his changing status at the court. Refer to specific fabrics, colours and at least one moment where the costume interacts with blocking or proxemics to create meaning.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Specific fabrics named (e.g. British woollen livery at arrival; silk or embroidered cotton Indian court dress after Victoria's patronage); colours chosen with symbolic rationale (muted British servant palette giving way to rich jewel tones of royal honour); at least one named moment in the play linked to a specific proxemics or blocking observation (e.g. court figures turning away from his Indian robes while Victoria moves toward him); audience effect clearly articulated throughout.

Secure: Fabrics and colours chosen with some specificity; at least one named moment referenced; proxemics or blocking mentioned; audience effect generally accurate.

Developing: Costume described in general terms (period robes, British uniform); limited reference to named moments; audience effect implied rather than stated.

Emerging: Broad idea of Indian versus British clothing; no specific fabrics, colours or named moments; descriptive rather than analytical.

practice_questions.text: Analyse the playwright's intentions in contrasting the physical environments of the East End and Windsor Castle in The Empress. What does Gupta want the audience to understand about power and imperial inequality?
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Multiple intentions analysed (audience positioned to feel the injustice of inequality; the physical contrast makes visible what official history hides; the rapid transition between worlds suggests the characters inhabit the same empire but in radically different conditions); linked to specific named scenes or moments; audience response addressed throughout; evaluates how design choices amplify Gupta's intentions; sustained and coherent.

Secure: Two or more intentions identified and explained with reference to named moments; some awareness of audience response; design briefly referenced.

Developing: Describes the contrast between the two worlds rather than analysing what Gupta intends; some relevant point but effect on audience implied rather than stated.

Emerging: Brief or plot-based description; limited engagement with playwright's intentions or audience effect.

practice_questions.text: You are the director of a GCSE production of The Empress. Discuss how you would stage the opening scene at Tilbury Docks, making specific choices about set design, lighting, sound and the performance of Rani, to communicate both the historical setting and the political isolation she faces. Refer to at least two design disciplines and one named performance choice.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Detailed and specific choices across two or more design areas (named scenic materials and set elements, lantern type and colour temperature with direction, soundscape elements layered to create the dockside texture) and at least one performer (vocal quality, posture, proxemics, eye contact at a specific moment); every choice justified with reference to what it communicates about Rani's historical and political situation; consistent directorial vision that draws the audience into solidarity with Rani; sustained throughout.

Secure: Choices across at least two disciplines and one performer; generally specific with some named elements; most choices justified; staging mostly coherent and directed.

Developing: Some choices made but generic (period set, sad lighting, period music); limited justification; staging lacks coherent vision.

Emerging: Lists ideas with little specificity or justification; description rather than analysis.

practice_questions.text: Name one staging configuration suitable for The Great Wave and explain one advantage it would offer for staging the play's two locations.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for naming a valid staging configuration (proscenium arch, thrust, end-on, in-the-round, traverse) with a brief explanation of its advantage for this play. Example: thrust — brings audience close to both worlds simultaneously, reducing comfortable distance from the injustice.

practice_questions.text: What is a lighting special in theatre design?
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying that a lighting special is a single focused lantern; 1 mark for explaining that it illuminates one specific area or performer against a darker surrounding stage, creating contrast and isolating the subject.

practice_questions.text: Explain how a set designer might use a minimalist set and levels to represent both Japan and North Korea without scene changes. Refer to specific set choices and their effect on the audience.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks: identification of minimalist approach — few scenic elements, location created through light and performer action (1); specific use of levels — e.g. a platform for the Japanese household and a lower, clinical floor for the North Korean compound (1); effect of simultaneous visibility on audience — both worlds are always present, reinforcing the play's parallel structure (1); link to meaning — the audience is never allowed to forget either location, holding the injustice in view throughout (1).

practice_questions.text: As a lighting designer, explain how you would design lighting for the scenes set in the North Korean compound in The Great Wave. Refer to specific lighting choices — including lantern type, colour, angle and intensity — and explain the effect on the audience.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: a fully specified lighting design — e.g. profile spotlights rigged steeply overhead (creating institutional surveillance shadows), Lee 201 Full C.T. Blue gel at 70% intensity (leaching warmth without losing visibility), a gobo of window bars projected across Hanako’s body (making captivity legible without scenic construction), and the surrounding stage in near-darkness so the spotlight functions as a searchlight. Every choice is anchored to a named moment (e.g. the first interrogation, a teaching scene) and the effect on the audience is explicitly stated: the audience feels Hanako is exposed and without protection.

Secure: at least two specific choices (lantern type and colour, or angle and gobo); at least one named moment; effect on audience present.

Developing: general lighting ideas (“cold blue lighting,” “harsh spotlights”) without specifying lantern type, gel, angle or intensity; effect is implied rather than stated.

Emerging: describes the desired “mood” of the lighting without any specific technical choices; no named moment.

practice_questions.text: Analyse Turnly's intentions in contrasting the physical environments of Japan and North Korea throughout The Great Wave. What does he want the audience to understand about the two worlds and the relationship between them?
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: analyses multiple intentions — the contrast between natural and institutional environments communicates the violence done to Hanako by the state; the sea as a shared but impassable element in both worlds embodies the theme of separation; the domestic warmth of Japan against the surveillance logic of North Korea is a political argument about the cost of state authoritarianism on individual life. Specific dramatic methods (stage directions specifying the sea, the contrast between open coastal setting and enclosed compound) are linked to specific intended audience effects. The response shows awareness that Turnly’s play is rooted in the real DPRK abductions and that the design choices must honour that reality.

Secure: identifies the contrast between locations and links it to themes of captivity and family loss; generally accurate about intended effect; at least one reference to a specific dramatic method.

Developing: describes the two locations and notes they are different; limited analysis of intention; effect on audience implied.

Emerging: lists features of each location without explaining what Turnly intends the contrast to communicate.

practice_questions.text: You are designing the full production of The Great Wave. Discuss how you would use set, lighting, sound and costume to differentiate between the Japan and North Korea scenes and to communicate the passage of over twenty years. Refer to specific design choices and their effect on the audience.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: a coherent design concept is proposed and applied across all four disciplines. Set: minimalist split stage, levels differentiating locations, cyclorama projection of sea for Japan and blank wall for compound. Lighting: warm amber wash for Japan versus steep overhead profile spots with cold gel and bar-gobo for North Korea; lighting state transitions signalling time. Sound: binaural wave soundscape for Japan, institutional drone and distant propaganda audio for compound, sea sound growing quieter over decades. Costume: period 1980s Japanese clothing for the family aging across decades versus Hanako’s costume becoming progressively more institutional in North Korea. All choices are specific (named gel, lantern type, fabric, silhouette), anchored to named moments, and linked to audience effect and directorial intention (the wave as controlling metaphor).

Secure: at least three design disciplines addressed with generally concrete choices; some named moments; effect on audience present.

Developing: general ideas across disciplines; few specific technical choices; limited sense of a coherent design concept.

Emerging: describes what each location “should look like” without specific design choices; no named moments; no discussion of audience effect.

practice_questions.text: Name one type of lantern a lighting designer might use to create a focused special on a performer in a garden scene.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for any of: profile lantern / profile spot / Fresnel / floor birdie. Accept any named lantern type.

practice_questions.text: What is a gobo in lighting design?
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying a gobo as a template inserted into a profile lantern; 1 mark for explaining that it projects a pattern of light onto the stage (e.g. leaf-break, branch pattern, geometric shapes) to suggest environment or texture.

practice_questions.text: Explain the effect of using a seasonal soundscape in the garden scenes of Things I Know to Be True. How might changing this soundscape across the four seasons contribute to the audience's experience?
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying the garden soundscape (cicadas, birdsong, wind, near-silence across the seasons); 1 mark for explaining the effect on audience at one or more specific seasonal points (e.g. summer cicadas communicate warmth and outdoor life; winter near-silence communicates coldness and exposure); 1 mark for connecting the soundscape to the emotional arc (the audience unconsciously reads the change in sound as the play's temperature dropping); 1 mark for a specific design choice (e.g. fading the soundscape to silence during the most charged dialogue moments to give the words acoustic clarity).

practice_questions.text: As a lighting designer working on Things I Know to Be True, explain how you would design the lighting for the winter garden to communicate the emotional state of a parent confronting a revelation they were not prepared for. Refer to specific lighting choices and their effect on the audience.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Specific design choices named for the winter garden: a cold, blue-white wash (Fresnel or wash bar, cool blue gel, reduced intensity compared to earlier seasons); the rose bush lit separately with a small warm unit (floor birdie, pale amber) to suggest it remains alive despite the cold; a profile special on the parent at the moment of confrontation (narrow beam, directed from above, cool white gel) to isolate them from the garden space. Every choice explained with specific effect on the audience at that moment. Silhouette considered: the parent standing still in the stark light, exposed.

Secure: At least two named lighting choices with some specification (lantern type or colour); both linked to the named moment; effect on audience mostly present. May not name all lantern types but shows understanding of how light creates meaning.

Developing: Lighting ideas present but generic ('cold blue light', 'bright spotlight'); one or two choices described without named elements; effect implied rather than explained.

Emerging: Basic mention of lighting with no named elements; no clear link to the named moment or the audience's experience.

practice_questions.text: Analyse how a set designer might use the coexistence of the kitchen and the garden on a shared stage to communicate the relationship between practicality and emotion in the Price family. Consider specific set elements and their symbolic function.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Detailed analysis of the kitchen/garden contrast as a spatial metaphor: the kitchen as Fran's domain of direct speech and practical action; the garden as Bob's private emotional territory. Specific set elements discussed (kitchen table and chairs, rose bush, earth ground cloth, levels); the symbolic function of the garden as Bob's inner life. The student analyses what Bovell and the designer want the audience to understand about the Price family's emotional geography. No plot summary.

Secure: Identifies both spaces and their contrasting qualities; explains the garden's symbolic function; names one or two specific set elements; some analysis of audience effect.

Developing: Describes the two spaces without sustained analysis of their symbolic relationship; may mention the rose bush but treat it as literal rather than symbolic.

Emerging: Basic description of the two spaces with little or no analysis of meaning or designer intention.

practice_questions.text: As a designer working across all four design disciplines for a production of Things I Know to Be True, explain how you would use set, lighting, sound and costume to communicate the progression from the spring opening to the winter ending of the play. Refer to specific design choices at two or more points in the seasonal arc and explain the intended effect on the audience.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: All four disciplines addressed across at least two seasonal moments. Set: specific elements for spring (rose bush in bloom, warm kitchen) vs winter (bare stems, stripped stage). Lighting: spring warm amber wash with gobo leaf-break vs winter cold blue-white Fresnel, gobo withdrawn. Sound: spring cicadas and birdsong vs winter near-silence or low wind underscore. Costume: lighter fabrics and warmer colours in spring/summer vs heavier, darker clothing in autumn/winter. Every choice anchored to the named seasonal moment with explanation of intended audience effect. Choices shown to work together as a unified design concept.

Secure: At least three of four disciplines addressed; at least two seasonal moments referenced; most choices specific (one or two named elements per discipline); audience effect mostly present.

Developing: Relevant design ideas across at least two disciplines; seasonal arc acknowledged but choices tend to be generic (e.g. 'warmer lighting in spring'); effect on audience implied not stated.

Emerging: List of design ideas with limited or no justification; one discipline or one season only; mostly descriptive.

practice_questions.text: Name the staging configuration in which the original New Vic production of Around the World in 80 Days was performed.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for: theatre in the round (accept in-the-round).

practice_questions.text: Define the term 'minimal scenography' as it applies to this production.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying that minimal scenography uses as few physical set elements as possible; 1 mark for explaining that lighting, sound and performance substitute for physical scenery, creating location through non-material means.

practice_questions.text: Explain how a lighting designer might use a warm amber wash and a gobo to create the atmosphere of the India sequence. Refer to the specific effect on the audience.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks: naming the warm amber wash and its association with heat and sunlight (1); naming the gobo and the specific pattern it would project (leaf shadow, sun dapple) (1); explaining the effect of the combination on the audience's sense of location (instant geographical orientation without set) (1); explaining the emotional or thematic effect (warmth, exoticism, contrast with London's grey) (1).

practice_questions.text: As a lighting and sound designer, explain how you would design the scene in which the company burns the ship's deck to fuel the engines during the Atlantic crossing. Refer to specific lighting and sound choices and their effect on the audience.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Specific lighting choices named and justified: floor-level warm orange flicker to suggest fire (floor lanterns or footlights), contrasted with cool steel-blue wash from above for the night-time Atlantic. Named effect on audience (visual tension between cold ocean and growing fire; desperation communicated without dialogue). Specific sound design: drone beneath the scene representing failing engines; crack and hiss of burning timber; non-diegetic string underscore rising in pitch to signal mounting stakes. Every choice anchored to this specific moment with a named effect on the audience. Design choices work together coherently.

Secure: At least two specific design elements named (one lighting, one sound) with effects. The moment is identified and the design is broadly coherent. Some use of technical vocabulary.

Developing: Design ideas are present but generic (exciting lights, dramatic music). Effects implied but not stated. Little technical vocabulary.

Emerging: Basic listing of design ideas (fire-coloured lights, sad music) with no justification or effect.

practice_questions.text: Analyse the playwright's intentions in using minimal scenography rather than a fully realistic set for this production. What is the audience meant to experience and understand?
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Analyses multiple intentions: the audience as active co-creators of each location; the theatrical self-awareness of the production (it celebrates storytelling as a craft, not illusion); the ensemble's skill is foregrounded as part of the meaning (watching the transformation is part of the pleasure). Identifies that the form mirrors the adventure's speed and energy: a naturalistic set would require pauses that would drain the pace Verne's narrative demands. Every point anchored to a named moment with a named audience effect. Awareness of the in-the-round configuration's design implications.

Secure: Identifies at least two reasons for the minimal set with generally accurate audience effects. At least one named moment. Some technical vocabulary.

Developing: States that the minimal set 'helps the audience imagine' without developing the idea. Limited reference to specific moments or design choices.

Emerging: Describes that there is not much set without analysing why this was chosen or what the audience experiences as a result.

practice_questions.text: As a director, explain how you would design the staging of the Reform Club opening scene and the transition to the first travel sequence. Cover your set, lighting, sound and costume choices, and explain how each communicates the play's themes of precision and adventure to the audience.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Full directorial design across all four disciplines, coherent and specific. Set: minimal furniture (a table, chairs) placed centre stage or on a raised platform; precise geometry of placement mirroring Fogg's world. Lighting: a neutral, slightly cool wash for London; naming of lantern type for the Reform Club interior (profile lanterns from above for formality and precision). Sound: specific soundscape elements (clock ticking, gentlemen's murmur, perhaps a distant foghorn signalling the journey to come). Costume: Fogg's consistent dark, precise base layer versus the ensemble's more varied accessories; the speed of the first role-switch from Club gentleman to customs official or ship's crew. Transition staging: how the lighting and soundscape shift to the first travel location, naming the new lighting wash colour and any specific sound cue. Every choice has a named effect on the audience. Directorial judgement about the overall intended impression (precision, control, the thrill of impending disorder).

Secure: Most disciplines covered with concrete choices. At least one named element per discipline. Some audience effect stated. The transition is acknowledged.

Developing: Some disciplines covered, choices are partly generic. Effects implied. The transition is mentioned but not designed.

Emerging: Basic listing of design ideas for one or two disciplines. Little effect, no transition discussion.

practice_questions.text: Name one physical theatre company whose work has influenced the staging of Romeo and Juliet.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for: Frantic Assembly (accept any correct physical theatre company with a valid link to the play).

practice_questions.text: What is proxemics?
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying it as the use of distance and space between performers; 1 mark for explaining that it is used deliberately to communicate emotional or social relationship (e.g. intimacy, power, conflict).

practice_questions.text: Explain how a performer playing Mercutio might use vocal and physical choices to communicate the tonal shift in the Queen Mab speech from playful mockery to feverish urgency.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for a specific vocal choice for the playful opening (e.g. quick pace, bright tone, voice projected to include the other characters); 1 mark for a specific vocal choice for the escalating section (e.g. pace accelerating, pitch rising, volume increasing toward the end); 1 mark for a specific physical choice for the opening (e.g. circling Romeo, relaxed posture, gestures contained); 1 mark for a specific physical choice for the feverish section (e.g. wider, less controlled movement, arms extending, the performer taking up more of the stage space).

practice_questions.text: As a performer playing Romeo in the balcony scene in Act 2 Scene 2, explain the vocal and physical choices you would make during his opening speech to communicate his wonder and urgency to the audience. Refer to a specific moment of the scene.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: The response names at least two specific vocal choices (e.g. entering breathless from the run across the Capulet garden, voice initially hushed and low in pitch, pace very slow as the speech begins — the haste of arrival giving way to a deliberate, wondering delivery; a rising inflection on key words; a pause before the famous address to Juliet as the sun, as if the thought arrives for the first time). The response names at least two specific physical choices (e.g. entering at speed from upstage, then arresting to complete stillness when Juliet appears; gaze fixed upward, head tilted slightly back, hands open at the sides in a gesture of submission; a single slow step forward on the couplet that ends the speech, halving the distance to the balcony). Every choice is anchored to a named moment and a named effect on the audience.

Secure: The student names at least one vocal and one physical choice with generally accurate effects; the moment is named.

Developing: The student describes Romeo's emotional state (wonder, love) without translating it into vocal or physical specifics; the moment is identified but choices are general.

Emerging: The student describes Romeo as passionate or in love without any vocal or physical choices; no named moment.

practice_questions.text: Analyse the playwright's intentions in staging Tybalt's entrance into the duel scene in Act 3 Scene 1. What is the audience meant to understand about Tybalt's character and the inevitability of the feud at this moment?
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: The response analyses what the playwright is designing the audience to feel and understand at Tybalt's entrance: the feud is not an abstraction but a physical force embodied in a real person, and that force is cold and deliberate, not hot and random. The student names specific performer choices for Tybalt (controlled posture, low steady voice, measured pace that contrasts with the energetic chaos of Mercutio's earlier scene) and explains the effect on the audience (Tybalt's control makes him more frightening than Mercutio's volatility; the audience understands that this encounter is different, that it will not resolve as earlier confrontations have). The student also considers design: how a sound designer might let the street noise drop slightly as Tybalt enters, or a lighting designer narrow the state, emphasising Tybalt as a focal point. A substantiated judgement about directorial intention is offered.

Secure: The student identifies Tybalt's threatening qualities and links them to at least one performer and one design choice with a named effect on the audience.

Developing: The student describes Tybalt as dangerous and angry without specific choices; reference to the audience's experience is implied rather than stated.

Emerging: The student describes Tybalt's character without linking it to any staging or performance choice.

practice_questions.text: You are directing the final sequence in the tomb in Act 5. Discuss your choices for the staging of Romeo's death, Juliet's waking, and their final tableau together. Refer to performer choices for both Romeo and Juliet, and to your lighting and sound design for this sequence, explaining the effect on the audience.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: The response covers Romeo's physical arc from entry to death (deliberate, low-energy movement signalling resolved grief; low-pitched, measured voice; touch and stillness as he places himself beside Juliet; the actual drinking of the poison staged as a quiet, private act rather than a theatrical one), Juliet's waking and rapid emotional transition (slow physical waking, then a sharp stillness as she sees Romeo; a silent moment before she speaks, the audience watching her understand; the final speech delivered at low volume and slow pace into near-silence), and the design frame (cold blue-white profile special from above, the rest of the stage in darkness; near-silence with a low string underscore fading to nothing; both performers in the costumes of their wedding night, the white now carrying grief rather than hope). The final tableau — both bodies lying together, the lighting state narrowing to a tight spot on them — is described with its effect on the audience. The Prince and family entering to break the image is addressed, with a choice about how that transition is lit.

Secure: The student covers both Romeo and Juliet with at least one concrete performer choice each; lighting and sound are addressed with at least one named element each; the final tableau is described.

Developing: The student describes the emotional arc of the scene but keeps performer and design choices generic; no named elements.

Emerging: The student retells what happens in the scene without making staging choices or identifying audience effects.

practice_questions.text: Name one vocal skill a performer might use to show Sephy's social discomfort in a scene with Callum.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for any one named vocal skill with brief justification: e.g. slowing pace when she recognises her privilege / dropping pitch and volume / pausing before key words / hesitation / quiet delivery.

practice_questions.text: What is meant by 'subtext' in acting and performance?
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for stating that subtext is what is implied or felt beneath the surface of the dialogue; 1 mark for explaining that a performer communicates subtext not by expressing the feeling openly but by performing the effort of containing or concealing it.

practice_questions.text: Explain the effect of proxemics in a scene between Sephy and Callum. In your answer, refer to a specific scene from the play and describe a specific staging choice, explaining what it communicates to the audience.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks: identification of proxemics as the use of physical distance and orientation between performers (1), description of a specific proxemic choice for a named scene (e.g. the two performers positioned close but body-angled away from each other in a confrontation scene) (1), explanation of what that choice communicates about the power gap or emotional tension between the characters (1), explanation of the effect this creates for the audience (1).

practice_questions.text: As a performer playing Callum in the interrogation scene, explain how you would use vocal and physical choices to communicate his attempt to maintain composure under pressure. Refer to specific choices and name the effect you want them to have on the audience.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (7-8): both vocal and physical choices named and specific; vocal: e.g. controlled, measured pace with deliberate pauses before responses, lowered pitch, reduced volume to signal control; physical: e.g. almost entirely still, weight settled, hands open and visible, only involuntary micro-movements betraying interior state, sustained but carefully chosen eye contact with the interrogator; each choice linked to the character's intention (to survive without giving anything away) and to the audience's experience (they feel the effort of containment, making the subtext palpable); named moment referenced.
Secure (5-6): both vocal and physical present; generally specific; at least one named moment; effect on audience identified.
Developing (3-4): relevant ideas but one dimension only (vocal or physical), or generic descriptors ('acts calmly', 'moves carefully'); effect implied.
Emerging (1-2): basic description of how the character feels with little or no translation into specific performance choices.

practice_questions.text: Analyse the playwright's and director's intentions in showing the relationship between Sephy and Callum through contrasting scenes of intimacy and confrontation. What do you think they want the audience to understand about love and inequality by placing these scenes alongside each other?
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (10-12): sustained analysis of intentional juxtaposition of intimacy and confrontation; argues that placing love and inequality in the same relationship forces the audience to confront the personal cost of systemic racism; at least two named scenes discussed; specific staging, vocal and physical implications explored; considers both Blackman's original intent and Cooke's adaptation choices; substantiated judgement about cumulative audience response.
Secure (7-9): clear analysis with some reference to intention; at least one named scene; generally accurate effect identified; good understanding of the relationship's central tension.
Developing (4-6): relevant but mostly descriptive; retells what happens in scenes rather than analysing intention; limited named moments.
Emerging (1-3): basic identification of the relationship with little or no analysis of intention.

practice_questions.text: Discuss how you would stage the beach scene (in which Sephy and Callum are together as young people, before the politics intensify) and a later confrontation scene of your choice. For each scene, describe the performers' positioning and physical choices, the lighting design and any sound or set elements that communicate the change in their relationship. Explain what effect you want these staging choices to have on the audience.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (17-20): detailed staging vision for both scenes; beach scene: open proxemics, warm lighting, spacious stage, performers' physical freedom and open body language; later confrontation: reduced proxemics or angled-away positioning, colder lighting state, physical containment and tension; at least one specific lighting element per scene (named gel colour or effect, lantern type); at least one sound or set element per scene; every choice anchored to named moment and explained in terms of audience effect; coherent directorial vision that shows awareness of the journey from openness to loss.
Secure (12-16): both scenes addressed; most design areas covered; at least one specific choice per area; named moments referenced; some justification.
Developing (7-11): relevant ideas but generic terminology; limited specificity; effects implied; may only address one scene in detail.
Emerging (1-6): basic staging ideas with little technical vocabulary; plot retelling may intrude.

practice_questions.text: Name one vocal skill a performer might use to communicate a character's emotional restraint in a quiet, charged scene.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for any valid vocal skill indicating restraint: e.g. low volume / near-whisper, slow pace, extended pause, soft tone, flat intonation. Accept any named vocal skill clearly linked to restraint.

practice_questions.text: What is meant by the term 'proxemics' in performance?
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying proxemics as the use of space/distance between performers; 1 mark for explaining how proxemics communicates meaning (e.g. close proximity suggests intimacy or confrontation; physical distance suggests emotional distance or tension).

practice_questions.text: Explain the effect of using stillness as a physical choice for Bob in the moment when he receives one of his children's revelations. How does this communicate his emotional state to the audience more effectively than overt physical reaction?
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying stillness as a deliberate physical choice (not absence of action); 1 mark for explaining what stillness communicates (restraint, suppressed feeling, the effort of holding oneself together); 1 mark for explaining why this is more effective than overt display (the audience is asked to read the emotion rather than being told it; the contrast between the stillness and the weight of the revelation creates tension); 1 mark for anchoring the choice to a named moment (e.g. Bob receiving the news in the garden).

practice_questions.text: As a performer playing Bob Price in the moment when he first hears about Mark's transition, explain the vocal and physical choices you would make to communicate his response to the audience. Refer to specific techniques and their intended effect.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two or more specific vocal choices named and justified (e.g. a slowing of pace so that each subsequent word takes longer to arrive, signalling that Bob is processing; a drop in volume to near-whisper when he finally speaks, so the audience must work to hear him; a pause of three or four beats before his response, in which the silence itself is expressive). Two or more specific physical choices named and justified (e.g. continuing to face the rose bush slightly rather than turning fully to face Mark, communicating difficulty in direct eye contact; a very slow, deliberate movement to place both hands flat on a surface, as if steadying himself; an almost imperceptible forward lean of the head). Both vocal and physical choices anchored to the named moment, with clear explanation of the effect on the audience.

Secure: At least one named vocal and one named physical choice for the named moment; choices generally specific (not just 'I would speak quietly'); audience effect present. May not achieve the depth of Mastering but shows clear understanding of technique.

Developing: Relevant choices mentioned but described in general terms ('I would be quiet and still'); limited specificity; audience effect implied rather than explained.

Emerging: Describes how Bob feels without naming specific vocal or physical techniques; no named moment; mostly descriptive.

practice_questions.text: Analyse how Bovell uses the contrast between Bob's restraint and Fran's directness to communicate the different kinds of love each parent offers their children. Consider how a performer might communicate this contrast through specific vocal and physical choices.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Analysis of Bovell's intention in creating two parents with contrasting emotional registers: Bob's restraint as an expression of the difficulty of speaking emotional truth; Fran's directness as an expression of love that refuses to withhold. The student explains what Bovell wants the audience to understand about the Price family's emotional dynamics, not just describe the characters. Specific performance techniques discussed for both characters. No plot summary.

Secure: Identifies the contrast between Bob and Fran, explains each character's emotional register with reference to performance choices, and makes some analysis of Bovell's purpose in the contrast. One or two specific techniques mentioned.

Developing: Describes Bob as quiet and Fran as direct without sustained analysis of what Bovell intends the audience to understand about parental love through this contrast.

Emerging: Basic descriptions of each character's personality with little or no analytical engagement with playwright's intentions.

practice_questions.text: As a director staging the final tableau of Things I Know to Be True, explain how you would use blocking, ensemble proxemics and at least one design choice to communicate the emotional state of the Price family in the aftermath of the play's final revelation. Refer to specific decisions and their intended effects on the audience.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Blocking and proxemics: specific positioning of named characters described and justified (e.g. Bob at centre, at floor level in the garden space, the four children arranged around him at measured distances that reflect their individual relationships to him — Rosie close, perhaps touching his arm; Mark/Mia at a slightly greater distance, standing tall and present; Ben further upstage, isolated; Pip equidistant). Physical contact specified (who touches whom, and why). Lighting: specific state described (e.g. a slow fade from a cold winter wash to a single warm amber pool centred on the rose bush, so the final image is held in the warmth of the garden rather than the chill of winter). Sound: specified (e.g. the cicada soundscape from the summer season returned at very low volume as an emotional memory, or absolute silence). Every choice justified with reference to the emotional content of the moment and its effect on the audience.

Secure: Most aspects addressed; at least two named characters' positions justified; one named lighting choice; sound considered; audience effect mostly present.

Developing: Relevant staging ideas but general in execution; positions described without clear justification; lighting present but not specific; audience effect implied.

Emerging: List of staging ideas without justification; one or two disciplines only; mostly descriptive.

practice_questions.text: In Around the World in 80 Days, what is the term for the physical distance between performers on stage, used to signal relationship and status?
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for: proxemics.

practice_questions.text: Define the term 'gestus' as used in performance analysis.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying that gestus refers to the social meaning embedded in a performer's movement or posture; 1 mark for explaining that it communicates character, status or a social/political position through a specific physical attitude.

practice_questions.text: Explain the effect on the audience of Fogg's stillness in contrast to Passepartout's kinetic energy. How does this physical contrast generate comedy?
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks: identifying the contrast between Fogg's stillness and Passepartout's expressiveness (1); explaining that Fogg functions as the straight man (1); explaining how the stillness sets up the comic reaction (Passepartout's energy lands against Fogg's lack of response) (1); explaining the audience effect (delight, surprise, a sense of the world's absurdity bouncing off Fogg's certainty) (1).

practice_questions.text: As a performer playing Fogg at the moment he is reunited with the Reform Club gentlemen at the London ending, explain the vocal and physical choices you would make to show his unchanged character despite the world-altering journey. Refer to specific performer skills.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Both vocal AND physical choices are specific and named, and both are anchored to the London ending moment. Vocal: measured pace, even pitch, consistent volume (no excitement in the voice — exactly the same as he left); possibly the same rhythm as the opening Reform Club scene to create a structural echo. Physical: the same precise erect posture, the same still hands; possibly the same pocket watch gesture as at the start, creating a circular staging pattern that mirrors the play's circular journey. Every choice is justified with a named effect on the audience (e.g. 'the audience laughs with recognition because his absolute consistency is the joke; the world has changed but Fogg has not').

Secure: At least one clear vocal and one clear physical choice, both anchored to the London ending. Effects are generally accurate. Some use of specific vocabulary.

Developing: Identifies that Fogg is calm and precise but does not translate this into specific vocal or physical choices. Effects implied.

Emerging: Describes Fogg's character ('he is unflappable') without any performer choices or named moment.

practice_questions.text: Analyse the playwright's intentions in constructing Passepartout as the audience's emotional proxy throughout the play. How does his performance function communicate meaning to the audience?
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Full analysis of Eason's intentions. Passepartout is designed to feel everything the audience feels: wonder at each location, alarm at each obstacle, warmth towards Aouda, admiration for Fogg. His emotional expressiveness allows the audience to have a relationship with the journey that Fogg's stillness denies. Identifies that his multi-roling also gives him a unique relationship with the audience: he can step in and out of minor roles and return to Passepartout without the audience losing track because his physical signature is unmistakable. Analyses how this dual function (emotional proxy + multi-roling pivot) serves Eason's overall theatrical intention of a co-created journey. Named moments. Named audience effects.

Secure: Identifies Passepartout's emotional proxy function with two or more audience effects. Some named moments. Awareness of multi-roling demands.

Developing: Identifies that Passepartout is 'the funny one' without developing the proxy function or analysing the playwright's intention.

Emerging: Describes Passepartout's character traits without analysing what the playwright intended or what effect this creates.

practice_questions.text: As a director, explain how you would stage the Hong Kong opium-house sequence to communicate Passepartout's physical and emotional disorientation. Discuss your performer direction, blocking, lighting and sound choices and their effect on the audience.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Full directorial vision. Performer direction: specific physical instruction for Passepartout (how disorientation manifests in the body: loss of controlled centre of gravity, unfocused gaze, slower and less deliberate gesture); the contrast with Fogg's maintained composure when he eventually arrives. Blocking: where Passepartout is placed in the space relative to other performers; how his movement pattern disrupts the usual orderly staging. Lighting: a specific state for the opium house (warm, hazy, possibly a Fresnel with a dimmed, low amber wash; possibly a gobo projecting diffuse shadow patterns to suggest smoke); named effect on the audience. Sound: a soundscape of the opium house (distant voices, a low drone, perhaps non-Western musical fragments); possibly underscore that deliberately disorients through rhythm. Every choice has a named effect on the audience. A directorial statement about what the audience is intended to feel.

Secure: Most disciplines covered, generally concrete choices. At least one named design element and one performer direction. Some audience effects stated.

Developing: Some disciplines covered, choices are partly generic. Effects implied. Limited performer direction specifics.

Emerging: Basic listing with little effect or directorial justification.

practice_questions.text: Name one vocal skill a performer might use to show that Hanako is deliberately suppressing her emotions in the interrogation scenes.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for any appropriate specific vocal skill: e.g. flat/even tone; measured pace; low pitch; controlled volume; strategic pausing.

practice_questions.text: What is stillness as a performance choice, and when might it be particularly effective in The Great Wave?
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for defining stillness as a deliberate choice to remain physically motionless at a significant moment; 1 mark for explaining when it would be effective — e.g. in the interrogation scenes, where Hanako’s absolute stillness communicates self-preservation and controlled concealment of her true feelings.

practice_questions.text: Explain how a performer might use vocal and physical choices to show the difference between Hanako on the beach in 1979 and Hanako in the North Korean compound a decade later.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks: specific vocal choice for the beach scene (high pitch, fast pace, full volume on the argument with Reiko; 1); specific physical choice for the beach scene (wide stance, outward gestures, blocking that cuts across the stage; 1); specific contrasting vocal choice for the compound (measured pace, low register, controlled neutrality; 1); specific contrasting physical choice for the compound (contained gestures, arms close to body, movements that do not claim space; 1).

practice_questions.text: As a performer playing Hanako, explain how you would use vocal and physical choices to communicate her internal state in the scene when she first confronts her new identity in the North Korean compound. Refer to at least one vocal and one physical choice and explain the effect on the audience.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: the response specifies concrete vocal choices (e.g. flat, even delivery at low volume — not dead but carefully neutral; measured pace with strategic pauses; a slight steadying of breath before each answer) AND specific physical choices (absolute stillness at centre stage; arms at sides, not held defensively; eye contact that is controlled rather than downcast — looking when safe, not when unsafe). The choices are anchored to the named scene (first interrogation) and the effect on the audience is stated: the audience reads Hanako’s stillness and neutrality as a strategy of self-preservation, understanding that she is spending as little of herself as possible. There is awareness of what this choice reveals about character.

Secure: at least one specific vocal and one specific physical choice; named moment; effect on audience present.

Developing: describes how Hanako is feeling (“scared,” “trying to be brave”) without translating feeling into specific vocal or physical choices.

Emerging: says “I would act scared” or similar; no specific choices; no named moment.

practice_questions.text: Analyse Turnly's intentions in showing the physical and vocal transformation of Hanako across the play's 24-year timeline. What does he want the audience to understand about the effect of captivity on an individual?
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: analyses Turnly’s intention to make captivity physically legible — not as melodrama but as a gradual, specific process of accommodation. The response links the performance arc (from the open, claiming physicality of the beach scene to the contained economy of the compound years) to Turnly’s political argument: what the DPRK abductions actually did to real people was not just imprison them but require them to perform a different self so thoroughly that the original self could only appear in private flashes. The analysis shows awareness of the play’s documentary roots and the ethical weight of staging a real person’s experience. Named moments are used (beach scene, first interrogation, teaching scenes, closing scenes).

Secure: identifies the transformation and links it to Turnly’s themes of identity erasure; generally accurate; at least one named moment.

Developing: describes the changes in Hanako without analysing what Turnly intends the audience to understand; effect is implied.

Emerging: retells plot events without analysis of playwright’s intention.

practice_questions.text: You are directing The Great Wave. Discuss how you would work with the performers playing Hanako, Reiko and Etsuko to show the passage of twenty-four years in their vocal and physical choices. Refer to specific performance choices for each character and their effect on the audience.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: a specific, differentiated performance brief for all three characters. Hanako: tracks accommodation and private resistance through changing proxemics, gesture size, vocal register, and the contrast between official and private voices across named scenes. Reiko: tracks grief hardening into advocacy — early scenes with high vocal tension and physical restlessness; later scenes with a brittle steadiness and forward-moving proxemics; vocal change from raw grief to controlled insistence. Etsuko: tracks the endurance of waiting — economical physicality, each movement deliberate; low, steady vocal quality that is endurance not defeat; subtle make-up and physical marks of ageing supporting but not replacing the performer’s choices. All choices are specific, named to moments, and linked to audience effect. The response shows directorial intention: these three transformations are the play’s argument about what state violence costs individual human lives.

Secure: at least two characters addressed with specific choices; generally concrete; effect on audience present.

Developing: general suggestions (“she gets older and sadder”) without specific vocal and physical choices; one or two characters addressed.

Emerging: describes what the characters go through rather than how a performer would communicate it; no specific choices.

practice_questions.text: Name the term for a completely still, held position on stage used to communicate a moment of intense emotion or decision.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for: tableau.

practice_questions.text: What is proxemics in performance?
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying that proxemics refers to the spatial distance between performers on stage; 1 mark for explaining how it communicates meaning, e.g. closeness can signal intimacy or threat, distance can signal emotional estrangement or power imbalance.

practice_questions.text: Explain how a performer might use physical stillness to communicate Proctor's controlled fury in the courtroom scene in Act 3.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for describing a specific physical choice (e.g. standing with feet planted wide, spine straight, arms by the sides or hands pressed flat on the court table); 1 mark for linking this to the emotional state being communicated (controlled fury held under a formal exterior); 1 mark for contrasting stillness with movement (explaining that stillness focuses audience attention more powerfully than restless pacing would); 1 mark for the audience effect (the effort of Proctor's restraint is visible and more frightening than an outburst, increasing dramatic tension).

practice_questions.text: As a performer playing John Proctor in the courtroom scene in Act 3, explain how you would use vocal and physical choices to communicate his moral conflict to the audience. Refer to at least one specific moment in the scene.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Names specific vocal choices (e.g. volume, pitch, pace, pause) AND specific physical choices (posture, gesture, proxemics, stillness, levels) for a named moment of the courtroom scene. Both sets of choices are anchored to that named moment. The performer explains the effect of each choice on the audience. There is a sense of the moral conflict — the gap between Proctor's knowledge of the truth and his inability to make the court hear it — communicated through the choices, not just described. The answer reads as a director's note, not a description of feelings.

Secure: Names at least one vocal and one physical choice for a named moment. Generally concrete. Connects choices to the moral conflict or the moment's meaning. Effect on audience explained.

Developing: Refers to character feeling angry or frustrated but expresses this as emotional description rather than translating into specific vocal and physical choices. 'I would look at Danforth to show my anger' — too vague for Secure. Limited sense of a named moment.

Emerging: States general emotional tone ('I would be angry and upset') without translating into any specific performance choices. No named moment. No vocal and physical distinction.

practice_questions.text: Analyse Miller's intentions in presenting Elizabeth Proctor's lie in the court scene. Consider what he wants the audience to understand about her character, the constraints she faces in Puritan society, and how a performer might communicate this through vocal and physical choices.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: States Miller's intention clearly (e.g. to show that Elizabeth is not cold but constrained — her lie is an act of love that costs her everything, and Miller wants the audience to understand the weight of patriarchal society on a woman's ability to speak freely). Analyses at least two specific performance choices for Elizabeth (e.g. the long pause before the lie, the downward gaze, the flattened voice) and links each to Miller's intention. Explains the role of dramatic irony (the audience knows what Elizabeth cannot say directly). Connects to the play's social context — the position of women in Puritan society. Reaches a substantiated judgement about why this is one of the play's most moving moments.

Secure: States Miller's intentions. Analyses at least two elements with generally concrete performance choices. Dramatic irony referenced. Context present.

Developing: Describes what happens in the court scene but does not consistently analyse Miller's intentions. Performance choices vague. Context present but not connected to the analysis.

Emerging: Retells the scene. No analysis of intentions. No specific performance choices. Descriptive.

practice_questions.text: You are directing the Act 4 jail scene, from the moment Proctor is offered the signed confession through to his decision to tear the paper. Discuss the performer choices for both Proctor and Elizabeth, the staging configuration, and at least two design choices (lighting and either sound or set). Explain how your overall production choices communicate Miller's final statement about integrity and the cost of conscience.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Covers performer choices for both Proctor and Elizabeth with named vocal and physical specifics (e.g. Proctor's voice dropping to near-monotone as he reads the confession, Elizabeth's stillness and her refusal to ask him to sign, the moment the paper is torn where both characters' voices are silent and only the physical action speaks). Staging configuration is chosen and justified (e.g. end-on or thrust, with both characters isolated in separate pools of light). At least two design choices are named and justified (e.g. cold blue-grey wash shifting to a single warm special on Elizabeth after the tearing; the sound of the off-stage drum growing slowly louder through the scene). Miller's final statement about integrity is explicitly connected to every choice. The answer reads as a coherent directorial vision.

Secure: Covers both characters with generally concrete performance choices. At least two design areas. Staging configuration named. Miller's intentions present.

Developing: Addresses one character thoroughly and the other briefly. Some design choices present but generic. Miller's intentions mentioned.

Emerging: Describes the scene. Few or no specific performance or design choices. No connection to Miller's intentions.

practice_questions.text: What term describes the spatial distance between performers on stage, used to communicate power or intimacy?
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for: proxemics.

practice_questions.text: What is meant by gestus in performance practice?
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying it as a term associated with Brecht's practice; 1 mark for explaining it as a physical attitude or stance that simultaneously reveals a character's social position and the playwright's comment on it.

practice_questions.text: Explain the effect on the audience of a performer playing Rani with deliberate stillness and reduced vocal volume when she is paid off at Tilbury Docks, rather than with visible anger.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks: identification that stillness and quiet communicate controlled resistance rather than reactive emotion (1); explanation that this creates audience sympathy and respect for Rani rather than pity (1); link to the play's argument about dignity under imperial power (1); comment on how the choice sets up the contrast with her freer register in the Ayahs' Home scenes (1).

practice_questions.text: As a performer playing Rani in the moment she is paid off by Mrs Wormwood at Tilbury Docks, explain how you would use vocal and physical choices to communicate both her vulnerability and her quiet dignity to the audience.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: At least one specific vocal choice (e.g. measured pace, reduced volume to near-inaudible, pauses of two beats before each reply, neutral tone without the upward inflection of deference) and at least one specific physical choice (e.g. feet planted at a fixed proxemic distance from Mrs Wormwood, controlled eye contact maintained throughout, hands loose at sides rather than clasped in service posture, upright spine), both anchored to the Tilbury Docks moment, both justified with reference to what they communicate to the audience about Rani's situation; sustained and coherent.

Secure: One vocal and one physical choice, both generally specific and anchored to the moment; audience effect addressed; mostly coherent.

Developing: Performer choices described but vague (e.g. 'she would speak quietly' without pace, pitch or proxemics); limited reference to named moment; effect implied rather than stated.

Emerging: Emotion described rather than performance choices; no named moment; descriptive.

practice_questions.text: Analyse the playwright's intentions in presenting Queen Victoria as simultaneously warm towards Abdul and the symbolic head of an Empire that marginalises characters like Rani. What is Gupta asking the audience to understand about how power and individual kindness coexist?
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Multiple intentions analysed (individual kindness does not dismantle structural power; warmth can make structural critique more devastating rather than less; audience forced to hold two responses simultaneously); anchored to named scenes (private lesson scenes versus public court politics); audience response addressed; performance and design choices referenced where relevant; evaluative judgement about why Gupta structures Victoria this way; sustained throughout.

Secure: Two or more intentions identified and explained; reference to named scenes; some awareness of audience response; generally coherent.

Developing: Describes Victoria as kind or as hypocritical without holding both truths in tension; some relevant content; limited analysis of playwright's purpose.

Emerging: Brief description of Victoria's character; little engagement with Gupta's intentions or audience effect.

practice_questions.text: You are directing a GCSE production of The Empress. Discuss how you would stage the contrast between Rani's servitude in the docks scenes and her belonging in the Lascar lodging-house scenes, making specific choices about performance, lighting and set to communicate her transformation to the audience.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Detailed choices about Rani's performance across both scenes (specific contrasting vocal and physical registers named and justified), lighting choices specific enough to be acted upon (named lantern, colour, direction, intensity for each scene), set choices that reinforce the performance contrast (materials, spatial arrangement, proxemics of characters within the space); every choice anchored to the contrast between servitude and belonging; consistent directorial vision; sustained throughout.

Secure: Choices across at least two disciplines and Rani's performance; generally specific; most choices justified with reference to the contrast; staging mostly coherent.

Developing: Some choices made but generic; contrast identified but not staging how it is produced; limited specificity.

Emerging: Lists general ideas; little specificity or directorial justification; descriptive rather than analytical.

practice_questions.text: Identify one physical technique a performer could use to distinguish playing Mickey at the age of seven from playing Mickey at the age of twenty-five in Blood Brothers.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for any valid physical technique showing contrast, such as: lower centre of gravity for the child vs contracted, inward posture for the adult; outward-radiating energy for the child vs inward, contained energy for the adult; impulsive proxemics for the child vs withdrawn proxemics for the adult.

practice_questions.text: What is meant by "proxemics" in the context of performance?
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying that proxemics relates to the physical distance between performers on stage; 1 mark for explaining that it is used to communicate character relationships, power dynamics or emotional states.

practice_questions.text: Explain how a performer playing Mrs Johnstone might use vocal and physical choices to show the ageing and exhaustion of her character across Blood Brothers.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for a specific vocal choice showing ageing (e.g. slower pace, rougher vocal quality, more effort on consonants); 1 mark for explaining its effect on the audience; 1 mark for a specific physical choice showing exhaustion (e.g. slower gait, weight lowering onto surfaces, less upright posture); 1 mark for explaining how together these choices communicate the toll of Mrs Johnstone's circumstances to the audience.

practice_questions.text: As a performer playing Mickey in the scene where he discovers the truth about his relationship with Edward, explain how you would use vocal and physical choices to communicate his emotional response to the audience. Refer to at least one specific vocal choice and one specific physical choice.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Both vocal and physical choices named precisely (e.g. vocal: pace drops to almost nothing, voice falls to a low flat pitch stripped of Liverpudlian inflection, a long pause before or after the key moment; physical: stillness replaces the usual kinetic quality, hands drop to the sides, eye contact with Edward is broken as the gaze goes blank, the body weight shifts backwards as though absorbing a physical blow); choices anchored to the specific moment of discovery; effect on audience named (e.g. the stillness after movement makes the audience feel the shock as a physical event); character motivation and given circumstances integrated.

Secure: Both vocal and physical choices present and generally specific; at least one choice anchored to the moment; effect on audience stated; some integration of character psychology.

Developing: Relevant choices but described generally ("I would sound shocked", "I would stand still"); little specificity of vocal or physical parameters; effect on audience implied not stated.

Emerging: Description of character feeling with little translation into physical or vocal specifics; no named moment; no effect on audience.

practice_questions.text: Analyse Russell's intentions in showing the physical and emotional contrast between Mickey and Edward across the play. What does he want the audience to understand about nature versus nurture and the British class system through the way the two performers should inhabit their characters?
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sustained analysis of Russell's intention to stage the nature versus nurture argument through contrasting performer vocabularies; specific reference to named moments where the physical contrast is most visible (e.g. the blood-brother oath, the teenage scenes, the final confrontation); analysis of how the audience is made to feel the tragedy through performer choices rather than through narrative; consideration of at least one design element that reinforces the contrast (costume, lighting); substantiated judgement about what Russell argues through the bodies of his two leads.

Secure: Clear analysis of Russell's intent with reference to class contrast and nature/nurture; at least two named moments; performance vocabulary addressed; effect on audience stated.

Developing: Relevant points about contrast between characters; intent partially addressed; descriptions of character rather than analysis of intention; effect on audience implied.

Emerging: Basic description of the two characters with little analysis of Russell's purpose.

practice_questions.text: A director is staging the sequence in Blood Brothers where Mickey and Edward meet as children for the first time and form their blood-brother pact, and then the same sequence after the time leap showing them as young adults in conflict. Discuss how a performer playing Mickey and a designer working in lighting and costume could use their skills to communicate both the joy of childhood friendship and the tragedy of adult estrangement in these two moments.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Full performer choices for Mickey at both ages (concrete vocal and physical vocabulary clearly distinguished between the child and the adult); specific lighting design choices for both moments (named lantern types, colour gels, intensity levels, transitions between the two states); specific costume choices showing Mickey's social arc; all choices anchored to the named moments with effects on audience stated; directorial intention articulated as a coherent argument about the play's themes; substantiated overall judgement.
