Secure: Performer and design choices present for both moments; generally concrete; at least one named lighting element and one costume choice; effect on audience stated for most choices.

Developing: Relevant ideas for both moments described generally; performer choices present but not fully specific; design mentioned without named elements; effect on audience implied.

Emerging: Basic description of both moments with few specific performance or design choices.

practice_questions.text: Name one vocal skill a performer might use to communicate Jo's vulnerability beneath her wit in A Taste of Honey.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for any of: pace (slowing), pause, volume (dropping), pitch (lowering), intonation, hesitation. Must be a named vocal skill.

practice_questions.text: What is proxemics in performance?
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying that proxemics concerns the use of space between performers; 1 mark for explaining that it communicates relationship, power, emotional closeness or distance.

practice_questions.text: Explain how a performer playing Geof might use stillness and proxemics in the lullaby moment to communicate his relationship with Jo. Refer to specific physical choices.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks: identification of stillness or tableau as a physical choice (1); specific description (e.g. seated near Jo but not touching, slight lean towards her, voice low and contained) (1); link to what this communicates about Geof's care without imposing (1); audience effect — tenderness, fragility, the sense of a family that is not quite a family (1).

practice_questions.text: As a performer playing Jo in the final scene with Helen, explain the vocal and physical choices you would make to communicate her emotional state to the audience. Refer to a specific moment in the scene.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Specific vocal choice named and described concretely (e.g. flatter delivery, reduced pace, slightly lowered pitch compared to earlier scenes, a pause before responding to Helen that was not there in Act 1) anchored to a named moment; specific physical choice named and described (e.g. less movement around the flat, more time seated or near the periphery of the space, a gesture that is contained rather than expansive — contrasting with Helen's wider physicality); both choices linked to Jo's exhaustion, resilience and the sub-text of what she is not saying; effect on audience named. Both vocal and physical skills present.

Secure: Named vocal and physical choices with some specificity; anchored to the final scene; link to character's emotional state; audience effect present.

Developing: Relevant choices but generic ("slow voice", "sad face"); some link to character; effect implied; may lack a named moment.

Emerging: Emotional description only ("Jo is scared"); no named skills; no named moment.

practice_questions.text: Analyse what Delaney intends the audience to feel at the end of the play when Jo and Helen are left alone together. Refer to the staging, the characters' relationship and the play's themes.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sustained analysis of Delaney's deliberate ambiguity — is this reunion or repetition? Analysis of the cyclical structure and what the final image (two women, the flat, the same world) is designed to make the audience feel; engagement with the play's major theme of women's limited options and the cycle Jo seems about to repeat; link to staging decisions that reinforce this ambiguity (proxemics, lighting state, the final jazz cue or its absence); analysis of Delaney's intention not to provide comfort or resolution. Substantiated judgement.

Secure: Clear analysis of the ending's ambiguity; themes engaged; some reference to staging; audience effect named.

Developing: Relevant points about the ending but described rather than analysed; theme present but thin; staging not engaged.

Emerging: Simple description of what happens; little analysis of why.

practice_questions.text: As a director, discuss how you would stage the final moments of A Taste of Honey to communicate your interpretation of the play's ending. Refer to performer choices, set, lighting and sound.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Full directorial vision with a clearly stated interpretive choice (reunion or repetition or deliberate ambiguity between them); blocking described specifically (where each character stands, whether they are touching, the proxemic distance as a visual statement); lighting state named and justified (e.g. same functional flat overhead wash as the opening — signalling nothing has changed; or a slightly warmer shift that leaves the interpretation open); sound choice (the final jazz phrase — its tempo, whether it ends before the blackout or continues; or silence — the musicians putting down their instruments); costume unchanged from earlier scenes, but perhaps adjusted (Helen having removed her coat — she is home); performer choices including vocal sub-text in the final exchanges; all choices linked to the specific interpretation being advanced. Substantiated and convincing.

Secure: Most areas addressed; staging configuration and blocking referenced; interpretive choice present; at least one specific design element alongside performer choices.

Developing: Design areas mentioned; limited specificity; interpretive choice present but underdeveloped.

Emerging: Listing of a few staging ideas; no clear interpretive direction.

before.exam_tip_html:
For 8-mark performer questions, the most common error is describing what the character is feeling (“Jo is scared and lonely”) rather than translating that feeling into specific vocal and physical choices for a named moment. The examiner wants to visualise what the performer is doing on stage. Name the skill (pace, pitch, volume, pause, posture, gesture, proxemics, facial expression), describe it concretely (“I would slow my pace to one or two words before a pause”), anchor it to a named moment (“when Jo realises Geof has left for good”), and explain the effect (“communicating her exhaustion beneath the surface composure, making the audience feel the weight of her isolation”). Both a vocal AND a physical choice must be present for the top band.

For 12-mark intentions questions, focus on what Delaney wants the audience to understand or feel — not what the characters feel. The play’s final scene is designed to leave the audience with unresolved ambiguity: is this reunion or repetition? Examiners reward students who engage with that deliberate ambiguity rather than forcing a single reading.

practice_questions.text: Name the Frantic Assembly co-director who worked with Andrew Bovell to develop Things I Know to Be True.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for: Scott Graham.

practice_questions.text: What is meant by 'given circumstances' in Stanislavski's acting approach?
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying given circumstances as information about a character's situation (who they are, where they are, when the scene takes place); 1 mark for explaining how given circumstances guide a performer's choices (they provide the specific context from which truthful action arises, shaping objectives and motivations).

practice_questions.text: Analyse how Frantic Assembly's physical theatre techniques communicate emotional content that the naturalistic dialogue scenes in Things I Know to Be True cannot reach on their own.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks: identification of Frantic Assembly's starting point (physical task rather than emotional display) (1); explanation of how this externalises subtext (shared weight and movement communicates what characters feel but cannot say) (1); reference to a specific technique (chair duet, lift, round-by-through-under) (1); explanation of the effect on the audience when the register shifts from dialogue to movement (the audience reads the physical interaction as emotional truth) (1).

practice_questions.text: As a performer playing Rosie in a Frantic Assembly movement sequence with Bob, explain the specific physical approach you would take to communicate the relationship between daughter and father. What would your choices of weight-sharing, spatial proximity and pace of movement communicate to the audience?
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Specific physical choices for the Frantic Assembly sequence: weight-sharing described in detail (e.g. beginning with Rosie offering her weight to Bob and him accepting it, establishing a physical trust; later in the sequence, Bob initiating a lift that Rosie resists slightly before yielding, suggesting the complexity of the relationship); spatial proximity managed carefully (close enough to communicate intimacy; not so close that it becomes claustrophobic, preserving the sense that this is a father and daughter rather than two people in crisis); pace of movement: beginning slower and increasing as the sequence builds, then resolving to stillness, so that the emotional trajectory is felt in the body before it is understood by the mind. Every choice anchored to the specific emotional content of the father-daughter relationship.

Secure: At least two specific physical choices for the sequence with justification; both anchored to the father-daughter relationship; audience effect present. May not achieve the precision of Mastering.

Developing: General movement ideas (e.g. 'we would move slowly and carefully'); limited specificity; audience effect implied.

Emerging: Describes the movement sequence without specific physical choices; no clear link to the father-daughter relationship.

practice_questions.text: As a lighting designer, explain how you would use a change in lighting state to support the transition from a naturalistic dialogue scene into a Frantic Assembly movement sequence in Things I Know to Be True. Refer to specific lighting choices and their effect on the audience's experience of the moment.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Specific lighting state described for the dialogue scene (e.g. a naturalistic interior warm wash, Fresnel cover from above, no moving lights, a sense of domestic ordinariness). Transition: a gradual dimming of the general wash (3-5 seconds) as the movement sequence begins, paired with the activation of one or two moving lights that track the performers, removing them from the fixed domestic world; gel shifts to a cooler, slightly less saturated tone (e.g. from warm 3000K to a neutral or slightly blue-tinted 4000K equivalent) to signal the shift to a more interior, subjective register. Return: the reverse at the sequence's end — the moving lights fade, the domestic wash returns, the gobo (if used for the garden) reinstates. Every choice explained with its effect on the audience.

Secure: At least two named lighting choices for the transition; both explained with audience effect; at least one named element (lantern type, gel colour, intensity). May not achieve the full precision of Mastering.

Developing: Lighting changes described in general terms ('I would dim the lights'); one or two choices; effect implied.

Emerging: Mention of lighting with no specific elements; no clear link to the transition moment.

practice_questions.text: As a director staging a scene from Things I Know to Be True that uses both Stanislavskian naturalistic dialogue and a Frantic Assembly movement sequence, explain how you would direct the performers across both registers and how the design would support the transition between them. Refer to specific practitioner techniques, performer choices and at least two design disciplines.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Both practitioners addressed with specific techniques. Stanislavski: the performer is anchored in given circumstances for the dialogue scene (specific objective named, e.g. Bob trying to hold the family together; specific physical grounding, e.g. hands in the soil, a physical task that is then released at the emotional peak). Frantic Assembly: the movement sequence described with named vocabulary (round-by-through-under, shared weight, a lift); the emotional content the sequence communicates named and justified. Design: lighting state for dialogue vs movement sequence (specific choices per phase); soundscape transition (diegetic domestic sounds for the dialogue; abstract underscore for the movement; return to diegetic on resolution). Costume contributes to the reading of the movement (e.g. a fabric that moves well, or a contrast between a character who is dressed more formally and one who moves with greater physical freedom). Every choice justified with reference to audience effect.

Secure: Both practitioners addressed; at least two design disciplines; specific choices made with justification. May not achieve the full integration of Mastering.

Developing: Both practitioners mentioned but not applied to specific moments; design present but general; audience effect implied.

Emerging: One practitioner only, or both practitioners described biographically without application to the staging task.

before.exam_tip_html:
For any question that asks you to apply practitioner techniques to this play, you must do more than describe the practitioner’s biography. Examiners are looking for the technique applied to a specific moment of the set play. The pattern to follow is: name the practitioner, name the technique, name the moment in the play where it applies, and explain what the technique achieves for the audience at that moment. For example: “Frantic Assembly’s chair-duet technique could be applied to the moment when Bob and a child are unable to speak directly to each other — the shared weight and negotiated movement of the duet communicates the effort of their relationship without any dialogue needing to name it, creating an emotional honesty the naturalistic scene cannot reach.”

For a 20-mark response, use the performer or designer perspective named in the question. Explain how the chosen technique shapes the performance or design choices for a specific moment and affects the audience.

practice_questions.text: Identify one Brechtian technique that Willy Russell uses in Blood Brothers.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for any valid Brechtian technique in Blood Brothers: the Narrator / a commentator who addresses the audience directly; songs that comment on rather than advance the action; the circular structure (prologue announces the ending); direct address / breaking the fourth wall.

practice_questions.text: What is meant by the "alienation effect" in Brecht's theatre?
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying that it is a technique for creating critical distance between the audience and the performance; 1 mark for explaining that it prevents emotional absorption and keeps the spectator analytically aware (or equivalent: it reminds the audience they are watching a constructed story about social conditions, not a slice of life).

practice_questions.text: Analyse how the use of the Narrator in Blood Brothers reflects Brecht's influence on Russell's dramatic method.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks: identification of the Narrator as a Brechtian device (1); explanation of one specific Brechtian function the Narrator performs (e.g. direct address, breaking the fourth wall, commenting on fate and class, functioning as a Greek chorus) (1); analysis of how this specific function prevents emotional absorption and prompts critical thinking in the audience (1); reference to how a performer or director might signal the Narrator's Brechtian register in staging or performance (1).

practice_questions.text: As a performer playing the Narrator in Blood Brothers, explain the vocal and physical choices you would make to communicate his Brechtian function as a moral commentator and social critic. Refer to a specific moment in the play.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Specific vocal choices named (e.g. low, measured pitch; deliberate slow pace; long pauses before key moral pronouncements; absence of emotional warmth in tone; no Liverpudlian accent, suggesting he exists outside the social world of the play); specific physical choices named (e.g. upstage centre stillness; eye contact held with the audience rather than with the characters; a slight turn of the body away from the action to signal his separation from it; gestus in a particular stance that communicates moral judgment); both choices anchored to a specific named moment; effect on audience stated (e.g. the audience feels watched and implicated, not simply entertained); Brechtian intent articulated.

Secure: Both vocal and physical choices present and generally concrete; Brechtian function addressed; at least one named moment; effect on audience stated.

Developing: Relevant choices but described generally; Brechtian function mentioned but not integrated into the choices; effect on audience implied.

Emerging: Description of the Narrator's role with little translation into specific vocal and physical performance choices.

practice_questions.text: As a lighting and sound designer, explain how you would design the moment in Blood Brothers when a song transitions from the realistic dialogue of a scene into a moment of Brechtian musical commentary. How would you signal to the audience that the theatrical register has shifted? Refer to specific design choices.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Specific lighting choices named (e.g. transition from local scene lighting to a full-stage colour wash in a cool or warm tone that removes naturalistic realism; Narrator caught in a separate profile spot with a contrasting colour gel; cross-fade rather than blackout to preserve the continuity of commentary); specific sound choices named (e.g. a brief silence before the musical introduction to signal the register shift; sparse acoustic arrangement using named instruments; removal of diegetic ambient sounds; the underscore during the Narrator's cue fading as the song begins); all choices anchored to the specific moment and to the Brechtian function; effect on audience stated concretely.

Secure: Both design disciplines addressed with generally concrete choices; at least one named lantern and one named sound element; Brechtian function addressed; effect on audience stated.

Developing: Relevant ideas for both disciplines but described generally; few named elements; Brechtian function mentioned; effect on audience implied.

Emerging: Basic mention of lighting and sound changes with no specificity; no Brechtian framing.

practice_questions.text: Discuss how a director of Blood Brothers might use Brechtian staging techniques alongside Stanislavskian performance approaches for the principal characters to create a production that is both critically engaging and emotionally powerful. Refer to specific moments in the play and specific design and performance choices across multiple theatrical disciplines.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Full directorial vision articulating the tension between Brecht (structural devices: Narrator, songs, direct address; staging choices: visible lighting rig, cool colour wash for song moments, Narrator in profile spot rather than warm wash) and Stanislavski (performer demands: Mickey's psychological arc from child to adult, Mrs Johnstone's emotion memory, Edward's given circumstances); specific named moments where each approach is most evident; concrete design choices across lighting, sound and costume supporting both modes; effect on audience articulated for both the Brechtian and Stanislavskian elements; substantiated directorial judgement about how the tension between the two modes creates the play's specific theatrical power.

Secure: Both Brecht and Stanislavski addressed with reference to specific techniques and moments; design choices present across at least two disciplines; effect on audience stated; directorial intent clear.

Developing: Relevant discussion of both practitioners but one treated more superficially; design choices present but generic; effect on audience implied; directorial intent present but underdeveloped.

Emerging: Basic mention of both practitioners with little application to specific moments or design choices.

practice_questions.text: Name the playwright who developed the concept of 'gestus' and the theatre tradition with which it is associated.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for: Bertolt Brecht / epic theatre / political theatre. Accept any one correct identification.

practice_questions.text: What is meant by 'given circumstances' in Stanislavski's system of acting?
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for stating that given circumstances are the specific social, historical and personal facts that define a character's world; 1 mark for explaining that a performer must fully inhabit these conditions to create genuine psychological truth in performance.

practice_questions.text: Analyse how the use of multi-roling for Cross authority figures in Noughts and Crosses creates a Brechtian effect. Refer to a specific moment or scene in your answer.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks: identification of multi-roling as a Brechtian device (1), explanation that it prevents individual character identification and presents authority as a social type rather than a person (1), analysis of how this creates a Brechtian distancing effect — the audience sees the system, not just individuals (1), reference to a named moment where multi-roling could be applied (e.g. officials, interrogators, guards sharing the same performer) (1).

practice_questions.text: As a performer playing Callum in the beach scene at the opening of the play, explain how you would use Stanislavski's concept of given circumstances to shape your vocal and physical choices. Refer to a specific moment in the scene.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (7-8): clear application of Stanislavski's given circumstances to Callum's specific situation; vocal choices: e.g. relaxed pace and natural rhythm in this scene, contrasting with the controlled register of Cross spaces — shows freedom before the political pressure; warmer, more open tone; physical choices: open posture, unconstrained movement, physical ease in the space, full and spontaneous eye contact with Sephy — communicating genuine connection before the social forces intrude; every choice anchored to the specific scene and justified by its effect on the audience (showing the audience what is at stake before the play takes it away); reference to given circumstances as the basis for each decision.
Secure (5-6): both vocal and physical present; generally accurate application of Stanislavski; at least one named moment; effect on audience identified.
Developing (3-4): relevant ideas but one dimension only, or generic; limited reference to Stanislavski; effect implied.
Emerging (1-2): describes the scene or character without genuine application of practitioner technique.

practice_questions.text: As a lighting and set designer, explain how you would use design to signal the shift between Brechtian political scenes and Stanislavskian intimate scenes in a production of Noughts and Crosses. Refer to specific design choices and explain the effect on the audience.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (7-8): clear and specific design language that distinguishes Brechtian scenes (institutional, frontal, colder lighting — e.g. a Lee 201 full CT blue general wash, hard-edged profile lanterns from front-of-house, minimal warm fill; set reduced to functional institutional pieces) from Stanislavskian scenes (warmer amber gel, softer Fresnel or flood wash, more intimate and enveloping light, set cleared to suggest private space); the cross-fade transition itself described as a design event with named timing and effect; every choice justified by its effect on the audience's emotional and critical engagement; a coherent system rather than isolated choices.
Secure (5-6): both modes addressed with generally appropriate choices; at least one named element per mode; effect on audience identified; transition mentioned.
Developing (3-4): relevant ideas but generic (warm and cold); limited specificity; effect implied; may not address the transition.
Emerging (1-2): basic distinction between the two types of scene with little design specificity or justification.

practice_questions.text: Discuss how a director might apply Brechtian and Stanislavskian principles in a production of Noughts and Crosses. In your answer, refer to specific scenes and staging choices, and explain what effect the combined use of both approaches has on the audience's response to the play's political and emotional content.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (17-20): detailed and coherent directorial vision that demonstrates genuine understanding of how both practitioners serve different aspects of the play; Brechtian application: named techniques (gestus, multi-roling, direct address as political device, design captions or projections, ensemble performance of authority figures) applied to named scenes with specific staging detail; Stanislavskian application: given circumstances for Sephy and Callum, moment-to-moment naturalism in the intimate two-handers, specific vocal and physical detail; the transition between modes described as a staging event with lighting and sound choices; sustained analysis of the cumulative effect on the audience — how the double awareness (emotional involvement + critical distance) is the play's intended effect; substantiated directorial judgement.
Secure (12-16): both practitioners applied to named scenes; most areas covered; generally accurate staging; at least one specific choice per practitioner application; effect on audience identified; some directorial coherence.
Developing (7-11): relevant ideas across both practitioners but largely biographical; limited application to named scenes; generic staging; effects implied.
Emerging (1-6): basic identification of practitioners with little or no application to the specific play; may describe what Brecht and Stanislavski believed without staging any of it.

before.exam_tip_html:
The most common error in practitioner questions is describing a practitioner’s biography without applying the techniques to a specific moment of the set play. Knowing that Brecht developed epic theatre and that Stanislavski created the system of naturalistic acting is not enough on its own — the mark scheme rewards application. Your answer must move quickly from ‘Brecht believed that…’ to ‘in the scene when Callum is interrogated, a director applying Brechtian principles might stage this by… because this would make the audience feel…’.

For extended staging questions that ask about practitioner influence, always show awareness of both practitioners: Brecht for the political, distancing, public scenes, and Stanislavski for the intimate, emotionally truthful private scenes. Show that you understand the production needs both. An answer that only discusses Brecht will miss the naturalistic dimension; one that only discusses Stanislavski will miss the political argument entirely.

practice_questions.text: Name the Northern Irish playwright who wrote The Great Wave.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for: Francis Turnly.

practice_questions.text: What is gestus in Brechtian theatre?
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying gestus as a performance technique involving a physical pose or attitude; 1 mark for explaining that it expresses the social relationship between characters at a given moment, making the power dynamic between them immediately readable to the audience.

practice_questions.text: Explain how a director could use one Brechtian technique to communicate the political dimension of The Great Wave to the audience. Refer to a specific moment in the play.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks: naming a Brechtian technique (direct address, projected titles, gestus, tableau, Verfremdungseffekt; 1); explaining how it would be applied to a specific moment of the play (e.g. projected date and location titles at each scene change to insist this is a documented event; 1); effect on the audience (positions them as witnesses to a political crime rather than spectators of a domestic drama; 1); link to Turnly’s intention (the play is about a real state act, not just individual suffering; 1).

practice_questions.text: As a performer playing Kum-Chol, Hanako’s husband in North Korea, explain how you would use vocal and physical choices to show that he is both complicit in the state system and recognisably human. Refer to at least one vocal and one physical choice and explain the effect on the audience.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: the response holds both dimensions simultaneously. Physical choices that signal systemic authority (upright bearing, formal proxemics, a gestus of institutional belonging — e.g. a particular way of standing in a doorway that signals ownership of the space) alongside physical choices that reveal humanity (a moment of stillness when listening to Hanako that suggests something other than pure official engagement; a fractionally longer pause before an order). Vocal choices similarly: a formal, even register for official transactions, but a shift in tone or pace in private exchanges. The response anchors these to named moments and explains the effect on the audience: they are held in a dual response, understanding him as a perpetrator and as a person, which is the play’s moral complexity.

Secure: at least one specific vocal and one physical choice; named moment; effect on audience present; some engagement with the dual character.

Developing: describes what Kum-Chol is feeling without translating into specific choices; or plays only one dimension (either evil or sympathetic, not both).

Emerging: generic emotional description; no specific choices; no named moment.

practice_questions.text: As a lighting or sound designer, explain how you could use design choices to reinforce the Brechtian political frame of The Great Wave. Refer to at least one specific design choice and its effect on the audience.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: the response proposes design choices that function as Brechtian devices — projected titles (dates, number of abductees, location) in a plain sans-serif typeface on the cyclorama at key transitions (interrupting the naturalistic fiction to insist on documentary reality); or a cold, high-contrast lighting state for the official scenes that makes them feel less naturalistic than the family scenes (a design “estrangement”); or a sound design that introduces institutional broadcast sound without the emotional preparation a naturalistic production would use (no gradual fade-in, just the sound arriving — a Brechtian shock cut). Every choice is named specifically (e.g. projected white sans-serif text at 80% opacity on the cyclorama; or a sudden cut to tinny propaganda audio at mid-volume from a single downstage speaker) and the effect on the audience is stated: the audience is reminded that this is a documented event, not a private story.

Secure: at least two specific design choices; at least one linked to Brechtian technique; effect on audience present.

Developing: general design ideas (“I would use cold lighting”) without linking to Brechtian technique or naming specific elements.

Emerging: describes the desired atmosphere without specific design choices; no link to practitioner.

practice_questions.text: You are directing The Great Wave. Discuss how you would apply both Brechtian techniques and Stanislavski's approach to different moments of the production to serve the play's dual purpose: political argument and emotional truth. Refer to specific moments of the play and specific staging choices.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: a clear directorial vision is articulated that uses both practitioners purposefully. Brechtian choices: direct address at the official announcement scenes (audience positioned as jury); gestus for the officials and Kum-Chol (making their social role legible); projected title cards at scene transitions (insisting on documentary reality); a design language for the North Korean compound that is slightly less naturalistic than the Japan scenes (harder edges, less texture, more institutional geometry). Stanislavskian choices: detailed given circumstances for Hanako’s arc (what she has lost, what she still has, what she wants from each encounter); specific vocal and physical choices for the teaching scenes with Jung Sun (warmth, however provisional); the emotional truth of Etsuko’s waiting given full interior life. The response explains why each practitioner is appropriate to which type of scene and shows awareness that the two approaches reinforce rather than contradict each other. Named moments throughout. Audience effect throughout.

Secure: both practitioners addressed with at least one specific application each; named moments; effect on audience present.

Developing: one practitioner addressed in detail, the other mentioned but not applied; general choices.

Emerging: describes what the practitioners believed without applying their techniques to the play; no named moments.

practice_questions.text: Name the Russian theatre practitioner whose system of actor training is based on objective, obstacle and the pursuit of psychological truth in performance.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for: Constantin Stanislavski (accept Stanislavski).

practice_questions.text: What is gestus in Brecht's theatre?
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying it as a moment in which a character's social attitude or relationship is made visible through a clear physical action; 1 mark for linking it to Brecht's aim to make the audience think critically rather than simply feel.

practice_questions.text: Analyse how a director applying Stanislavski's objective method to Juliet in the potion soliloquy scene in Act 4 might shape the performer's vocal and physical choices differently from a director using a heightened, stylised approach.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks: identification of Stanislavski's objective method (what Juliet wants at this moment — e.g. to survive, to trust Friar Lawrence, to reach Romeo) (1); explanation of how a specific objective shapes a vocal choice (e.g. her pace is unsteady, catching and restarting, because the objective is constantly threatened by doubt) (1); identification of the heightened approach (the soliloquy delivered as a formal verse performance, each image spoken outward to the audience as a deliberate act of shared imagination) (1); comparison of the two effects on the audience (the naturalistic approach makes the audience feel Juliet's private terror; the heightened approach makes them co-witnesses to a ritual decision) (1).

practice_questions.text: As a performer playing Romeo, explain how you would use Stanislavski's objective method to shape your vocal and physical choices in the tomb scene. Refer to a specific moment of the scene.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: The response names a clear, specific objective for Romeo in the tomb (e.g. to say goodbye properly; to ensure Juliet knows she was the only real thing in his life). The student explains how this objective shapes specific vocal choices (e.g. slow, deliberate pace because he is not rushing — he has decided; low pitch and controlled volume because he is past anger; brief pauses as if choosing each word carefully, not from uncertainty but from the weight of what he is saying). The student names specific physical choices (e.g. moving to kneel beside Juliet rather than standing, closing the physical distance for the last time; hands touching her face, then releasing; the body language of someone who has resolved, not panicked). Every choice is anchored to the named moment of the tomb scene and the effect on the audience is named.

Secure: The student names an objective and links it to at least one vocal and one physical choice with a named moment and a generally accurate effect.

Developing: The student describes Romeo's grief without translating it into Stanislavski's method; choices are general (he would seem sad).

Emerging: The student mentions Stanislavski but does not apply his technique; no named moment.

practice_questions.text: As a lighting and sound designer, explain how you would design the technical elements for a production of Romeo and Juliet that uses a Brechtian approach: one that keeps the audience thinking critically about the feud rather than simply feeling the romance. Refer to specific design choices and their effect on the audience.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: The response names specific lighting choices consistent with a Brechtian approach (e.g. exposed lighting rig, no softening gels, a cool white open flood that prevents the romantic warmth of amber washes; lighting changes made visibly as a technical operation rather than a seamless transition, reminding the audience they are watching theatre). The response names specific sound choices (e.g. non-diegetic sound cues introduced at moments of feud violence that are documentary or newsreel-like in texture, rather than romantic underscore; or a recurring motif, a recurring drumbeat or chord, every time a Montague or Capulet act perpetuates the feud). Every choice is explained with reference to its effect on the audience (e.g. the exposed rig prevents emotional absorption; the newsreel sound reminds the audience that this violence is systemic, not just personal). Specific named moments of the play are referenced (the prologue, the brawl, the duel).

Secure: The student names at least one lighting and one sound choice consistent with a Brechtian aesthetic, explains the effect on the audience, and references at least one moment of the play.

Developing: The student describes Brechtian ideas generally (less emotional lighting, more exposed set) without naming specific elements or moments.

Emerging: The student describes Brecht without connecting his techniques to specific design choices.

practice_questions.text: You are directing Romeo and Juliet. Discuss how you would approach the production, choosing between psychological realism (Stanislavski), physical theatre and the heightened style of the Globe tradition. Refer to the impact of your chosen approach on performer choices, staging configuration and design, anchored to at least two named moments of the play.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: The response articulates a clear directorial concept and defends it: e.g. a hybrid approach in which the lovers' scenes are played in a Stanislavskian register (internal truth, naturalistic physical behaviour, conversational verse) while the feud scenes use physical theatre (stylised, choreographed violence, movement that externalises the social mechanics of inherited aggression). The staging configuration is chosen to serve this concept (e.g. a thrust stage allows the intimacy of naturalistic scenes while the extended platform allows physical theatre sequences to read in three dimensions). Specific scenes are addressed: the balcony scene (Stanislavskian, close, direct, verse nearly transparent); the duel (physical theatre, choreographed, stylised, nearly silent except for a percussion soundscape); the tomb (a return to interiority, Stanislavskian stillness). Design choices are consistent across the hybrid concept: costume moves from naturalistic period detail for the lovers to more stylised, colour-coded garments for the families; lighting transitions from warm specials for private scenes to a harsher, more functional state for feud scenes. A substantiated justification for the hybrid choice is offered, explaining what it achieves that a single-approach production would not.

Secure: The student articulates a clear approach, names at least two practitioners, anchors choices to two named scenes, and covers performer and design elements with at least one concrete element each.

Developing: The student describes one practitioner approach with general choices; design is addressed but remains generic; only one moment of the play is referenced.

Emerging: The student describes practitioners' biographies without applying techniques to specific staging choices; no named moments.

practice_questions.text: Name the practitioner most closely associated with the theatrical concept of the 'alienation effect'.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for: Bertolt Brecht.

practice_questions.text: What is meant by the term 'super-objective' in Stanislavski's system of actor training?
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying it as a character's driving desire or overall goal; 1 mark for explaining that it shapes all the character's choices throughout the play, providing through-line and consistency.

practice_questions.text: Analyse how a director applying Theatre Workshop's methods might approach the rehearsal of the flat-cleaning scenes between Jo and Geof. Refer to specific techniques and their effect on the performance.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks: identification of Theatre Workshop's devised, improvisational approach (1); application to the specific scenes (e.g. allowing performers to discover the domestic rhythms of shared life through improvisation rather than formal blocking) (1); link to what this produces in performance (texture of genuine shared intimacy, discoveries that a scripted rehearsal might miss) (1); link to audience effect (the scenes feel lived-in and truthful) (1).

practice_questions.text: As a performer playing Jo, explain how you would apply Stanislavski's approach to emotional truth to a moment when she is alone in the flat, preparing for the baby's arrival. Refer to vocal and physical choices.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Specific application of Stanislavskian principles (internal justification, emotional truth, drawing on personal experience or imagination to motivate the physical and vocal choices); named vocal choice described concretely (e.g. a quiet monologue-like delivery, minimal volume, pace that has no audience to perform for — Jo alone with herself); named physical choice described concretely (e.g. slow, deliberate actions with the baby's things, a stillness that is exhausted rather than peaceful, gestus that communicates the weight of her situation); link to super-objective (Jo wants to survive and be seen — and here, briefly, no one is watching); audience effect named. Both vocal and physical skills present; Stanislavski explicitly applied.

Secure: Named skills with some Stanislavskian framing; vocal and physical choices present; link to the moment and its meaning; generally concrete.

Developing: Emotional description or general practitioner biography without clear application; some named skills but thin.

Emerging: Emotional description only; no named skills; Stanislavski mentioned but not applied.

practice_questions.text: As a lighting and sound designer, explain how you would apply Brechtian principles to the staging of a transition between two scenes in A Taste of Honey. Refer to specific design choices and their effect on the audience.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Specific application of Brechtian visible staging (e.g. keeping the house lights at a low level during scene changes so the audience sees the transition happening; jazz musicians playing an audible transitional phrase that comments ironically on the mood change; lighting rig partially visible — not hidden by borders); named lighting choice for the transition (e.g. a slow cross-fade without a blackout, with one area fading up as another fades down); named sound choice (jazz musicians responding to the transition's emotional content with a specific phrase — muted trumpet, walking bass); explanation of how these choices remind the audience they are watching a performance, maintaining critical awareness; audience effect named. All choices linked to Brechtian intent.

Secure: Named design choices with some Brechtian framing; lighting and sound both addressed; audience effect present; generally specific.

Developing: General design ideas with Brecht mentioned but not clearly applied; limited specificity.

Emerging: Basic design description; Brecht not meaningfully applied; no specific design elements.

practice_questions.text: As a director, discuss how you would apply the methods of Theatre Workshop and Brecht to stage the moment when Jo directly addresses the audience about her pregnancy. Refer to performer choices, staging configuration, lighting and sound.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Full directorial vision drawing explicitly on Theatre Workshop methods (rehearsal process informing the rawness of the moment; devised quality to the delivery) and Brechtian devices (direct address isolated by a lighting special; jazz musicians pausing or playing quietly underneath, making their presence audible as a Brechtian reminder of the theatrical frame); staging configuration named and justified (e.g. end-on proscenium so the direct address is a clear downstage move into the audience's space); lighting design specific (narrow profile special from front, dropping the domestic wash behind so Jo stands apart from the flat); sound design specific (musicians stop or play a single sustained note; the pause before they resume registers as loaded); performer choices include vocal (direct, conversational tone of direct address — not theatrical projection but intimate confidence) and physical (downstage, turned away from the flat and towards the audience — the body language of confession); all choices linked to what Brecht and Littlewood wanted: an audience who witnesses rather than simply watches, who holds both feeling and thought. Stanislavski also invoked for the internal emotional truth that makes the moment land. Substantiated throughout.

Secure: Most disciplines addressed; Brechtian and Littlewood methods named and applied to specific choices; performer and design choices present; staging configuration referenced.

Developing: Practitioner names mentioned but applied generally; design choices present but thin; staging limited.

Emerging: Basic staging ideas; practitioner biography without application.

practice_questions.text: Name the German theatre practitioner who developed the concept of epic theatre and the alienation effect.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for: Bertolt Brecht.

practice_questions.text: What is the alienation effect (Verfremdungseffekt) as used by Brecht?
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying it as a technique that creates critical distance between audience and action; 1 mark for explaining that it prevents emotional immersion and encourages the audience to reflect politically on what they are seeing.

practice_questions.text: Analyse how a director could use Brechtian gestus to stage the British court figures' response to Abdul Karim's growing position at Windsor Castle.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks: identification that gestus is a stylised physical stance exposing social role (1); description of a specific gestural choice for the court figures (e.g. synchronised backward lean, collective turning of backs) (1); explanation that the choreographic quality makes the court read as a social institution rather than individual characters (1); link to the Brechtian purpose of making structural power visible to the audience (1).

practice_questions.text: As a performer playing Rani in the scene when she first delivers a direct address to the audience, explain how you would use vocal and physical choices to create a Brechtian witness moment rather than a naturalistic scene. Refer to a specific vocal choice and a specific physical choice.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: At least one specific vocal choice in the Brechtian mode (e.g. slightly elevated, clear projection directly out to the audience, slowing pace to allow the audience to process rather than be swept along, no emotional quaver — the voice of a witness, not a victim) and at least one specific physical choice (e.g. stepping downstage centre to break the tableau of the dock scene, turning squarely to face the audience, arms at sides rather than in narrative gesture, eye contact sweeping the auditorium rather than locking to one person), both anchored to the direct address moment, both justified with reference to the Brechtian distancing effect and what it communicates to the audience; sustained.

Secure: One vocal and one physical choice, both generally specific and anchored to the moment; Brechtian intent addressed; mostly coherent.

Developing: Choices offered but without the Brechtian frame; may describe the scene naturalistically rather than as a witness address; limited reference to practitioner technique.

Emerging: Emotion described rather than vocal/physical choices; no reference to practitioner technique; descriptive.

practice_questions.text: As a designer working on a production of The Empress that draws on Brechtian staging principles, explain how you would design the set and lighting for the Tilbury Docks scene to make visible the historical and political context of Rani's situation. Refer to specific design choices and their effect on the audience.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Specific Brechtian set choices (bare stage, minimal symbolic props named with their symbolic function, visible lighting rig, possible use of projected captions with historical context) and lighting choices (cool, even wash rather than atmospheric special, visible lanterns, no attempt at naturalistic illusion), each justified with reference to the Brechtian principle of theatrical visibility and the audience's role as critical witness; named moment anchored; audience effect articulated; sustained.

Secure: Set and lighting choices with some Brechtian rationale; generally specific; audience effect addressed; mostly coherent.

Developing: Design choices described but without Brechtian framing; some relevant content but limited reference to practitioner technique or audience effect.

Emerging: General design ideas listed; no reference to Brechtian principles; descriptive.

practice_questions.text: You are the director of a GCSE production of The Empress. Discuss how you would use Brechtian techniques at the structural level of the production and Stanislavskian performance at the individual character level to communicate both the historical argument and the personal truth of Rani's story. Refer to at least two staging choices and at least one named performance moment.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Clear articulation of the two practitioners operating at different levels (Brecht: structure, framing, audience address, design visibility; Stanislavski: individual performer truth, inner motivation, psychological specificity); at least two specific staging choices that demonstrate Brechtian technique (named design element, direct address moment staged with specific lighting and physical performance choice); at least one named Stanislavskian performance moment (specific vocal and physical choice rooted in Rani's inner life at a named scene); both approaches integrated into a coherent directorial vision that justifies why the play needs both; audience effect articulated throughout; sustained.

Secure: Both practitioners addressed with some specificity; at least one staging choice and one performance moment named; mostly coherent integration of the two approaches.

Developing: Practitioners described separately without integration; some staging and performance content but limited specificity or justification.

Emerging: Brief mention of Brecht and/or Stanislavski without application to specific staging choices; descriptive.

practice_questions.text: Name the Brechtian term for a physical gesture or attitude that defines a character's social function rather than their individual psychology.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for: gestus.

practice_questions.text: What is the alienation effect (Verfremdungseffekt) in Brechtian theatre?
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying that the alienation effect prevents the audience from losing themselves emotionally in the story; 1 mark for explaining its purpose — to keep the audience critically aware so they think about the social and political implications of what they are watching, rather than simply empathising with characters.

practice_questions.text: Analyse how a director might use Brechtian gestus in staging Judge Danforth in the courtroom scene.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for defining gestus or explaining the Brechtian technique at stake (making the social function visible through a repeated physical signature); 1 mark for a specific gestus choice for Danforth (e.g. a mechanically repeated gavel motion, a pointed finger, the reflex of a raised hand dismissing testimony); 1 mark for linking the staging position to the gestus (e.g. Danforth upstage centre on a raised platform, the gavel always at a fixed height, communicating automated institutional authority); 1 mark for the audience effect (the audience reads Danforth not as a conflicted individual but as the body of a system that cannot admit error, which is more politically frightening than personal malice would be).

practice_questions.text: As a performer playing John Proctor, explain how you would use a Stanislavskian approach to bring emotional truth to the linen scene in Act 2. Refer to given circumstances, specific vocal choices and specific physical choices.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Names specific given circumstances that Proctor carries into the linen scene (the affair, the guilt, Elizabeth's distrust, his private scepticism about the witch trials). Translates these into named vocal choices (e.g. a deliberately lowered pitch, a controlled pace that flattens his emotional register, a brief pause before he speaks her name) AND physical choices (e.g. slow deliberate movement across the kitchen, remaining on the opposite side of the table, avoiding direct eye contact until the emotional pressure makes it unavoidable). Explains how the Stanislavskian approach creates emotional authenticity that the audience can feel rather than simply observe. Links to a named moment in the scene.

Secure: Names at least one given circumstance and translates it into at least one vocal and one physical choice for a named moment. Generally concrete. Effect on audience explained.

Developing: Refers to Proctor's feelings but does not apply Stanislavski's specific techniques. Choices are present but generic. Not anchored to a named moment.

Emerging: States 'I would play Proctor as guilty' without any vocal or physical translation. No reference to given circumstances or emotion memory. No named moment.

practice_questions.text: You are staging a production of The Crucible using a hybrid approach — Stanislavskian intimacy for the domestic scenes and Brechtian staging for the courtroom. Discuss how you would stage both the linen scene in Act 2 and the courtroom confrontation in Act 3, explaining which practitioner approach you are applying in each scene, the specific staging and performance choices you would make, and why this hybrid serves Miller's dual purpose of emotional tragedy and political argument.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Clearly articulates the hybrid rationale (Stanislavski for domestic intimacy because the audience must feel the emotional cost; Brecht for the courtroom because the audience must think about the political machinery). Linen scene choices are Stanislavskian: named given circumstances carried into the scene, specific vocal and physical choices for both Proctor and Elizabeth, staging that creates intimate proximity (centre stage, table as barrier, warm amber lighting from a low angle Fresnel, restrained underscore or silence). Courtroom choices are Brechtian: Danforth with gestus (gavel, pointed finger, raised upstage platform), the girls' chorus as a deliberate ensemble rather than individual psychology, cold white top light, the audience in thrust configuration so they feel the court's jurisdiction, sightlines managed so Proctor is always visually isolated. Miller's dual purpose is explicitly argued. A coherent directorial vision sustains both scenes.

Secure: Both scenes covered with generally concrete choices. Practitioner labels applied with some accuracy. At least one design and one performer choice per scene. Miller's dual purpose referenced.

Developing: One scene stronger than the other. Practitioner references present but not consistently translated into staging choices. Miller's intentions mentioned but not argued.

Emerging: Describes both scenes. Little practitioner application. No named staging or performance choices that could be attributed to either practitioner approach.

practice_questions.text: As a designer, explain how you would use staging configuration and lighting to make the Brechtian political argument visible in the courtroom scene of The Crucible. Refer to specific design choices and their effect on the audience.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Selects and justifies a staging configuration (e.g. thrust, so the audience feel themselves surrounded by the courtroom — positioned as jurors rather than spectators). Describes at least two named lighting choices with specific elements (e.g. cold white profile lanterns steeply angled to create downward shadows across all faces; a tight special on Danforth from above using a profile spot without gel, emphasising his institutional authority; a gobo projecting a grid or lattice pattern onto the stage floor suggesting a cage or a scaffold). Explains how each design choice communicates the Brechtian intention (the audience cannot get lost in individual sympathy — the staging keeps reminding them of the political structure). Links to the allegory explicitly.

Secure: Names at least two design choices in at least two disciplines (configuration + lighting) with generally concrete elements. Effect on audience explained in terms of the Brechtian approach. Generally specific.

Developing: Refers to 'Brechtian staging' and 'harsh lighting' without naming specific elements. Configuration mentioned but not justified. Effect on audience implied.

Emerging: States that the courtroom should look serious or imposing. No named design elements. No connection to Brecht or to Miller's intentions.

practice_questions.text: Name one physical theatre company whose ensemble methods are directly relevant to staging Around the World in 80 Days.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for: Frantic Assembly (accept Complicite).

practice_questions.text: Define the term 'Verfremdungseffekt' as it applies to theatrical performance.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying that Verfremdungseffekt (alienation effect) is a technique associated with Brecht; 1 mark for explaining that it involves reminding the audience they are watching a theatrical construction, preventing passive emotional identification and encouraging critical thinking.

practice_questions.text: Analyse how Complicite's principle of object transformation could be applied to the scene in which chairs become a railway carriage. What must the performers do for the transformation to be successful?
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks: identifying Complicite's principle that object transformation is achieved through the performer's physical relationship to the object, not through the object's appearance (1); describing specific physical choices the performer must make (the sway of a moving carriage, holding an imaginary armrest, gaze from an invisible window) (1); explaining what happens if the commitment breaks (the fiction collapses, the audience loses the transformation) (1); explaining the effect on the audience when it succeeds (collective reading of the chairs as carriage through the performers' physical logic) (1).

practice_questions.text: As a performer working in a Frantic Assembly-influenced rehearsal for the train attack sequence, explain the vocal and physical choices you would make to play an ensemble member caught in the chaos. Refer to Frantic Assembly's working methods and to specific performer choices for this moment.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Both vocal AND physical choices specific and named, anchored to the train attack sequence. Physical: reference to Frantic Assembly's contact choreography principles (bodies reacting to each other's physical initiatives); specific physical choices for the chaos (disorganised centre of gravity, low levels — crouching or falling — contrasting with the earlier organised train rows); how the body communicates fear or urgency without overacting (specific postural choice, e.g. pulling arms in, chin down, rapid weight transfer). Vocal: how voice changes under duress (increased pace, shorter phrases, possibly fragmented syntax); reference to the silence of mime sections. Both choices justified with named effect on the audience. The Frantic Assembly context is applied to a specific moment, not just described in general.

Secure: At least one vocal and one physical choice named, both anchored to the train attack. Frantic Assembly is referenced meaningfully. Some audience effect stated.

Developing: Describes the chaos of the scene physically but without specific choices or Frantic Assembly methodology. Effects implied.

Emerging: Describes what happens in the scene without any performer choices or practitioner reference.

practice_questions.text: As a lighting and sound designer working from Complicite's aesthetic principles, explain how you would design the Atlantic crossing scene. Refer to how your design choices support the company's physical storytelling rather than competing with it.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Specific lighting choices that serve the physical storytelling (not competing with it): a minimal, clean wash (Complicite’s aesthetic is rarely overlit); named lantern choices; a specific gobo or effect for the ocean surface; transitions that respond to the physical action rather than leading it. Sound: a specific soundscape that enhances the physical vocabulary (creaking timbers, water sound built from below); how the non-diegetic underscore supports the physical rhythm of the ensemble rather than overriding it; named instruments or textures. Every choice is justified as serving the physical storytelling. Named effect on the audience.

Secure: At least two named design elements (one lighting, one sound) with effects, and at least one is connected to supporting rather than competing with the physical work.

Developing: Design choices are present but the connection to Complicite's principles is not made. Generic descriptions.

Emerging: Basic listing of design ideas with no practitioner context.

practice_questions.text: As a director drawing on the traditions of Frantic Assembly, Complicite and the music-hall form, explain how you would stage the opening Reform Club scene and the moment the wager is made. Cover your approach to performer direction, staging configuration, lighting, sound and the performer-audience relationship.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Full directorial vision drawing coherently on the three practitioner traditions. Frantic Assembly: the physical precision of the Reform Club ensemble — how the company moves as a social unit (shared weight, status physicality, a Frantic Assembly-devised movement score for the club's rituals). Complicite: the narrator stepping forward to address the audience; objects already becoming symbols (the chairs as club furniture, the pocket watch as the play's central image). Music hall: the awareness of the audience's presence even in this early scene; perhaps a direct address to the front row at the moment the wager is proposed, recruiting the audience as judge. Staging configuration: the choice of formation for the Reform Club (upstage semicircle with Fogg downstage, OR a cluster with Fogg central); the lighting state (precise, formal, slightly cold for London precision); sound (a clock ticking, perhaps a distant locomotive whistle as the wager is made, foreshadowing). The performer-audience relationship is explicitly addressed. Every choice has a named effect. A directorial statement about the overall intended experience.

Secure: Most disciplines covered, with at least two of the three practitioner traditions meaningfully applied. Concrete choices. Some audience effect.

Developing: Some disciplines covered; practitioner references are general rather than specific to the moment. Effects implied.

Emerging: Basic description of the scene with little practitioner application or design specifics.

before.exam_tip_html: When applying a practitioner to a set play, the most common error is to describe the practitioner’s biography or general philosophy without showing how a specific technique applies to a specific moment of the play. The examiner wants you to say: “Using Frantic Assembly’s contact choreography approach, the director would develop the elephant sequence through physical improvisation in rehearsal, allowing the ensemble to find a shared weight and rhythm that makes the creature credible — the physical logic of the movement, not a visual representation, persuades the audience.” That is a practitioner applied to a moment. Compare: “Frantic Assembly like physical theatre” — that is biography, not application. For the 8-mark practice questions in this lesson, make sure your performer or designer response also demonstrates how the practitioner’s principles shape the specific choices you make.
